slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: What an intangible asset is
slides.html:
An intangible asset has no physical form but is expected to bring future benefits; for a lawyer, its core is the set of legal rights Indian law recognises.

Intangible assets are resources that have no physical form but are expected to bring future benefits to a business. Lawyers and managers draw the boundary in different places, and the difference decides what can later be valued, traded or used as security.

For a law student, the core of intangible assets is the set of legal rights recognised by Indian law:

  1. Patents under the Patents Act, 1970
  2. Copyright under the Copyright Act, 1957
  3. Trade marks under the Trade Marks Act, 1999
  4. Designs under the Designs Act, 2000
  5. Geographical indications under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
  6. Confidential information, protected through contract and equity

Management takes a wider view. It also counts know-how, software, data, brand reputation, customer relationships and the skills of employees, even when no registered right exists.

Keep both views in mind. The legal view tells you what the firm can enforce; the management view tells you what actually earns money. Part of IP management is securing items on the wider list as rights or contracts the firm controls, a point that returns with Ind AS 38 on the next slide.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: The accounting definition in Ind AS 38
slides.html:
Ind AS 38 counts an intangible only if it is identifiable, controlled and expected to give future economic benefits, so IP law shapes what accounts can show.

Ind AS 38. An intangible asset is an identifiable non monetary asset without physical substance.

Identifiable

It can be separated from the business, or it arises from contractual or legal rights.

Controlled

The business must control it, which in practice usually means owning a legal right or a contractual right.

Future benefits

The business must expect future economic benefits from it.

Why does a lawyer care about an accounting definition? Because two of its three tests are met through law. Identifiability can come from a contractual or legal right, and control usually means owning one.

The chain of reasoning is short: a right that is not legally secured is often not controlled, and what is not controlled cannot be an asset. The law of IP therefore decides much of what accounting can recognise.

Remember: ICF: Identifiable, Controlled, Future benefits. No secure right, no control; no control, no asset.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: How intangibles behave differently
slides.html:
Intangibles behave unlike land or machinery: they can be shared without being used up and copied cheaply, so their value rests on legal exclusivity or secrecy.

  1. Shared use: knowledge can be used by many people at the same time without being used up.
  2. Copying: once created, it can be copied at very low cost.
  3. Imitation: others can easily imitate it, so its value depends on legal exclusivity created by IP law or on secrecy.
  4. Returns: its future returns are uncertain.
  5. Markets: it is rarely bought and sold in open markets.
  6. Dependence: its value depends on complementary assets such as manufacturing, distribution and brand.
  7. Obsolescence: it can become obsolete quickly.
  8. People: much of it sits in the minds of employees, who are not owned by the firm and may leave.

Granstrand adds a portfolio point. The value of an IP portfolio is not simply the total of the values of its separate rights, because rights support and overlap each other.

Each feature returns later in this Part. Uncertain returns and the lack of an open market are why measuring is difficult. Dependence on complementary assets is the heart of Teece’s framework in 1.4. The portfolio point is developed in 1.6.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: The four levels of measuring
slides.html:
Measuring intangibles happens at four levels: identify what the firm has, classify it, quantify it with indicators, and only then value it in money.

  1. Identification: listing what the firm has, usually through an IP register.
  2. Classification: grouping assets by type, technology, business or legal status.
  3. Quantification: using non money indicators such as the number of patents, citations, staff turnover or customer retention.
  4. Valuation: putting a money value on an asset for a stated purpose and date.

Why this order? Each level uses the one before it. An asset that has not been identified cannot be classified, and a money value is only as sound as the list and the indicators beneath it.

Notice that valuation is tied to a purpose and a date. A value is an answer to a particular question asked at a particular time, not a permanent fact about the asset.

Remember: “I Can Quote Value”: Identification, Classification, Quantification, Valuation.

Exam focus. Do not use “measurement” and “valuation” as synonyms. Valuation is only the fourth level of measuring.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: Why measurement matters
slides.html:
Measurement matters legally and commercially: managers, parties to deals, courts, lenders, tax authorities, accountants and investors all need it, and it exposes hidden risks.

Who needs itWhat for
ManagementTo identify sources of competitive advantage; to divide budgets between R&D, marketing and IP; to decide which rights to renew, license, sell or abandon
Parties to legal transactionsLicences, assignments, mergers, joint ventures and technology transfer agreements need a price
CourtsA basis for damages in infringement suits
LendersBefore accepting IP as security
Tax authoritiesFor royalties and transfer pricing
AccountantsFor acquisitions and impairment tests
InvestorsTo judge knowledge companies; better information can lower the cost of capital

Measurement also reveals risks, such as dependence on one patent, one licence or a few key inventors. A firm that has never listed its rights cannot see that its whole business rests on one of them.

Remember: What is not measured is usually not managed.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: Why measuring is difficult
slides.html:
Intangibles are hard to measure because knowledge is tacit, comparables are rare, benefits lie in an uncertain future, and the legal right itself may fail.

The practical difficulties come first:

  1. Much knowledge is tacit and undocumented.
  2. Comparable market transactions are rare.
  3. The benefits lie in an uncertain future.
  4. The contribution of one asset is difficult to separate from others.
  5. Results depend on assumptions about royalty rates, discount rates and useful life.

Then there is legal uncertainty, the lawyer’s contribution to the problem:

Patent

May be revoked.

Trade mark

May become generic.

Trade secret

May leak.

Every money value quietly assumes that the right behind it will survive. If validity, distinctiveness or secrecy fails, the value built on it fails too, which is why the legal position must be checked before any figure is trusted.

Exam focus. Question 1 asks for the “legal and practical difficulties”. Give the practical ones, then legal uncertainty with its three examples.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: What Ind AS 38 lets the accounts show
slides.html:
Accounting recognises few intangibles: research is always expensed, development qualifies only on six conditions, and internally generated brands and goodwill are never recognised.

Accounting aims at reliable financial statements and follows Ind AS 38 or AS 26. Its rules are deliberately strict:

ItemRule under Ind AS 38
Research costAlways an expense (para 54)
Development costAn asset only when six conditions are met (para 57)
Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer listsNever recognised (para 63)
Internally generated goodwillNever recognised (para 48)
Bought intangiblesRecorded at cost and amortised over their useful life if that life is finite

The six conditions in para 57 for development cost:

  1. technical feasibility
  2. intention to complete
  3. ability to use or sell
  4. probable future benefits
  5. adequate resources
  6. reliable measurement of cost

Companies outside Ind AS follow AS 26, which takes a similar approach.

Remember: “Tired Interns Always Prefer Adequate Rest”: Technical feasibility, Intention to complete, Ability to use or sell, Probable future benefits, Adequate resources, Reliable measurement of cost.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: Accounting recognition versus management measurement
slides.html:
Accounting recognition and management measurement are different exercises: one seeks audited reliability under Ind AS 38, the other seeks better decisions and covers every intangible.

AspectAccounting recognitionManagement measurement
AimReliable financial statementsBetter decisions
RulesInd AS 38 or AS 26Voluntary
CoverageFew intangibles, under strict testsAll intangibles, including human capital
Standard of proofAudited reliabilityUsefulness for decisions, not audited reliability

Why keep two systems? Financial statements are relied on by investors and checked by auditors, so they accept only what can be measured with confidence. Managers need the whole picture to decide, so they accept estimates and indicators.

The price of strict accounting is that the balance sheet shows few internally created IP rights. The next slide shows how that gap appears in the market.

Exam focus. Never say that an asset missing from the balance sheet has no value. It may simply fail the accounting tests while being central to management.

slides.part: 1.1 Meaning and Importance of Measuring Intangible Assets
slides.title: The market to book ratio
slides.html:
Because the balance sheet omits most internally created IP, a knowledge firm’s market value is often far above its book value; the market to book ratio measures the gap.

Because of the recognition rules, the balance sheet shows few internally created IP rights, so the market value of a knowledge firm is often far above its book value.

Market to book ratio = Market value of equity ÷ Book value of net assets

Market value is what investors pay for the firm’s shares; book value is what its accounts record as net assets. The further the ratio is above 1, the more of the firm’s value the accounts do not record.

Worked example

  1. Market value of equity = ₹10,000 crore.
  2. Book value of net assets = ₹2,000 crore.
  3. Ratio = 10,000 ÷ 2,000 = 5.

The gap partly reflects unrecorded intangibles, but it also reflects growth expectations and market mood.

Exam focus. The ratio cannot be treated as an exact value of the firm’s IP. Say this whenever you use the market to book gap.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: What public policy covers and why the State cares
slides.html:
Public policy here means the State’s rules on how intangibles are recognised, valued, disclosed, audited, taxed, financed and counted, because intangibles now drive business value.

Public policy on this subject consists of the rules made by government, regulators and standard setters on how intangible assets are recognised, valued, disclosed, audited, taxed, financed and counted in national statistics.

Why should the State care how a company counts its patents? The notes give six reasons:

  1. Intangibles now form a large share of business value.
  2. Investors need reliable information.
  3. Firms rich in IP but poor in physical assets struggle to borrow.
  4. R&D benefits society beyond the firm.
  5. IP can be shifted easily to low tax countries.
  6. IP and data can create market power.

Each concern points to a branch of law covered next: accounting and audit protect investors, finance law addresses borrowing, tax law addresses profit shifting and incentives for R&D, and competition law addresses market power.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: The central choice: relevance or reliability
slides.html:
The central policy choice is between relevance and reliability; most standard setters keep recognition strict and ask instead for better disclosure.

The central policy choice is between relevance and reliability. Each side has a real case:

Relevance: recognise more

Accounts become more realistic, investors are helped, and the cost of capital for knowledge firms falls.

Reliability: keep it strict

Values of intangibles are often estimates that are hard to audit, can be manipulated to inflate balance sheets, and may rise and fall sharply.

Most standard setters therefore keep recognition strict and encourage better disclosure of non money indicators and narrative explanation. In short, they tell investors more rather than book more.

This choice explains the rest of the section. India’s framework applies the reliability side, the implications are the price of that choice, and the international trend repeats it.

Remember: Strict on recognition, generous on disclosure.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: India’s framework: accounting, valuation and audit
slides.html:
India follows a conservative recognition rule under Ind AS 38 and AS 26, requires registered valuers for company law valuations, and makes auditors report on intangible records.

AreaRuleSource
RecognitionA conservative recognition ruleInd AS 38, notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015; AS 26 for other entities
Who valuesValuations required under company law must be done by registered valuerss. 247, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017
How to valueA valuation standard for intangiblesICAI Valuation Standards 2018, including VS 302 on intangible assets
AuditThe auditor reports whether the company keeps proper records of its intangible assets, and reports on any revaluationCompanies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020 (CARO 2020)

Read the four rows together. The accounts show little, but whenever company law needs a value it must come from a regulated professional, the valuation standard guides the method, and the auditor checks the records. Reliability is protected at every step.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: India’s framework: tax, finance and policy
slides.html:
Outside the accounts, Indian law treats IP as valuable property: acquired intangibles are depreciable, Indian patent royalty is taxed concessionally, IP can secure loans, and policy promotes commercialisation.

AreaRuleSource
Tax: depreciationDepreciation on acquired intangibles such as know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences and franchises, but not goodwillIncome Tax Act, 2025, s. 33(1)(b)
Tax: patent royaltyRoyalty from patents developed and registered in India taxed at a concessional 10 per cents. 194(1)
Finance: securityIntangible assets are included in the definition of property; security interests over them are registered with CERSAISARFAESI Act, 2002
PolicyLists commercialisation of IPR as an objective, including valuation and IP based financingNational IPR Policy, 2016
Start-up supportSupports start-ups with IP filingsThe SIPP scheme

Notice the contrast with the previous slide. Accounting books little internally created IP, yet tax law depreciates acquired IP, finance law lets IP secure loans, and policy wants IP commercialised. The State encourages IP through these routes rather than through the balance sheet.

The Quick Revision calls the concessional 10 per cent rate on Indian patent royalty the 10 per cent patent box.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: Implications of the strict rules
slides.html:
Strict recognition has knock-on effects: investors may misprice firms, lenders see little security, start-ups depend on equity, and the State must use incentives.

WhoImplication
InvestorsMust estimate intangible value themselves and may misprice firms
LendersFind little security on the balance sheet, so IP backed lending remains small
Start-upsReport losses because R&D is expensed, and therefore depend on equity
GovernmentMust use tax incentives and grants to encourage R&D
Tax authorities and taxpayersDispute royalty values in transfer pricing
BoardsManage valuable assets that do not appear in the accounts
National statisticsMay understate investment in knowledge

Trace each effect back to its cause in 1.1. Research is expensed (para 54), internally generated goodwill is never recognised (para 48), and neither are internally generated brands and customer lists (para 63). The value is real but invisible, and every implication in the table is a cost of choosing reliability over relevance.

slides.part: 1.2 Public Policy on Measuring Intangible Assets and Its Implications
slides.title: The international position
slides.html:
Internationally, the trend is towards better disclosure rather than wider recognition; IAS 38 is under review but unchanged.

Law update. The International Accounting Standards Board is reviewing IAS 38 as a research project, but no change had been made by 7 November 2026. Any change would reach India only through Ind AS.

Integrated reporting encourages firms to report on six capitals:

  1. financial
  2. manufactured
  3. intellectual
  4. human
  5. social and relationship
  6. natural

WIPO runs a programme on IP finance and publishes country reports.

The overall trend is towards better disclosure rather than wider recognition. That is the same answer standard setters gave to the relevance and reliability choice, so the whole section points one way: report more about intangibles, but book few of them.

Remember: The six capitals: “Five Men In Hats Sell Nuts”: Financial, Manufactured, Intellectual, Human, Social and relationship, Natural.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: What intellectual capital is
slides.html:
Intellectual capital is the knowledge, skills, systems and relationships a firm can turn into value, and it has three components: human, structural and relational capital.

Intellectual capital (IC) is the knowledge, skills, systems and relationships of a firm that can be converted into value.

Granstrand divides a firm’s capital into physical, financial and intellectual capital, and treats IC as including IP rights, human competence and goodwill.

Human capital

The knowledge and skill of employees. The firm does not own it, and it leaves when people leave.

Structural capital

What remains in the firm: processes, databases, systems, culture and IP rights.

Relational capital

The value of relationships with customers, suppliers and partners, including brand and reputation.

The split has a practical lesson. Knowledge held only in employees’ heads can walk out of the door, while knowledge captured in documents, systems and IP rights stays with the firm. Written assignments and confidentiality agreements, met again in 1.5, help keep it.

Remember: HSR: Human (in people’s heads), Structural (stays in the firm), Relational (with outsiders).

Intellectual capital is the knowledge, skills, systems and relationships a firm can turn into value, and it has three components: human, structural and relational capital. slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: The Skandia value scheme
slides.html:
The Skandia scheme splits a firm’s market value step by step, showing exactly where intellectual capital and its parts sit.

Market value = Financial capital + Intellectual capital

Intellectual capital = Human capital + Structural capital

Structural capital = Customer capital + Organisational capital

Organisational capital = Innovation capital + Process capital

Read it from the top. Each line takes one item from the line above and splits it into two.

How does this fit the three components on the previous slide? Skandia puts customer capital inside structural capital, while the three-component view treats relationships as a separate relational capital. The labels differ, but both cover the same ground: people, what stays in the firm, and relationships with customers.

Exam focus. Draw the scheme as a tree. Four lines show where human, customer, innovation and process capital sit within market value.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: IC accounting and its legal use
slides.html:
IC accounting identifies, measures and reports intellectual capital, mainly for internal management; it is voluntary and outside the statutory accounts, but published claims carry prospectus liability.

IC accounting is the identification, measurement and reporting of intellectual capital, mainly for internal management. It is voluntary and is not part of the statutory financial statements.

Why does it matter to a lawyer? It connects IP rights with the people, systems and relationships that make them valuable. That connection supports three legal tasks:

  1. IP audits
  2. due diligence
  3. valuation

ss. 34 and 35, Companies Act, 2013. These sections impose liability for misstatements in a prospectus. Where a company chooses to publish IC information in a prospectus, the information must not be untrue or misleading.

Voluntary does not mean unregulated. A company is free to decide whether to report IC, but once that information goes into a prospectus, the ordinary liability for misstatements applies.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: The five IC frameworks
slides.html:
Five frameworks measure intellectual capital: the Balanced Scorecard, Skandia Navigator, Intangible Assets Monitor, Technology Broker and IC Index. Learn each one’s author and structure.

FrameworkAuthorStructure
Balanced ScorecardKaplan and NortonFour perspectives (financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth), linked through cause and effect
Skandia NavigatorEdvinsson and MaloneFive focus areas (financial, customer, process, renewal and development, and human), with human capital at the centre
Intangible Assets MonitorSveibyExternal structure, internal structure and competence of people, each measured through indicators of growth, efficiency and stability
Technology BrokerBrookingIC divided into market assets, human centred assets, IP assets and infrastructure assets
IC IndexRoosCombines indicators into one index and tracks changes over time

To tell them apart, count the boxes. The Scorecard has four perspectives, the Navigator five focus areas, the Monitor three areas each read through three kinds of indicator, the Broker four types of asset, and the IC Index a single number.

Remember: 4, 5, 3, 4, 1: Scorecard, Navigator, Monitor, Broker, Index.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: Sveiby’s four families of methods
slides.html:
Sveiby groups the methods of measuring intellectual capital into four families: direct, market capitalisation, return on assets and scorecard methods.

Direct methods

Value each part of IC.

Market capitalisation methods

Use measures such as market value minus book value.

Return on assets methods

Capitalise excess profit.

Scorecard methods

Use non money indicators.

The families sort the tools of this Part by how they work, not by who invented them. Applying the definitions: the Balanced Scorecard, Skandia Navigator and Intangible Assets Monitor work through indicators, which is the scorecard approach. The market to book ratio from 1.1 compares market value with book value, which is the market capitalisation approach.

Two of the formulas that follow fit the map: Tobin’s q starts from the market’s price, like the market capitalisation family, and Calculated Intangible Value capitalises excess profit, like the return on assets family. VAIC starts from value added and does not map cleanly onto any of the four.

Remember: “Don’t Make Rash Scores”: Direct, Market capitalisation, Return on assets, Scorecard.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: Tobin’s q
slides.html:
Tobin’s q compares the market value of a firm with the cost of replacing its assets; a q above 1 suggests intangibles that replacement cost misses.

Tobin’s q = Market value of the firm ÷ Replacement cost of its assets

A q above 1 suggests that the market sees valuable intangibles that replacement cost does not capture.

Compare the market to book ratio from 1.1. Both put the market’s view of the firm on top; only the bottom line differs. The market to book ratio divides by the book value of net assets, while Tobin’s q divides by the replacement cost of the firm’s assets.

Because both rest on market value, the warning given for the market to book ratio applies here too: market value also moves with growth expectations and market mood, so q only suggests intangibles and does not price them.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: VAIC
slides.html:
VAIC adds three efficiency ratios, for human capital, structural capital and capital employed, to show how much value a firm adds from its resources.

VAIC = HCE + SCE + CEE

HCE = VA ÷ HC; SCE = (VA − HC) ÷ VA; CEE = VA ÷ CE

Here VA is value added, HC is employee cost and CE is capital employed. HCE is value added per unit of employee cost; SCE is the share of value added left after employee cost; CEE is value added per unit of capital employed. The higher the total, the more value the firm adds from its people and capital.

Worked example

VA is 200, HC is 80 and CE is 400.

  1. HCE = 200 ÷ 80 = 2.5
  2. SCE = (200 − 80) ÷ 200 = 120 ÷ 200 = 0.6
  3. CEE = 200 ÷ 400 = 0.5
  4. VAIC = 2.5 + 0.6 + 0.5 = 3.6

Exam focus. The usual slip is SCE. Subtract employee cost from value added first, then divide by value added, not by employee cost.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: Calculated Intangible Value
slides.html:
Calculated Intangible Value treats profit above the industry’s normal return on tangible assets as earned by intangibles, and capitalises that excess into a value.

Under the Calculated Intangible Value method, the logic runs in three moves: work out what the firm’s tangible assets would normally earn, treat anything above that as earned by intangibles, and capitalise the after-tax excess.

Excess profit = Average pre tax profit − (Industry return × Tangible assets)

CIV = Excess profit × (1 − Tax rate) ÷ Cost of capital

Dividing by the cost of capital turns a yearly excess profit into a single capital value.

Worked example

  1. The firm earns average pre tax profit of 90 on tangible assets of 500; the industry earns 12 per cent.
  2. Normal profit = 12 per cent of 500 = 60.
  3. Excess profit = 90 − 60 = 30.
  4. After 25 per cent tax: 30 × 0.75 = 22.5.
  5. Divide by a 15 per cent cost of capital: 22.5 ÷ 0.15 = CIV of 150.

This is what Sveiby’s return on assets family means by capitalising excess profit.

slides.part: 1.3 Intellectual Capital Accounting as a Management Tool
slides.title: Uses and limits of IC accounting
slides.html:
IC accounting helps strategy, resource allocation and investor communication, but it has no common standard, can be manipulated and assumes cause and effect.

Uses

Helps managers form strategy, allocate resources, measure performance beyond profit, manage knowledge and risks, and communicate with investors.

Limits

There is no common standard; indicators can be manipulated; cause and effect is assumed rather than proved; money values depend heavily on assumptions.

The limits explain where IC accounting sits. They are the same worries about estimates, manipulation and audit that keep Ind AS 38 strict in 1.2. That is why IC accounting stays a voluntary management tool outside the statutory financial statements.

The uses explain why firms bother anyway. A board that manages assets missing from the accounts needs some other way to see them.

Exam focus. In Question 3, end with the limits. They show that you understand why IC accounting is a management tool and not an accounting standard.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Creating value versus extracting it
slides.html:
Creating knowledge is not the same as earning from it: value extraction converts knowledge into money or market power, and many inventive firms fail at it.

Value creation
The production of new knowledge and inventions.
Value extraction
The conversion of that knowledge into money or market power.

Many firms create valuable knowledge but earn little from it. The notes give three reasons. They lack:

  1. a clear IP policy;
  2. legal protection;
  3. complementary assets.

The rest of this section takes up each gap. Teece explains why legal protection and complementary assets decide who profits. The methods of extraction show the routes available and their legal structure. Granstrand’s model IP policy shows what a clear policy looks like, and the legal limits show where extraction must stop.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Teece: who profits from innovation
slides.html:
Teece explains that the innovator profits only if three conditions favour it: the appropriability regime, the dominant design and complementary assets.

Appropriability regime

Strong legal protection, such as valid patents or well kept secrets, allows the innovator to profit, while weak protection helps imitators.

Dominant design

Once a standard design emerges, competition moves to price and scale.

Complementary assets

Manufacturing, distribution, service and brand. If imitators own these and protection is weak, they may capture most of the profit.

Read the three together. Legal protection decides whether the innovator can stop copying. The dominant design decides when the contest shifts to price and scale. Complementary assets decide who wins that contest.

So an innovator with weak protection and no complementary assets is exposed: imitators who own the factories, distribution and brand may take most of the profit. This is the commercial reason why IP law and complementary assets matter together.

Remember: ADC: Appropriability, Dominant design, Complementary assets.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: The IP value hierarchy
slides.html:
Harrison and Sullivan’s IP value hierarchy shows firms progressing through five stages, from using IP defensively to a visionary stage where IP shapes the firm and its industry.

Harrison and Sullivan describe an IP value hierarchy in which firms progress:

  1. Defensive: using IP defensively.
  2. Cost control: controlling IP costs.
  3. Profit centre: treating IP as a profit centre.
  4. Integrated: integrating IP with business strategy.
  5. Visionary: IP shapes the future of the firm and the industry.

One way to read the ladder is that each stage asks more of IP than the one below. First IP only protects, then its costs are managed, then it must earn, then it serves the whole strategy, and finally it shapes where the firm and the industry go.

Use it to diagnose a firm in a problem question: ask which stage it is at and what the next stage would require. Compare Granstrand’s four stages of corporate IP management in 1.7, which also move IP from a legal matter to a strategic one.

Remember: “Don’t Count Pennies, Imagine Victory”: Defensive, Cost control, Profit centre, Integrated, Visionary.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Own use and transfer of rights
slides.html:
The basic ways to earn from IP are to use it yourself or to transfer rights by licence, assignment, franchise or technology transfer, each with its own formalities.

The simplest method is own use: IP keeps competitors out, and protected features, designs and marks support higher prices. The other basic methods transfer rights, and for revision they can be grouped as the transactional methods:

MethodWhat it doesLegal formality
LicensingOthers use the IP for a royalty; the licensor keeps ownershipPatent licence: in writing and registered to be relied upon (Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69). Copyright licence: in writing (Copyright Act, s. 30)
AssignmentTransfers ownership for a pricePatents: writing and registration. Copyright: writing (s. 19). Trade marks: registration (Trade Marks Act, s. 45)
FranchisingLicenses a business system with marks and know-howThe franchisor must control quality to protect the mark
Technology transferCombines patent licences with know-how and technical assistanceIts patent licences follow the licence rules above

Exam focus. Licence and assignment are the classic pair. A licensee gets permission to use and the licensor keeps ownership; an assignee becomes the owner.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Collaborative and financial methods
slides.html:
Value can also be extracted with partners, through joint ventures, alliances, research collaborations and open innovation, or with financiers, by borrowing against IP or selling royalty streams.

FamilyMethodHow it works
CollaborativeJoint venturesPartners contribute IP to a new company
Strategic alliancesCooperation based on contracts
Research collaborationsWith universities and firms
Open innovationFirms buy in outside ideas and sell out unused ones
FinancialLoansUsing IP as security for loans
Royalty saleSelling future royalties
SecuritisationSecuritising royalty streams

Why choose these routes? Collaboration brings in what a firm lacks: the notes advise licensing or partnership for a firm lacking capital or market access. Financial methods turn IP, or the royalties it earns, into money.

The financial routes rest on the framework in 1.2: the SARFAESI Act, 2002 treats intangible assets as property, and security interests over them are registered with CERSAI.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Enforcement, defensive and other routes
slides.html:
IP also yields value through enforcement, defensive publication, standards, pools and copyright societies, and through new business models, spin-offs, disposals and cross-licence bargaining.

  1. Enforcement: infringement suits can produce damages or licences.
  2. Defensive publication: keeps a field free by making an invention public so that nobody can patent it.
  3. Technical standards: patents included in standards earn royalties from all implementers.
  4. Patent pools: let several owners license related patents together.
  5. Copyright societies: license works collectively.
  6. Firms may also build data and software based business models,
  7. create spin off companies,
  8. sell or donate non core patents to save renewal fees,
  9. and use patents as bargaining chips to obtain cross licences and freedom to operate.

Notice that some routes bring in no income directly. Defensive publication and bargaining chips secure freedom to work in a field, and giving up non-core patents saves cost. Extracting value includes avoiding loss and keeping the road open, not only earning royalties.

Remember: The notes’ revision list: own use, licensing, assignment, collaboration, finance, enforcement, standards and collective licensing. “Only Lawyers Always Collect Fees, Even Settling Contracts.”

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Choosing the route
slides.html:
The right route depends on the firm’s complementary assets, the strength of its protection and whether the asset is core, always within tax, competition and exchange rules.

If the firm…It usually does best by…
Owns manufacturing and distributionUsing its IP itself: it usually earns most by own use
Lacks capital or market accessLicensing or partnership
Has strong legal protectionLicensing, which strong protection makes safer
Has weak legal protectionSpeed, secrecy and own use
Holds a core assetKeeping it
Holds a non-core assetLicensing or selling it

The choice must also account for tax, competition law and foreign exchange rules for cross-border payments.

This is Teece applied. Owning the complementary assets favours own use; a strong appropriability regime makes licensing safer; and weak protection pushes a firm towards speed and secrecy.

Exam focus. In a problem question, run the tests in order: core or non-core, own complementary assets or not, strong or weak protection, then tax, competition and foreign exchange.

slides.title: Granstrand’s model IP policy
slides.html:
Granstrand distinguishes a policy, a long lasting general guideline, from a strategy, a specific plan of action, and sets out a model IP policy.

Policy
A long lasting general guideline.
Strategy
A specific plan of action.

His model IP policy:

  1. makes business managers responsible for building and using IP;
  2. uses several types of protection for each business;
  3. seeks a strong patent position in core businesses;
  4. requires checking others’ patents before entering a new field;
  5. encourages early filing, or “speed to patent”;
  6. adopts open licensing for a proper royalty, with active cross licensing;
  7. requires respect for others’ IP.

Why business managers rather than lawyers? Extraction is a business decision, so the policy places IP with the people who decide how products reach the market. The same shift appears in the IA manager’s role in 1.7.

slides.part: 1.4 Extracting Profits from Intellectual Capital: Policy and Practice
slides.title: Legal limits on extracting value
slides.html:
The law limits extraction: competition law protects only reasonable conditions, s. 140 voids restrictive licence terms, and an unworked patent risks a compulsory licence.

s. 3(5)(i), Competition Act, 2002. Protects only reasonable conditions needed to protect IP rights.

s. 140, Patents Act. Makes certain restrictive conditions in patent licences void, such as:

  1. tying the licensee to buy unpatented goods from the licensor;
  2. exclusive grant backs;
  3. preventing challenges to validity;
  4. coercive package licensing.

s. 84, Patents Act. A patent that is not worked in India may attract a compulsory licence after three years from grant.

That is why the statement of working in Form 27 is important. Cross-border royalty payments must also comply with foreign exchange and tax rules.

The common thread is that an IP right gives exclusivity, not unlimited freedom to extract. Licence terms that go beyond protecting the right, and rights left unworked, invite the law to step in.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: Why intellectual capital matters in a start-up
slides.html:
In a start-up almost all value is intangible, so investors judge it mainly on its intellectual capital, yet that capital is hardest to measure there.

A start-up’s value lies in its founders, its technology, its business idea and its early customers. Investors therefore judge the company mainly on its intellectual capital.

Measuring it is difficult because:

  1. there is no past performance and often no revenue;
  2. uncertainty is high;
  3. the business depends on a few founders;
  4. patents are usually pending rather than granted;
  5. ownership of IP is often unclear.

Granstrand adds two warnings:

“Hubris”

Founders tend to overvalue their own ideas.

The one-patent belief

The mistaken belief among small firms that one good patent is enough.

Both warnings point the same way: measure a start-up with evidence rather than founder belief, beginning with who actually owns the IP.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: Ownership first: the legal foundation
slides.html:
The first question in measuring a start-up’s intellectual capital is ownership: the company must actually hold the inventions, works and know-how that investors are paying for.

AssetRuleWhat the start-up must do
Founders’ inventionsA patent application may be filed by the true and first inventor or by an assignee (Patents Act, s. 6)Founders assign their inventions to the company in writing, and the assignment should be registered (ss. 68 and 69)
Employees’ workCopyright in work made by an employee in the course of employment generally belongs to the employer (Copyright Act, s. 17)The company generally owns it
Consultants’ and freelancers’ workBelongs to them unless assigned in writing (s. 19)Take a written assignment

Three further checks complete the legal picture:

  1. Confidentiality agreements protect know-how.
  2. A trade mark search avoids conflicts.
  3. A freedom to operate check shows whether the product may infringe others’ patents.

Why ownership first? An investor valuing the IP is buying into the company, so any right that sits with a founder, consultant or freelancer is value the company does not hold.

Exam focus. The trap is the outside contributor: an employee’s work generally belongs to the employer, but a freelancer’s belongs to the freelancer unless assigned in writing.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: What to measure in a start-up
slides.html:
A start-up’s intellectual capital is measured across five areas: its team, structural capital, IP position, relational capital and market traction.

AreaWhat to look at
TeamFounders’ experience, completeness of the team, advisers
Structural capitalStage of the prototype, documented technology, data and processes
IP positionOwnership, filings, countries, claim scope, secrecy controls and freedom to operate
Relational capitalPilot customers, partners and letters of intent
Market tractionMarket size, users, revenue and growth

This is the general model of intellectual capital from 1.3 adapted to a young firm. The team plays the part of human capital, and structural and relational capital keep their names. Two areas are added: the IP position, which brings in the legal checks from the previous slide, and market traction.

The IP position row repeats the ownership point: ownership is listed first because the other items in that row only count if the company owns the rights.

Remember: “The Smart Investor Reads Metrics”: Team, Structural capital, IP position, Relational capital, Market traction.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: The scorecard and Berkus methods
slides.html:
The scorecard method adjusts the average value of similar funded start-ups by weighted factors; the Berkus method gives value for five risk-reducing elements.

The scorecard method starts with the average value of similar funded start ups and adjusts it by weighted factors:

FactorWeight
Team30 per cent
Size of opportunity25 per cent
Product and technology15 per cent
Competition10 per cent
Sales channels10 per cent
Need for further funding5 per cent
Others5 per cent

Value = Average value of similar funded start ups × Weighted score

A weighted score above 1 means the start-up scores better than the average on the weighted factors. The team carries the largest weight, which fits a business that depends on a few founders.

Worked example

Average value ₹20 crore; weighted score 1.155. Value = 20 × 1.155 = ₹23.1 crore.

The Berkus method gives value for five risk reducing elements: a sound idea, a prototype, a good team, strategic relationships and a product launch or sales.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: The venture capital and First Chicago methods
slides.html:
The venture capital method works backwards from the expected exit value at the investor’s target return; the First Chicago method weights best, normal and worst cases.

The venture capital method works backwards from the expected exit value:

Post money value = Expected exit value ÷ (1 + target return)years

Pre money value = Post money value − Investment

Post money value is the company’s value including the new investment; pre money value is its value before it. The investor’s share is the investment divided by the post money value.

Worked example

  1. Exit value ₹200 crore in five years; target return 50 per cent a year; investment ₹10 crore.
  2. (1 + 0.5)5 = 1.55 = 7.594.
  3. Post money value = 200 ÷ 7.594 = ₹26.34 crore.
  4. Pre money value = 26.34 − 10 = ₹16.34 crore.
  5. Investor’s share = 10 ÷ 26.34 = about 38 per cent.

The First Chicago method weights values in best, normal and worst cases by their probabilities. It answers the high uncertainty of a start-up by valuing several futures instead of one.

Exam focus. Pre money is post money minus the investment. Subtract the ₹10 crore; do not add it.

slides.part: 1.5 Intellectual Capital Measurement for Start Ups
slides.title: Indian support for start-up IP
slides.html:
Start-ups recognised by DPIIT get help with IP filings, including SIPP facilitators and fee support, lower patent fees and expedited examination.

  1. Start-ups recognised by DPIIT receive help with IP filings.
  2. The SIPP scheme provided facilitators and fee support and was extended up to 31 March 2026.
  3. Start-ups pay lower patent fees.
  4. They may request expedited examination of patent applications.

Why does the State help? The implications in 1.2 give the reason. Start-ups report losses because R&D is expensed, depend on equity, and offer lenders little security on the balance sheet. Cheaper and faster filings help them build the IP position that investors measure.

This support links back to the National IPR Policy, 2016, which lists commercialisation of IPR, including valuation and IP based financing, as an objective.

slides.part: 1.6 The IP Portfolio as a Competitive Tool
slides.title: What a portfolio is and what it does
slides.html:
An IP portfolio is the whole group of rights a firm owns or controls, managed together; because the rights support each other, the portfolio gives more power than single rights.

An IP portfolio is the whole group of IP rights that a firm owns or controls, managed together. Legally, it is a bundle of territorial rights with different terms, owners and conditions.

Because the rights support each other, a portfolio gives more power than single rights. It:

  1. keeps competitors out of markets;
  2. differentiates products;
  3. strengthens the firm’s position in licensing negotiations;
  4. protects freedom to operate, because others hesitate to sue a firm that can sue back;
  5. blocks rivals’ research directions;
  6. gives influence in technical standards;
  7. earns licensing income;
  8. provides access to others’ technology through cross licences;
  9. attracts investors and lenders;
  10. reveals competitors’ strategies.

This is Granstrand’s point from 1.1 at work: the value of a portfolio is not simply the total of its separate rights.

slides.part: 1.6 The IP Portfolio as a Competitive Tool
slides.title: Why firms patent
slides.html:
Granstrand’s survey found that large Japanese firms value patents for protection, bargaining and image, and least for internal reasons; large portfolios create retaliatory power.

Granstrand’s survey of large Japanese corporations found that firms value patents for:

  1. Protection: of products above all, of processes, and to threaten counter attack;
  2. Bargaining: licensing, cross licensing, R&D cooperation and standard setting;
  3. Image;
  4. and, least, internal reasons such as motivating inventors or measuring R&D.

Retaliatory power

Firms depend on each other’s patents, so a strong portfolio deters attack.

“Patent extortionists”

A party that holds one patent but has no manufacturing to be counter attacked can make demands on large firms.

The two tiles are linked. Retaliation works only against a firm that makes products and so can be sued back; a party with no manufacturing is out of its reach.

BlockingSecures
Offensive blockingMarket freedom
Defensive blockingDesign freedom

Remember: PBII: Protection, Bargaining, Image, Internal (least).

slides.part: 1.6 The IP Portfolio as a Competitive Tool
slides.title: Granstrand’s patent strategies
slides.html:
Granstrand’s patent strategies range from a few ad hoc patents to deliberate patent networks, and patenting itself may be sporadic or continuous.

StrategyWhat it is
Ad hoc blockingA few patents for one use; easy to invent around
Strategic patentOne patent that is too costly for rivals to invent around
Blanketing or floodingCovers a field with many patents
FencingA row of patents across several research paths
SurroundingMany small patents around a rival’s key patent to force a cross licence
Patent networkDifferent patents combined deliberately
PatentingMeaningTrade-off
SporadicCovers only key inventionsCosts less, protects less
ContinuousFiling throughout the product lifeCosts more but gives wider and longer protection

A way to picture them: ad hoc blocking and a strategic patent are single barriers, one weak and one strong; blanketing, fencing and surrounding use many patents in a pattern; a network combines different patents on purpose.

slides.part: 1.6 The IP Portfolio as a Competitive Tool
slides.title: Facing a blocking patent
slides.html:
A firm blocked by another’s patent has legal options, namely opposition, revocation and compulsory licence, and commercial ones such as inventing around, buying, licensing or cross licensing.

Legal optionWhen or howPatents Act
Oppose before grantBefore grants. 25(1)
Oppose after grantWithin one year from publication of the grants. 25(2)
RevocationSeek the patent’s revocations. 64
Compulsory licenceApply where the conditions of s. 84 are mets. 84

The commercial options are to:

  1. invent around it;
  2. buy or license it;
  3. offer a cross licence;
  4. wait for expiry;
  5. leave the field.

Timing narrows the legal choice. Opposition under s. 25(1) is possible only before grant, and opposition under s. 25(2) only within one year from publication of the grant; revocation under s. 64 is a separate route.

A cross licence is realistic only if the firm has patents the other side needs, which is the retaliatory power of the previous slide.

slides.part: 1.6 The IP Portfolio as a Competitive Tool
slides.title: Size is not value
slides.html:
A few patents usually carry most of a portfolio’s value, so its real strength lies in quality, not in the number of patents.

A few patents usually carry most of the value of a portfolio. Its real strength depends on:

  1. validity
  2. claim scope
  3. use in products
  4. countries covered
  5. remaining life
  6. fit with strategy
  7. cost of maintenance

Unused patents are not merely wasted. They also carry legal risk, since non working can support a compulsory licence (s. 84, seen in 1.4).

Granstrand records that leading Japanese firms moved from quantity to quality by seeking “strategic patents”, the single patents too costly for rivals to invent around.

Exam focus. In Question 6, do not praise a portfolio for its size alone. Close the portfolio half of the answer with the quality factors and the risk of non-working.

slides.part: 1.7 The Role of the Intellectual Asset Manager
slides.title: Who the IA manager is and how the role evolved
slides.html:
The intellectual asset manager manages IP as a business asset, and Granstrand’s four stages show the role moving from legal administration to business strategy.

The intellectual asset manager, also called IP manager or chief IP officer, manages IP as a business asset by identifying, protecting, using and defending it in line with business strategy.

Granstrand describes four stages in the evolution of corporate IP management:

  1. First stage: IP is ignored.
  2. Second stage: inventors are rewarded and IP is left to the legal department.
  3. Third stage: patenting becomes selective, licensing happens when needed and patent positions are reviewed.
  4. Fourth stage: IP becomes part of business strategy, engineers rotate through the IP department and licensing is based on business needs.

The role therefore moves from legal administration to business strategy.

The same movement runs through this Part: Harrison and Sullivan’s value hierarchy in 1.4 and Granstrand’s model policy, which makes business managers responsible for IP, both pull IP out of the legal department and into strategy.

Remember: “I Leave Selection to Strategy”: Ignored, Legal department, Selective, Strategy.

slides.part: 1.7 The Role of the Intellectual Asset Manager
slides.title: What the IA manager does
slides.html:
The IA manager’s work spans policy, the portfolio, deals and contracts, risk and records, and people, linking the legal, R&D, finance, tax and business teams.

Policy and strategy

Frames the firm’s IP policy and runs an IP committee; aligns IP strategy with business strategy; plans IP budgets.

Portfolio

Collects invention disclosures and maintains an IP register; decides which form of protection to seek and in which countries; reviews the portfolio and decides on renewal, licensing or abandonment.

Deals and contracts

Negotiates licences and sales; drafts and manages IP clauses in employment, consultancy, research and supply contracts.

Risk and records

Checks freedom to operate; monitors infringers; coordinates valuation, due diligence and audit; keeps records and deadlines.

People

Trains staff; runs inventor reward schemes; links the legal, R&D, finance, tax and business teams.

Skills. The role requires IP law, technical understanding, business and financial skills, negotiation and communication.

Organisation. The function may be organised centrally, within business units, or through a mix of central policy and unit level managers.

slides.title: The IA manager’s compliance checklist
slides.html:
The IA manager keeps the firm compliant: working statements in Form 27, renewal fees, registration of transactions, permission for foreign filing, trade mark renewals and CARO records.

DutyRuleSource
Statement of workingForm 27 filed once for every period of three financial yearsPatents Rules, rule 131, as amended in 2024
Renewal feesPaid on time; a 10 per cent reduction applies when fees are paid online four or more years in advanceNo section cited in the notes
RegistrationAssignments and licences of patents are registeredPatents Act, s. 69
Foreign filingPermission is obtained before filing abroad first, for inventions made in India by residentss. 39
Trade marksRenewed every ten yearsNo section cited in the notes
Audit recordsRecords must support the auditor’s report on intangible assetsCARO 2020

Each duty protects value measured earlier in this Part. Form 27 guards against the compulsory licence risk for unworked patents (1.4 and 1.6). Registration under s. 69 lets the firm rely on its licences and assignments (1.4). The records support the auditor’s reporting described in 1.2.

Remember: Form 27 every three financial years; marks every ten years; 10 per cent off for paying four years ahead online.

slides.title: Part One in eight points
slides.html:
Part One in a sentence: accounts recognise few intangibles, so firms measure them more widely, extract value by many routes and manage portfolios within legal limits.

  1. Intangible assets are non physical resources that bring future benefits. Under Ind AS 38 they must be identifiable, controlled and expected to give economic benefits.
  2. Because research is expensed and internally generated brands and goodwill are never recognised, accounts show few intangibles. Management therefore relies on wider measurement through identification, classification, indicators and valuation.
  3. Public policy balances relevance against reliability. India combines strict recognition (Ind AS 38 and AS 26) with registered valuers, ICAI VS 302, CARO 2020 reporting, depreciation on acquired intangibles, a 10 per cent patent box, SARFAESI and CERSAI security and the National IPR Policy.
  4. Intellectual capital consists of human, structural and relational capital and is measured through the Balanced Scorecard, Skandia Navigator, Intangible Assets Monitor, Tobin’s q, VAIC and CIV.
  5. Profits are extracted through own use, licensing, assignment, collaboration, finance, enforcement, standards and collective licensing, within the limits of s. 140 of the Patents Act, s. 3(5)(i) of the Competition Act and the working requirement behind compulsory licensing.
  6. Start-ups are measured by team, ownership, filings, freedom to operate and traction, and valued by scorecard and venture capital methods.
  7. A portfolio is a competitive tool through protection, bargaining and retaliatory power, but its value depends on quality rather than size.
  8. The intellectual asset manager has moved from legal administration to business strategy and must keep the firm compliant with Form 27, renewals and registration.

slides.html:
1. Explain the meaning and importance of measuring intangible assets and the legal and practical difficulties involved.
  2. Discuss public policy on the measurement of intangible assets and its implications in India.

slides.title: Answer plans: Questions 1 and 2
slides.html:
Questions 1 and 2 reward a definition first, then a structured list, then the accounting or policy rule that explains the problem, then a balanced conclusion.

Q1. Explain the meaning and importance of measuring intangible assets and the legal and practical difficulties involved.

  1. Define intangible assets: no physical form, future benefits. Name the legal rights (Patents Act, 1970; Copyright Act, 1957; Trade Marks Act, 1999; Designs Act, 2000; GI Act, 1999; confidential information) and contrast management’s wider view.
  2. Give the Ind AS 38 definition and its three tests, and explain why IP law decides what accounts can recognise.
  3. Explain what measuring involves: identification, classification, quantification, valuation.
  4. Importance: management decisions; prices for licences, assignments, mergers, joint ventures and technology transfer; damages; lenders; tax and transfer pricing; acquisitions and impairment; investors and the cost of capital; hidden risks.
  5. Difficulties: tacit knowledge, few comparables, uncertain future, separating contributions, assumptions; then legal uncertainty (revocation, a mark becoming generic, a leaked secret).
  6. Show the accounting gap: para 54, para 57, para 63, para 48 and AS 26; work the market to book example (₹10,000 crore ÷ ₹2,000 crore = 5) and give its caveat.
  7. Conclude: accounting is strict for reliability, so management measurement fills the gap; what is not measured is usually not managed.

Q2. Discuss public policy on the measurement of intangible assets and its implications in India.

  1. Define public policy on measuring intangibles and give the State’s six concerns.
  2. Explain the central choice of relevance and reliability and why standard setters prefer strict recognition with better disclosure.
  3. Indian framework, accounts and valuation: Ind AS 38 (Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015), AS 26, registered valuers under s. 247 and the 2017 Rules, VS 302, CARO 2020.
  4. Tax, finance and policy: s. 33(1)(b) and s. 194(1) of the Income Tax Act, 2025; SARFAESI Act, 2002 and CERSAI; National IPR Policy, 2016; SIPP.
  5. Implications for investors, lenders, start-ups, government, transfer pricing, boards and national statistics.
  6. International position: IAS 38 under review with no change by 7 November 2026; integrated reporting’s six capitals; WIPO.
  7. Conclude: the trend is towards better disclosure rather than wider recognition.

slides.title: Answer plans: Questions 3 and 4
slides.html:
Questions 3 and 4 reward named frameworks and worked formulas, and then the legal structure and limits; always end with the limits.

Q3. Explain intellectual capital accounting as a management tool with reference to the main frameworks.

  1. Define intellectual capital; give Granstrand’s physical, financial and intellectual capital and the three components (human, structural, relational).
  2. Set out the Skandia value scheme as a tree.
  3. Define IC accounting: voluntary, internal, outside the statutory statements; its legal use in IP audits, due diligence and valuation; prospectus liability under ss. 34 and 35 of the Companies Act, 2013.
  4. Explain the five frameworks with their authors (Balanced Scorecard, Skandia Navigator, Intangible Assets Monitor, Technology Broker, IC Index) and Sveiby’s four families of methods.
  5. Work the formulas: Tobin’s q (above 1); VAIC = 3.6; CIV = 150.
  6. Give the uses, then the limits.
  7. Conclude: a valuable management tool that complements, but cannot replace, the strict accounts.

Q4. Explain the methods of extracting profits from intellectual capital and the legal limits on them.

  1. Distinguish value creation from value extraction, and give the three reasons firms earn little.
  2. Explain Teece’s three conditions and Harrison and Sullivan’s IP value hierarchy.
  3. Own use, then licensing (ss. 68 and 69; s. 30), assignment (s. 19; s. 45), franchising and technology transfer.
  4. Collaborative and financial methods; then enforcement, defensive publication, standards, pools, copyright societies, business models, spin-offs, disposal of non-core patents and bargaining chips.
  5. How to choose the route, and Granstrand’s policy and strategy with his model IP policy.
  6. Legal limits: s. 3(5)(i) of the Competition Act, 2002; s. 140 of the Patents Act; compulsory licence under s. 84 after three years from grant and Form 27; foreign exchange and tax rules.
  7. Conclude: extraction is a business choice that the law permits only within reasonable limits.

slides.title: Answer plans: Questions 5 and 6
slides.html:
Questions 5 and 6 reward putting ownership and quality before numbers, then the valuation methods or strategies, then compliance.

Q5. How can a start up measure and value its intellectual capital?

  1. Explain why IC matters in a start-up and why it is hard to measure; give Granstrand’s “hubris” and the one-good-patent belief.
  2. Put ownership first: s. 6 and ss. 68 and 69 of the Patents Act; s. 17 and s. 19 of the Copyright Act; confidentiality agreements, trade mark search, freedom to operate.
  3. Set out what to measure: team, structural capital, IP position, relational capital, market traction.
  4. Explain the scorecard method with its weights and the ₹23.1 crore example, and the Berkus method.
  5. Work the venture capital method (₹26.34 crore post money, ₹16.34 crore pre money, about 38 per cent) and explain the First Chicago method.
  6. Note Indian support: DPIIT recognition, SIPP, lower patent fees, expedited examination.
  7. Conclude: a credible value rests on clean ownership and evidence, not on founder belief.

Q6. Explain the IP portfolio as a competitive tool and the role of the intellectual asset manager.

  1. Define the IP portfolio as a bundle of territorial rights, and list its functions.
  2. Why firms patent: Granstrand’s Japanese survey; retaliatory power; “patent extortionists”; market freedom and design freedom.
  3. Patent strategies: ad hoc blocking, strategic patent, blanketing, fencing, surrounding, network; sporadic or continuous patenting.
  4. Options against a blocking patent: s. 25(1), s. 25(2), s. 64, s. 84, and the commercial options.
  5. Size is not value: the quality factors, the non-working risk and the Japanese shift to strategic patents.
  6. The IA manager: definition, Granstrand’s four stages, responsibilities, skills and organisation.
  7. Compliance: Form 27 (rule 131, as amended in 2024), renewals and the 10 per cent online reduction, s. 69, s. 39, trade mark renewal every ten years, CARO 2020.
  8. Conclude: the portfolio is a competitive tool only if the IA manager keeps it valid, aligned with strategy and compliant.

slides.title: The menu of IP rights in India
slides.html:
Indian law offers a menu of IP rights, each with its own subject matter, term and formality, so strategy starts by knowing exactly what each right covers.

Each right is built for a different kind of asset. A firm can only combine rights well if it knows what each one protects, how long it lasts and how it arises.

RightStatuteProtectsTermHow it arises
PatentPatents Act, 1970Inventions that are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application, subject to the exclusions in s. 320 years from filingFiling and grant
DesignDesigns Act, 2000The shape, pattern or appearance of an article10 years, extendable by 5Registration
Trade markTrade Marks Act, 1999Signs that distinguish goods or servicesRenewable periods of 10 years, without limitRegistration
CopyrightCopyright Act, 1957Literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, films, sound recordings and softwareGenerally life of the author plus 60 yearsAutomatically
Trade secretsNo statute in IndiaConfidential informationAs long as it remains secretContracts and the equitable duty of confidence

Geographical indications protect goods linked to a place, and separate laws protect semiconductor layout designs and plant varieties.

Exam focus. Remember the contrast in terms: a patent is fixed at 20 years, a trade mark can be renewed without limit, and a trade secret lasts only while secrecy lasts. These differences drive every strategy choice that follows.

slides.title: What a protection strategy decides
slides.html:
A protection strategy decides which right to use, when, where and how much, so that IP supports the business at the lowest total cost and risk.

Owning rights is not the goal; supporting the business is. Every right costs money to file, renew and enforce, so the strategy weighs that cost against the protection it really gives.

The choice of right depends on:

  1. the type of innovation;
  2. whether rivals can copy it by examining the product;
  3. the length of its commercial life;
  4. whether infringement can be detected and proved;
  5. the cost of filing, renewal and enforcement;
  6. the need to avoid disclosure;
  7. the markets and competitors involved; and
  8. the legal exclusions.

s. 3(d), Patents Act, 1970. Bars patents on new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy.

s. 3(k), Patents Act, 1970. Excludes computer programs as such and business methods.

The exclusions show how law shapes strategy. Because s. 3(k) closes the patent route for much software, it pushes software firms towards copyright, secrecy and contracts.

slides.title: Patent or trade secret?
slides.html:
A patent buys a strong 20-year right at the price of full public disclosure; a trade secret needs no disclosure and can last indefinitely, but protects only against misuse.

FeaturePatentTrade secret
Duration20 yearsCan last indefinitely
DisclosureFull public disclosure requiredNo disclosure needed
Protects againstEveryone, even independent inventorsOnly misuse of confidential information
Independent discovery or reverse engineeringStill covered by the exclusive rightNo protection

Granstrand identifies four situations in which secrecy may be the better choice:

  1. the firm has a large lead over rivals;
  2. the secret is hard to discover, for example a process that leaves no trace in the product;
  3. infringement of a patent would be hard to detect; and
  4. a patent could easily be invented around.

The logic is the same in each: the patent would give little real protection, yet its price, full disclosure, would still be paid.

Remember: when to HIDE an invention: Head start (large lead), Invisible (hard to discover), Detection of infringement hard, Easy to invent around.

Granstrand also notes that the legal protection of secrets is weak, so firms must rely on their own measures. In India these are confidentiality clauses in employment and supply contracts, non disclosure agreements and access controls.

s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872. Makes most post employment non compete restraints void, so a firm cannot simply bar a leaving employee from joining a rival; it must guard the information itself.

slides.title: Multi protection and defensive publication
slides.html:
Strong positions combine several rights around one business, and a firm can even publish an invention deliberately so that nobody else can patent it.

Granstrand recommends multi protection, which means combining several rights around one business. Each right covers a different part of the offering, so the business is not left exposed when one right is weak or expires.

Secret formula

Trade secret: lasts while it stays secret.

Patented machinery

Patent: a 20-year exclusive right.

The container

A registered design for its appearance.

The brand

A registered trade mark.

Trade marks deserve special attention because they can be renewed without limit and grow in value. Long after the machinery patent expires, the brand can keep the business distinctive.

Defensive publication is the deliberate publication of an invention so that nobody can patent it. It is a cheap way of keeping freedom to operate, because published matter forms prior art that defeats later patent claims.

Exam focus. Contrast defensive publication with secrecy: the firm gives up exclusivity, but in return no rival can patent the idea and block it.
slides.plain: Multi protection and defensive publication. Strong positions combine several rights around one business, and a firm can even publish an invention deliberately so that nobody else can patent it. Granstrand recommends multi protection , which means combining several rights around one business . Each right covers a different part of the offering, so the business is not left exposed when one right is weak or expires. Secret formula Trade secret: lasts while it stays secret. Patented machinery Patent: a 20-year exclusive right. The container A registered design for its appearance. The brand A registered trade mark. Trade marks deserve special attention because they can be renewed without limit and grow in value . Long after the machinery patent expires, the brand can keep the business distinctive. slides.title: Timing and territory of filing
slides.html:
Timing is critical: file before any public disclosure, use the priority periods to file abroad, and seek rights where the firm sells, manufactures and competes.

  1. File before any public disclosure. Indian law allows only limited exceptions for prior disclosure, so a public talk, sale or paper before filing can cost the right.
  2. Use the priority period. A first filing gives a priority period of 12 months for patents and 6 months for designs and trade marks to file abroad under the Paris Convention.
  3. Or use the PCT route. It allows one international application, with entry into the Indian national phase at 31 months from priority.
  4. Choose the territories. Rights should be sought where the firm sells, where it manufactures and where competitors operate, because those are the places where copying would hurt.

s. 39, Patents Act, 1970. A resident inventor must obtain permission before filing abroad first.

Read the steps together: the first filing fixes the priority date, and the priority period or the PCT route then gives time to decide which countries are worth the cost.

Exam focus. Learn the three time figures as a set: 12 months (patent priority), 6 months (design and trade mark priority), 31 months (PCT national phase in India).

slides.part: 2.2 IP Categorisation: Business, Technical and Legal Perspectives
slides.title: Why categorise: three perspectives
slides.html:
Categorisation turns a list of registrations into information for decisions, by grouping rights from the business, technical and legal perspectives.

A bare list of patents and marks says nothing about what to do. Categorisation shows which rights matter to the business, which only cost money, where the legal risks lie and what action each asset needs.

PerspectiveRights are grouped by
Business perspectivecore or non core; strategic, defensive or offensive; revenue earning or merely cost generating; product line, business unit or market
Technical perspectivetechnology field (IPC or CPC classes); basic technology or application; product or process; basic invention or improvement; stage of maturity
Legal perspectivetype; registered or unregistered status; legal status (pending, granted, opposed, lapsed); countries covered and remaining term; ownership; licences and security interests already granted; strength in terms of validity, claim scope and enforceability

A widely used business practice sorts patents into those the business is using, those it will use and those it will not use. The last group is licensed, sold, donated or abandoned.

s. 50, Patents Act, 1970. A joint owner of an Indian patent cannot grant a licence or assign a share without the consent of the other owners.

This is why joint ownership needs particular care in the legal view: a co-owned patent may look like a licensing asset, yet one owner cannot license it alone.

slides.part: 2.2 IP Categorisation: Business, Technical and Legal Perspectives
slides.title: The portfolio matrix
slides.html:
A portfolio matrix scores each asset for business value and legal strength, and the quadrant it lands in tells the firm what to do with it.

Strong legal positionWeak legal position
High business valueCrown jewels: maintain, enforce and extendWeak core: strengthen through further filings, secrecy or better contracts
Low business valueCandidates for licensing or saleShould be dropped by abandonment, sale or donation

Remember: Keep, Fix, Sell, Drop: crown jewels are kept, the weak core is fixed, strong but low-value rights are sold or licensed, and rights weak on both are dropped.

The review is a cycle, not a one-off:

  1. List all assets.
  2. Score them with input from business, technical and legal staff.
  3. Decide the action for each.
  4. Repeat the review before renewal fees fall due.

Renewal makes sense only where the expected benefit exceeds the cost. Abandonment saves money but may free the technology for competitors, so the saving must be weighed against what a rival gains.

s. 60, Patents Act, 1970. A lapsed patent can be restored only within the period and conditions allowed by law, so a mistaken abandonment may not be reversible.

Firms should also avoid depending on a single patent, licensee or market.

slides.title: Evaluation before valuation
slides.html:
Evaluation judges the quality and importance of an IP asset and valuation fixes its value in money, so evaluation comes first: valuing a weak right is meaningless.

EvaluationValuation
What it doesA judgement of the quality and importance of an IP assetFixes a value in money
Expressed asScores or ratingsAn amount, for a stated purpose and date
Used forPortfolio decisions and screeningSales, licences, accounts, tax, loans and damages
OrderComes firstFollows evaluation

Evaluation comes first, because a valuation of a weak or invalid right is meaningless. If a patent would not survive a challenge, the income it is said to protect is not really protected.

Evaluation looks at five groups of factors:

Legal

Validity, scope, enforceability, remaining term, territory and ownership.

Technical

Novelty, substitutes and ease of inventing around.

Commercial

Market size, growth, margins and competition.

Strategic

Fit with business plans and blocking power.

Risk

The risks attached to the asset.

Remember: Let The Company See Risk: Legal, Technical, Commercial, Strategic, Risk.

slides.title: Why IP is valued, and the legal basis
slides.html:
IP is valued for deals, reporting, tax, disputes, insolvency and finance, and several of these purposes impose a legal requirement on how the valuation is done.

Valuation is needed for:

  1. licensing and royalty setting, assignment, mergers and acquisitions and investment;
  2. financial reporting, tax and transfer pricing;
  3. damages in infringement suits and insolvency proceedings;
  4. loans secured on IP; and
  5. internal portfolio decisions.

Several of these have a legal basis, so the valuation must meet a legal standard and not just a commercial one:

ContextLegal basisWhat it requires
Company lawCompanies Act, 2013, s. 247Registered valuers for statutory valuations
TaxIncome Tax Act, 2025, ss. 161 to 173Related party royalties at arm's length
AccountingInd AS 103, Ind AS 36 and Ind AS 113Fair values in acquisitions and impairment tests
InsolvencyInsolvency proceduresEstimates of fair value and liquidation value
Valuation standardICAI Valuation Standard 302 (VS 302)Deals specifically with intangible assets

Exam focus. When a question asks why valuation matters legally, cite these five bases in one sentence each: s. 247, ss. 161 to 173, the three Ind AS, insolvency values and VS 302.

slides.title: The three valuation approaches
slides.html:
IP is valued by what it would cost to replace (cost), what comparable deals paid (market), or the present value of the income it will generate (income).

ApproachValues the asset atStrengthWeakness
Cost approachWhat it would cost to recreate or replace it, less obsolescenceSimple; suits early stage technology and softwareCost is not the same as value
Market approachPrices or royalty rates in comparable transactionsPersuasive when good comparables existTrue comparables are rare and deal terms are usually confidential
Income approachThe present value of the future income it will generateLooks forward to what the asset will earnDepends on forecasts of that income

The income approach has five methods:

Discounted cash flow
The present value of the forecast future cash flows.
Relief from royalty
The royalties saved by owning the asset rather than licensing it.
Excess earnings
Business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used.
With and without
The difference in business value with and without the asset.
Premium profit
The extra price or cost saving due to the asset.

Remember: the income methods DREW a Profit: DCF, Relief from royalty, Excess earnings, With and without, Premium profit.

Real option models, empirical models and index scores complement these approaches; they are taken up in 2.4 to 2.6.
