slides.title: Choosing a method and doing a sound valuation
slides.html:
Each method suits a particular asset, and a sound valuation fixes its purpose, uses at least two methods, tests sensitivity and states its assumptions.

SituationMethod that suits it
Early patents with no incomeCost approach or real options
Established brands and technologiesRelief from royalty
The core technology of a businessExcess earnings
Non compete agreementsWith and without method
Licence negotiationsComparable royalties combined with discounted cash flow

The pairings follow the definitions: with no income yet there is little to discount, an established brand has royalty rates to borrow, and core technology earns the profit left after a fair return on everything else.

Value is affected by remaining legal life, economic life, exclusivity, claim scope, enforceability, market size, competition, complementary assets, territorial coverage and licences already granted.

A sound valuation:

  1. fixes the purpose, basis and date;
  2. identifies the legal rights;
  3. evaluates them;
  4. collects data;
  5. uses at least two methods;
  6. tests the sensitivity of the result; and
  7. states its assumptions clearly.

Exam focus. In a valuation answer, match the method to the asset and say why, then name a second method as a cross-check.

slides.title: What an IP value index measures
slides.html:
An IP value index is a single score that ranks patents or portfolios by quality by combining several indicators; it screens and compares but does not fix a price.

Because the score is relative, it answers "which portfolio is stronger?" and not "what is it worth in rupees?". It is a tool for screening and comparison, not for fixing a price, and there is no statutory IP value index in Indian law.

IndicatorWhat it measuresWhat it signals
Forward citationsLater patents citing the patentTechnical importance
Family sizeNumber of countries in which protection is soughtExpected commercial value
Number of claimsHow much the patent claimsBreadth

Other typical indicators are grant lag, backward citations, remaining term, renewals and the history of licensing and litigation.

Each indicator is only a sign of value, which is why an index combines several rather than relying on one.

slides.title: The Patent Asset Index
slides.html:
The Patent Asset Index of Ernst and Omland multiplies each family's Technology Relevance by its Market Coverage, then adds the results across the portfolio.

It is the best known example, used in commercial patent analytics. Each patent family receives two scores:

Technology Relevance
Based on citations, with an average of 1.
Market Coverage
Based on the size of the markets in which it is protected, with a granted United States patent equal to 1.

Competitive Impact = Technology Relevance × Market Coverage

Patent Asset Index = Σ Competitive Impact

A family scores highly only if it is both technically important and protected in large markets. The index adds these family scores, so it rewards quality per family, not the number of families.

Worked example

Portfolio A has three families with Competitive Impact of 3.6, 0.15 and 1.08: index = 3.6 + 0.15 + 1.08 = 4.83.

Portfolio B has ten families of 0.2 each: index = 10 × 0.2 = 2.0.

So the smaller portfolio is stronger: three good families beat ten weak ones.

Exam focus. Use this example whenever you need to show that portfolio size is not value.

slides.title: Other indices, building one, and the limits
slides.html:
Other quality indices exist; all are built by choosing, normalising, weighting and combining indicators, and none of them gives a money value.

IndexBuilt from
OECD patent quality indexForward citations, family size, claims and generality; an extended version adds backward citations and grant lag
Lanjouw and Schankerman compositeSeveral indicators; found forward citations most informative
Technology strength measuresPatent counts multiplied by citation impact
Granstrand's indirect valuationPatent volume, patent shares, citations, renewal fees and the age profile of patents

An index is built in five steps:

  1. Choose indicators.
  2. Normalise them.
  3. Weight them.
  4. Combine them.
  5. Test the result against real outcomes.

Its limits:

  1. it gives no money value;
  2. citations take years to accumulate;
  3. weights are subjective;
  4. indicators can be manipulated; and
  5. legal validity is not checked.

The last limit links back to 2.3: an index can rank a patent highly even if it would not survive a challenge, so evaluation of legal strength is still needed.

slides.title: Empirical models and the market value model
slides.html:
Empirical models estimate the value of IP from real data on large numbers of patents and firms, rather than from forecasts for a single asset.

Granstrand cautions that patent data alone cannot value a portfolio because patent values are highly uneven. Patent data must be combined with stock market data, panel data or survey evidence.

The market value model relates the stock market value of firms to their tangible assets and knowledge assets:

V = q × (A + γK)

V is market value, A is tangible assets, K is the knowledge stock (R&D or patents) and γ shows how the market values knowledge relative to tangible assets.

How to read it: estimated across many firms, a high γ means investors pay a lot for each unit of knowledge stock, which tells us what the market thinks knowledge is worth.

The model works on averages across firms, which is both its strength and its limit: it shows how markets price knowledge in general, not what one patent is worth.

The model works on averages across firms, which is both its strength and its limit: it shows how markets price knowledge in general, not what one patent is worth.

slides.title: Renewal, citation, survey, event and transaction models
slides.html:
Each empirical model reads value from a different trace in the data, and together they show that a few patents hold most of the value.

Renewal models
Owners keep paying renewal fees only while a patent is worth more than the fee, so renewal data reveal how values are spread. The main finding: most patents are worth little while a few are worth a great deal.
Citation models
Show that highly cited patents tend to be more valuable.
Survey models
Ask owners to estimate the value of their patents.
Event studies
Measure share price reactions to patent grants or court outcomes.
Transaction models
Use prices from patent sales and licences.
Empirical models
Useful forPolicy, screening and benchmarking; they inform assumptions in individual valuations
LimitsThey give averages rather than the value of one patent, depend on available data and show association rather than cause

Exam focus. The key line: empirical models inform an individual valuation but cannot replace it, because they give averages, not the value of one patent.

slides.title: A patent as a real option
slides.html:
A patent gives the right but not the obligation to exploit an invention exclusively, so, like a call option, it is worth more than a fixed-plan forecast suggests.

Like a call option in finance, a patent lets the owner wait for information and invest only if conditions are favourable, or expand, license, switch use or abandon.

Ordinary discounted cash flow assumes a fixed plan and ignores this flexibility, so it can undervalue early and uncertain IP.

SymbolMeaning in the patent analogy
SThe present value of expected cash flows from using the invention
KThe investment needed to commercialise it
TThe time until the decision must be taken, limited by the remaining patent term
σThe uncertainty of the project's value
rThe risk free rate

Each renewal fee can also be seen as buying an option to keep the patent for another year.

Exam focus. Explain the why: DCF treats the decision as already made, while an option model values the choice to wait, which is exactly what an early patent gives.

slides.title: The Black and Scholes model
slides.html:
The Black and Scholes model gives the value of the option a patent offers; in the notes' example the right to wait is worth 28.11 though investing now loses 20.

C = S × N(d1) − K × e−rT × N(d2)

d1 = [ln(S ÷ K) + (r + σ2 ÷ 2) × T] ÷ (σ√T); d2 = d1 − σ√T

C is the option value. N( ) is the cumulative normal probability, and K × e−rT is the present value of the investment K.

Worked example

S = 100, K = 120, T = 3 years, σ = 0.40 and r = 0.07.

  1. d1 = [ln(100 ÷ 120) + (0.07 + 0.16 ÷ 2) × 3] ÷ (0.40 × √3) = 0.3864.
  2. d2 = d1 − σ√T = −0.3065.
  3. N(d1) = 0.6504 and N(d2) = 0.3796.
  4. Present value of K = 120 × e−0.21 = 97.27.
  5. C = 100 × 0.6504 − 97.27 × 0.3796 = 65.04 − 36.93 = 28.11.

Investing immediately would have an NPV of −20 (100 − 120), yet the right to wait is worth 28.11.

The value rises as uncertainty rises: the owner keeps the upside if the market turns out well and simply does not invest if it turns out badly.

slides.title: The binomial model
slides.html:
The binomial model assumes value moves up or down by set factors, and values the option with a risk neutral probability, discounting at the risk free rate.

p = (1 + r − d) ÷ (u − d)

Option value = [p × up payoff + (1 − p) × down payoff] ÷ (1 + r)

p is the risk neutral probability of the up move, u and d are the up and down factors, and the payoff in each state is the value minus K, or nothing if that is negative.

Worked example

S = 100, up factor u = 1.4, down factor d = 0.7, risk free rate 7 per cent, K = 110.

  1. Up state: value 100 × 1.4 = 140, so the option pays 30 (140 − 110).
  2. Down state: value 100 × 0.7 = 70, below K, so it pays nothing.
  3. Risk neutral probability = (1.07 − 0.7) ÷ (1.4 − 0.7) = 0.5286.
  4. Option value = 0.5286 × 30 ÷ 1.07 = 14.82.

Why it works: once the probability is set this way, the expected payoff can simply be discounted at the risk free rate, without having to guess a risk premium.

Exam focus. Show the four lines of working in the exam. The marks are in the payoffs (30 and nothing) and the probability (0.5286), not just the answer.

slides.title: Decision trees and the limits of option models
slides.html:
A decision tree gives the same insight: keeping the choice to launch only if the market is good adds value, here 18.18.

Worked example

A pilot costs 20 now. Next year the market is good (value 180) or bad (value 40) with equal chance. Launch costs 80 and the discount rate is 10 per cent.

StrategyWorkingNPV
Commit to launch in both cases−20 + [0.5 × (180 − 80) + 0.5 × (40 − 80)] ÷ 1.107.27
Launch only in the good case−20 + [0.5 × (180 − 80)] ÷ 1.1025.45
Value of flexibility25.45 − 7.2718.18

The flexibility is worth exactly the loss it avoids. Launching into a bad market would lose 40 (value 40 less launch cost 80); weighted by its 0.5 chance and discounted, 0.5 × 40 ÷ 1.10 = 18.18.

Option models value flexibility and suit early, risky IP. Their limits:

  1. the analogy with traded options is imperfect;
  2. uncertainty is hard to estimate;
  3. rivals may invent around the patent; and
  4. the patent may be revoked.

slides.html:
Measuring gives a picture of intellectual capital at one point in time; monitoring tracks it regularly through indicators and targets so that management can act early.

slides.title: Building a monitoring system
slides.html:
A monitoring system starts from strategy and uses a few clearly defined indicators with owners and targets, while guarding against gaming.

  1. Start from strategy.
  2. Select a small number of clearly defined indicators, each with a named owner and data source.
  3. Set targets.
  4. Report results in a dashboard or IC statement.
  5. Review the indicators regularly.

The Danish model of IC statement combines a knowledge narrative, management challenges, initiatives and indicators.

Its main problems are:

  1. poor data;
  2. weak comparability between firms;
  3. the assumption that indicators cause results; and
  4. gaming, where people improve the number rather than the reality, for example by filing weak patents to raise patent counts.

Gaming explains why the system uses few, clearly defined indicators: the fewer and clearer they are, the harder it is to improve the figure without improving the reality.

OrganisationMonitors
Start upsMilestones and the team
Established firmsPortfolio quality and licence income
UniversitiesDisclosures, licences and spin offs
Service firmsExpertise and client relationships

slides.part: 2.8 Understanding and Managing Knowledge Assets for Competitive Advantage
slides.title: From data to knowledge assets
slides.html:
Knowledge assets are the stocks of useful knowledge a firm holds, and because knowledge cannot be taken back once disclosed, IP rights are needed to trade it.

  1. Data are facts.
  2. Information is data with meaning.
  3. Knowledge is information combined with experience that allows action.

Knowledge assets are the stocks of useful knowledge a firm holds: know how, skills, processes, designs, software, customer insight and IP.

Tacit knowledgeExplicit knowledge
Where it isLives in people's headsWritten or coded
TransferHard to expressEasy to transfer

Knowledge is not used up when shared, spreads easily, builds on itself and cannot be taken back once disclosed. These properties make it valuable and also easy to lose.

Arrow's information paradox explains why IP rights matter: a buyer cannot judge knowledge without seeing it, but once it is seen it has been given away. Patents and confidentiality agreements allow disclosure without loss of protection.

slides.part: 2.8 Understanding and Managing Knowledge Assets for Competitive Advantage
slides.title: How knowledge creates competitive advantage
slides.html:
Knowledge gives competitive advantage when it is valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable, and firms build it through competencies, capabilities and learning.

Remember: Barney's VRIN test: knowledge must be Valuable, Rare, hard to Imitate and Not substitutable.

Core competencies

Prahalad and Hamel: forms of collective learning that open many markets, add customer value and are hard to copy.

Dynamic capabilities

Teece: the ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure resources.

Absorptive capacity

Cohen and Levinthal: the ability to recognise and use outside knowledge.

Knowledge management means creating, capturing, storing, sharing, using and protecting knowledge.

The SECI model of Nonaka and Takeuchi explains how knowledge is created by converting it between tacit and explicit forms:

ModeConversion
SocialisationTacit to tacit
ExternalisationTacit to explicit
CombinationExplicit to explicit
InternalisationExplicit to tacit

slides.part: 2.8 Understanding and Managing Knowledge Assets for Competitive Advantage
slides.title: Protecting knowledge assets in law
slides.html:
Knowledge assets are protected by IP rights and contracts, but because Indian law voids most non compete clauses, firms also rely on keeping their people.

Legally, knowledge assets are protected through:

  1. IP rights;
  2. trade secret policies;
  3. non disclosure agreements; and
  4. confidentiality and assignment clauses in employment contracts.

Granstrand found that an internal secrecy policy was the most important secrecy measure in large Japanese firms.

s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872. Post employment non compete clauses are generally void.

So Indian firms rely on confidentiality duties and retention measures such as incentives, career paths and succession planning. If knowledge lives in people's heads and they cannot be barred from joining a rival, the firm must give them reasons to stay.

Knowledge that includes personal data is also subject to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Exam focus. This is the same s. 27 point as in 2.1: link the two in answers on trade secrets and on knowledge management.

slides.part: 2.9 Knowledge Assets in Innovation and Product Development
slides.title: IP at each stage of product development
slides.html:
New product development turns knowledge into products, and IP management must be built into every stage, from recording ideas to enforcing rights after launch.

New product development turns knowledge about customers, technology and markets into products. Firms that reuse knowledge through platforms and standard components innovate faster and at lower cost.

IP management must be built into each stage of development:

  1. Idea: record ideas and search patent literature for existing solutions.
  2. Concept: check patentability and freedom to operate.
  3. Design: decide between patenting and secrecy, and file before any disclosure.
  4. Testing: non disclosure agreements should bind testers, and improvements should be filed.
  5. Launch: register trade marks and designs and do a final clearance.
  6. After launch: file improvements, watch competitors and enforce the firm's rights.

Exam focus. Notice the thread through the stages: disclosure risk peaks at design, testing and launch, which is why filing and NDAs sit exactly there.

slides.part: 2.9 Knowledge Assets in Innovation and Product Development
slides.title: Granstrand's guidance and the Indian legal points
slides.html:
Granstrand says check others' patents, file early, patent continuously and use patent maps; Indian law adds rules on disclosure, exclusions, foreign filing and joint ownership.

Granstrand's guidance fits this process:

  1. check others' patents before entering a new field;
  2. file early ("speed to patent");
  3. patent continuously through the product life; and
  4. use patent maps to generate ideas, track rivals, plan R&D and strengthen bargaining.

He reports that Toshiba reviews patents at every step of the innovation process.

Legal point in IndiaEffect on development
Public disclosure before filingUsually destroys novelty
Exclusions in s. 3(d) and s. 3(k)Affect pharmaceutical and software inventions
s. 39, Patents ActResidents need permission before filing abroad first
s. 50, Patents ActJoint development requires clear agreement on ownership

These are the same provisions met in 2.1 and 2.2, now applied at the point where products are actually being built.

slides.title: Patent stocks and how they are counted
slides.html:
A patent stock is the accumulated number of patents of a firm, industry or country, used to measure its stock of technical knowledge; how it is counted changes the answer.

It can be counted as:

  1. a simple number of applications or grants;
  2. patent families (one invention counted once across countries);
  3. active patents still in force;
  4. a citation weighted count;
  5. a quality adjusted count; or
  6. a depreciated economic stock.

The depreciated stock gives less weight to older patents because knowledge becomes outdated:

Kt = (1 − δ) × Kt−1 + Pt

K is the stock, P is new patents in the year and δ is the yearly rate of decline, often taken as about 15 per cent. Each year the old stock shrinks by δ and the new patents are added.

Worked example

A firm obtains 10, 12, 15, 9, 20, 18 and 22 patents from 2019 to 2025. The simple count is 106, but the depreciated stock in 2025 is only 74.20. Working, with δ = 15 per cent and a stock of zero before 2019:

YearNew patentsStock = 0.85 × last year + new
20191010.00
20201220.50
20211532.43
2022936.56
20232051.08
20241861.42
20252274.20

slides.title: Revealed technological advantage, uses and limits
slides.html:
Revealed technological advantage compares a firm's share of patents in a field with the world's share; a high ratio shows the firm specialises in that field.

Patent stocks also support the measure of revealed technological advantage:

RTA = (Firm's patents in a field ÷ Firm's total patents) ÷ (World patents in the field ÷ World total patents)

A value of 1 means the firm patents in the field in the same proportion as the world; the higher the value, the stronger the specialisation.

Worked example

If 20 per cent of a firm's patents are in a field that has 5 per cent of world patents, RTA = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.0, showing strong specialisation.

Patent stocks
Used toMeasure innovation, explain firm value, compare competitors and screen acquisition targets
LimitsIndustries patent at different rates; patent values are highly uneven; strategic filing inflates counts; publication is delayed by about 18 months; company names vary

Exam focus. Granstrand insists that the counting unit must always be stated: 106 patents and a stock of 74.20 describe the same firm.

slides.title: Why copyright is managed collectively
slides.html:
Copyright societies license works for many owners, collect royalties and distribute them, because licensing thousands of works one owner at a time would be impossibly costly.

Collective management is the system in which copyright societies license works on behalf of many owners, collect royalties and distribute them.

Users such as radio and television broadcasters, hotels, restaurants, event organisers and digital platforms use thousands of works. Negotiating separately with every owner would be impossibly costly, while individual owners cannot monitor use across the country.

A society therefore:

  1. grants blanket licences covering its whole repertoire;
  2. sets tariffs and collects royalties;
  3. tracks use and distributes income to members;
  4. enforces rights; and
  5. makes reciprocal arrangements with foreign societies.

Societies commonly manage performing rights in music and lyrics, rights in sound recordings, performers' rights, reprographic rights and rights in scripts.

Voluntary

Owners choose to manage their rights through a society.

Extended

Extended to non members by law, as in Nordic countries.

Mandatory

Required for certain rights.

slides.title: Regulating copyright societies in India
slides.html:
Because one society tends to dominate each class of works, the Copyright Act, 1957 regulates societies' registration, tariffs, administration, control by owners and accounts.

Dominance raises concerns about high tariffs, unfair treatment of users, unclear distribution and high costs, which is why the law regulates collective management.

ProvisionRule
s. 33The business of issuing or granting licences in works may be carried on only by or through a registered copyright society; owners keep the right to license their own works individually; ordinarily only one society for each class of works; registration lasts five years
s. 33AEach society must publish its tariff scheme
s. 34Governs the administration of rights entrusted to the society
s. 35Gives owners and authors control over the society
s. 36Requires returns and audited accounts
Copyright Rules, 2013Add detailed procedures

The 2012 amendments required societies to register afresh, strengthened the control of authors and gave authors of works used in films and sound recordings a right to share in royalties.

Organisations active in India: IPRS for music and lyrics, PPL and RMPL for sound recordings, ISRA for performers and IRRO for reprographic rights.

Law update. The current registration status of these organisations should be checked with the Copyright Office.

Internationally, CISAC links authors' societies, and the European Union regulates the governance and transparency of collective management through Directive 2014/26/EU.

slides.part: 2.12 The Role of Intellectual Capital in Valuing Knowledge Companies
slides.title: Why accounts understate knowledge companies
slides.html:
Knowledge companies draw most of their value from technology, data, brands, people and relationships, yet their financial statements understate that value.

Knowledge companies, such as software, pharmaceutical, media and platform businesses, derive most of their value from technology, data, brands, people and relationships. Granstrand calls them IC firms.

Their financial statements understate their value because:

  1. research and brand building are expensed under Ind AS 38;
  2. employees are not shown as assets;
  3. assets are carried at historical cost; and
  4. network effects, data and future opportunities are not captured.

Their value is driven by IP, key people, data, software, research pipelines, brands, customer bases, processes, growth and scalability, together with the risks attached to each.

So the balance sheet is the wrong starting point: a valuer must look at what these drivers will earn, and at the risks attached to each driver.

Exam focus. Link this to Part One: the Ind AS 38 recognition rules are the reason the accounts miss most of an IC firm's value.

slides.part: 2.12 The Role of Intellectual Capital in Valuing Knowledge Companies
slides.title: Measures of value and how knowledge companies are valued
slides.html:
Keep five measures of value apart, from enterprise value to non money IC indicators, and value knowledge companies mainly from cash flows, multiples, parts and options.

Enterprise value
The value of the business to all providers of capital; it equals equity value plus net debt.
Equity value
The value to shareholders.
Asset value
The value of individual assets.
IP value
The value of the legal rights and the income they protect.
IC indicators
Non money measures of intellectual capital.

Enterprise value = Equity value + Net debt

Enterprise value belongs to all providers of capital, so the claims of lenders (net debt) are added to the shareholders' equity value.

Knowledge companies are usually valued by:

  1. discounted cash flow with scenarios;
  2. market multiples such as enterprise value to revenue;
  3. adding up the values of their parts;
  4. real options for research pipelines; and
  5. customer lifetime value.

These methods are sometimes applied after treating R&D as an investment rather than an expense, which undoes the Ind AS 38 expensing that hides much of their value.

slides.part: 2.12 The Role of Intellectual Capital in Valuing Knowledge Companies
slides.title: Why the residual method is unreliable
slides.html:
The residual method treats market value minus book value as the value of intellectual capital, but that gap moves with market mood, not with the firm's IC.

Value of IC (residual method) = Market value − Book value

The whole gap is credited to intellectual capital, which is the source of the problem.

The method is unreliable because the gap:

  1. includes market mood and growth expectations;
  2. ignores undervalued tangible assets and hidden liabilities, which also sit inside the gap; and
  3. changes every day.

Worked example

Market value is ₹10,000 crore and book value ₹2,000 crore, so the gap is ₹8,000 crore.

If the share price then falls by 20 per cent, market value becomes ₹8,000 crore and the gap becomes ₹6,000 crore, although nothing inside the firm has changed.

Exam focus. Conclude any answer on knowledge companies with the notes' line: they must be valued from cash flows rather than from the gap between market and book value.
slides.plain: Why the residual method is unreliable. The residual method treats market value minus book value as the value of intellectual capital, but that gap moves with market mood, not with the firm's IC. Value of IC (residual method) = Market value − Book value The whole gap is credited to intellectual capital, which is the source of the problem. The method is unreliable because the gap: includes market mood and growth expectations ; ignores undervalued tangible assets and hidden liabilities , which also sit inside the gap; and changes every day . slides.title: Part Two in brief: protection to option models
slides.html:
Choose the right protection, sort the portfolio, evaluate before valuing, and use each further tool (index, empirical model, option model) for the job it does.

  1. Protection strategy chooses among patents, designs, marks, copyright and trade secrets according to visibility, life, cost and enforceability, and Granstrand's four situations explain when secrecy is better: large lead, hard to discover, infringement hard to detect, easy to invent around.
  2. Portfolios are categorised from business, technical and legal perspectives and managed through a matrix of crown jewels, weak core, licensing candidates and assets to drop.
  3. Evaluation judges quality before valuation fixes money value by the cost, market or income approach.
  4. An IP value index such as the Patent Asset Index ranks portfolios but does not price them.
  5. Empirical models show that patent values are highly uneven.
  6. Option models value the flexibility a patent gives.

slides.title: Answer plans: protection strategy and categorisation
slides.html:
Open each answer with a definition, build through the notes' lists in order, cite the Patents Act and Contract Act provisions, and close with a clear strategic conclusion.

Q1. Explain IP protection strategy and the choice between patent and trade secret.

  1. Define protection strategy: deciding which right to use, when, where and how much, so IP supports the business at the lowest total cost and risk.
  2. Set out the menu of rights with terms: patent (Patents Act, 1970, 20 years), design (10 + 5 years), trade mark (10-year renewals without limit), copyright (life plus 60 years), GIs, layout designs, plant varieties, and trade secrets (no statute; contracts and duty of confidence).
  3. List the factors behind the choice and cite s. 3(d) and s. 3(k), using the software example.
  4. Compare patent and trade secret in a table: disclosure, duration, independent discovery and reverse engineering.
  5. Give Granstrand's four situations favouring secrecy, the weakness of secret protection and the Indian measures, citing s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872.
  6. Add multi protection, defensive publication and timing: file before disclosure; Paris priority of 12 and 6 months; PCT at 31 months; s. 39.
  7. Conclude: the choice is rarely either/or; the best strategy combines rights, keeps secrets only where Granstrand's situations apply and files where the firm sells, manufactures and competes.

Q2. Explain IP categorisation and the portfolio matrix.

  1. Define the purpose: categorisation turns a list of registrations into information for decisions (what matters, what only costs, legal risks, action needed).
  2. Explain the business perspective, including the using / will use / will not use practice.
  3. Explain the technical perspective (IPC or CPC classes, product or process, basic invention or improvement, maturity).
  4. Explain the legal perspective (status, term, ownership, licences, strength), stressing joint ownership under s. 50.
  5. Draw the 2 × 2 matrix of business value against legal strength: crown jewels, weak core, licensing or sale, drop, with the action for each.
  6. Describe the review cycle (list, score with business, technical and legal input, decide, repeat before renewal fees) and the renewal test; note that abandonment may free the technology and restoration is limited by s. 60.
  7. Conclude: avoid depending on a single patent, licensee or market; categorisation turns the portfolio from a cost into a managed asset.

slides.title: Answer plans: valuation approaches and models
slides.html:
Valuation answers score on the distinction drawn first, the approaches set out in a table, and at least one worked figure from the notes.

Q3. Distinguish evaluation and valuation and explain the main valuation approaches.

  1. Define both: evaluation judges quality through scores for portfolio decisions; valuation fixes a money value for a stated purpose and date. Evaluation comes first.
  2. List the evaluation factors: legal, technical, commercial, strategic and risk.
  3. Give the purposes and legal bases: Companies Act, 2013, s. 247; Income Tax Act, 2025, ss. 161 to 173; Ind AS 103, 36 and 113; insolvency values; ICAI VS 302.
  4. Explain the cost approach (replacement less obsolescence; cost is not value) and the market approach (comparables; rare and confidential).
  5. Explain the income approach and its five methods: DCF, relief from royalty, excess earnings, with and without, and premium profit.
  6. Match the method to the situation (early patent, established brand, core technology, non compete, licence negotiation) and list the value drivers.
  7. Conclude with the steps of a sound valuation: purpose, basis and date; rights; evaluation; data; at least two methods; sensitivity; stated assumptions.

Q4. Explain the IP value index, empirical models and option based models.

  1. Introduce them as complements to the three approaches: an index ranks, empirical models benchmark, and option models value flexibility.
  2. IP value index: a single quality score, not a price; no statutory index in India; indicators such as forward citations, family size and claims.
  3. Patent Asset Index: Competitive Impact = Technology Relevance × Market Coverage; the A (4.83) against B (2.0) example; other indices; the steps of building one; its limits.
  4. Empirical models: Granstrand's caution; the market value model V = q × (A + γK); renewal, citation, survey, event and transaction models; uses and limits.
  5. Option models: the right but not the obligation; why DCF undervalues; the S, K, T, σ and r analogy; renewal fees as options.
  6. Work the numbers: Black and Scholes 28.11 against an NPV of −20; binomial 14.82; decision tree flexibility 18.18.
  7. Conclude with the limits of option models (imperfect analogy, uncertainty hard to estimate, inventing around, revocation) and with the point that no single tool is enough.

For IC and knowledge questions, define the key distinction first, then move from frameworks to practical systems, and end on the legal limits in India.

Q5. Explain how intellectual capital is measured and monitored.

  1. Distinguish measuring (a picture at one point in time) from monitoring (regular tracking through indicators and targets so management can act early).
  2. Classify indicators: inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes, with the notes' examples; then leading against lagging.
  3. Give the indicators for human, structural, innovation and relational capital.
  4. Set out the steps of a monitoring system, from strategy to regular review, and describe the Danish model IC statement.
  5. Discuss the problems: poor data, weak comparability, assumed causation and gaming (weak patents filed to raise counts).
  6. Show tailoring: start ups, established firms, universities and service firms.
  7. Conclude: a few clear indicators tied to strategy, watched for gaming.

Q6. Explain the role of knowledge assets in competitive advantage and product development.

  1. Define data, information and knowledge, then knowledge assets; contrast tacit and explicit knowledge and list the properties of knowledge.
  2. Explain Arrow's information paradox and why patents and confidentiality agreements matter.
  3. Explain advantage through VRIN (Barney), core competencies (Prahalad and Hamel), dynamic capabilities (Teece) and absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal).
  4. Describe knowledge management and the four SECI modes (Nonaka and Takeuchi).
  5. Cover legal protection: IP, secrecy policies, NDAs and employment clauses; Granstrand on Japanese firms; s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872 and retention measures; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
  6. Move to product development: platforms and standard components; the IP action at each stage from idea to after launch.
  7. Add Granstrand's guidance (speed to patent, patent maps, Toshiba) and the Indian points (novelty, s. 3(d), s. 3(k), s. 39, s. 50).
  8. Conclude: knowledge creates advantage only when it is managed and protected at every stage.

Q7. Explain patent stocks and copyright collective management in India.

slides.title: Invention, innovation and diffusion
slides.html:
An invention is a new idea; it becomes an innovation only when it succeeds in the market, and diffusion is how it then spreads among users.

Invention
a new idea or device.
Innovation
the successful introduction of a new or improved product, process, service or business model into the market.
Diffusion
the spread of an innovation among users.

The three stages matter because value arrives late. An invention earns nothing until it is introduced into the market and adopted, so IP management has to follow the idea from the laboratory all the way to the customer.

Schumpeter described innovation as "new combinations" of goods, methods, markets, sources of supply and forms of organisation. He called the result "creative destruction", in which new products and firms replace old ones. Innovation is therefore an opportunity for entrants and a threat to incumbents at the same time.

Innovation may be classified in four ways:

Classified byTypes
Objectproduct, process, service, business model or organisation
Degreeincremental or radical
Market effectsustaining or disruptive
ArchitectureHenderson and Clark's four types (next slide)

Remember: four lenses, O-D-M-A: Object, Degree, Market effect, Architecture.

slides.title: Henderson and Clark, and where innovation comes from
slides.html:
Henderson and Clark sort innovation by two questions: are the core ideas replaced, and are the links between components changed?

TypeCore ideasLinks between components

Modularreplacedunchanged
Architecturalkeptchanged
Radicalchangedchanged

Read the table as a 2 × 2 grid: change neither, change only the core ideas, change only the links, or change both. Answering the two questions places any example in one box.

Innovation arises from two forces:

Technology push

New science creates products, and a market is then found for them.

Market pull

Customer needs drive development.

Does market power help or hurt innovation? The two classic views conflict:

ViewClaim
Schumpeterlarge firms with market power innovate more
Arrowcompetition gives stronger incentives
In practicethe relationship varies by industry

Exam focus. Present both views and then say that the relationship varies by industry; a one-sided answer loses marks.

slides.title: Diffusion, S curves and dominant designs
slides.html:
Innovations spread through adopter groups, improve along an S curve and settle on a dominant design, after which competition shifts to price and process.

Rogers explains diffusion through five adopter groups, which together make up the whole market:

Adopter groupShare of adopters
Innovators2.5 per cent
Early adopters13.5 per cent
Early majority34 per cent
Late majority34 per cent
Laggards16 per cent

A technology usually follows an S curve: it improves slowly, then rapidly, then levels off. Markets often settle on a dominant design, after which competition shifts to price and process, because the product itself is no longer the battleground.

In networked markets, products become more valuable as more people use them, and patents included in standards earn royalties from all implementers. That is why a place in a standard is so valuable to a patent owner.

Granstrand adds two lessons for incumbents. Firms strong in an old technology are often slow to build patent positions in a new one, which gives entrants an opening. And old technologies may improve under threat, the "sailing ship effect".

Remember: Rogers' five groups run 2.5 – 13.5 – 34 – 34 – 16, which add up to 100.

slides.title: IP as the link between innovation and market
slides.html:
IP links innovation to the market, and on Granstrand's strategy ladder IP strategy sits below business strategy, so IP choices should follow business choices.

IP does four jobs for an innovator:

Capture returns

It allows innovators to capture returns from what they create.

Trade

It makes technology tradeable through licences and assignments.

Signal

It signals capability to investors.

Finance

It supports financing.

Granstrand places IP strategy on a "strategy ladder" below the firm's business, innovation, technology and commercialisation strategies. Read from the top:

  1. Business strategy
  2. Innovation strategy
  3. Technology strategy
  4. Commercialisation strategy
  5. IP strategy

Each rung serves the one above it, which means that IP choices should follow business choices. A filing decision should start with the question: which business aim does this right serve?

Exam focus. Close any answer on innovation and IP with the strategy ladder. It shows the examiner that you treat IP as a business tool, not an end in itself.

slides.title: What makes an innovation radical
slides.html:
A radical innovation is a major technical change that creates a new technology base, a large jump in performance or an entirely new market.

A radical innovation replaces the old technology base rather than improving it. Two examples from the notes:

Transistors

Transistors replaced vacuum tubes.

Digital mobile

Digital technology replaced analogue mobile telephony.

Its features follow from the size of the jump:

  1. high uncertainty and cost
  2. long development
  3. the obsolescence of existing skills
  4. frequent entry by newcomers
  5. it often creates new industries

Because development is long and uncertain, radical projects need patient finance such as venture capital, government grants or staged corporate investment. Investors must wait years for returns, and staging lets them stop if the technology fails.

Radical projects face four main risks: technical failure, slow adoption, lack of complementary assets and regulatory delay.

Exam focus. Link the features to newcomers: because existing skills become obsolete, incumbents lose their advantage, which is why newcomers enter so often.

slides.title: IP strategy for radical innovation
slides.html:
A radical innovator should file early with broad claims, secure strategic patents and then win the second race for surrounding patents.

  1. File early with broad claims, so that the pioneer position is secured before rivals arrive.
  2. Seek strategic patents that rivals cannot easily invent around.
  3. Quickly file follow up patents, because Granstrand describes a second race for surrounding patents around a key patent.

Breadth has a price. Broad claims attract opposition and revocation attempts, so drafting must withstand the inventive step requirement in s. 2(1)(ja) of the Patents Act. A claim drawn too wide can be lost entirely.

Patents are not the only tool:

ToolWhat it protects in a radical innovation
Pioneer and strategic patentsthe core technology
Follow up (surrounding) patentsthe ground around the key patent
Trade secretsthe processes
Trade marksthe new brand

Exam focus. If asked why radical innovators file broad claims, give both sides: breadth blocks rivals, but it invites opposition and revocation under the inventive step test of s. 2(1)(ja).

slides.title: How disruption works
slides.html:
Disruption, as Christensen explains it, is a process by which a smaller firm with fewer resources successfully challenges established firms.

Disruptive innovation is a process, not a product. It unfolds in stages:

  1. Established firms improve their products for their most demanding and profitable customers, which is sustaining innovation, and in doing so overshoot the needs of other customers.
  2. The entrant starts either at the low end, serving customers the leaders neglect, or in a new market, serving people who were not buying at all.
  3. It offers a simpler, cheaper or more convenient product that is "good enough".
  4. It then improves and moves into the main market.
  5. Disruption is complete when mainstream customers adopt it.
EntrantEstablished firms it challenged
Steel minimillsintegrated mills
Personal computersminicomputers
Netflixvideo rental chains

The test is where the entrant starts. Christensen and his co authors argue that Uber was not disruptive, because it began in the main market with a better service.

Remember: two footholds only: the low end (neglected customers) or a new market (people not buying at all).

slides.title: Disruption, novelty and IP
slides.html:
A disruptive product is usually worse at first but cheaper or easier to use, so disrupters rely more on business model, speed and network effects than on patents.

Disruption should not be confused with mere technical novelty. A disruptive product is usually worse at first on conventional measures but cheaper or easier to use, and leaders ignore it because its margins are low.

s. 3(k), Patents Act. Business methods as such are not patentable in India.

This shapes the IP position of both sides:

DisrupterIncumbent
Relies onbusiness models, speed and network effectspatent portfolios built for sustaining innovation
IP protectioncopyright in software, trade secrets, brands and contractsits portfolio may not block a new business model
What it must dorely on speed, since business methods as such are not patentable (s. 3(k))watch low end and new market entrants, create separate units, or invest in or acquire the newcomers

Exam focus. Explain why patents matter less here: s. 3(k) closes the patent route for business methods, so the disrupter's advantage lies in its model and speed, protected by copyright, secrets, brands and contracts.

slides.title: Sustaining versus sustainable innovation
slides.html:
The syllabus term may mean sustaining innovation (Christensen) or environmentally sustainable innovation; state your meaning, and beside the other three types, sustaining is the likely one.

Exam focus. An answer should state which meaning it uses. Beside radical, disruptive and incremental innovation, sustaining innovation is the likely meaning; environmentally sustainable innovation is the alternative.

Sustaining innovation improves existing products for existing customers, whether by small steps or major breakthroughs. Established firms usually win these contests because they have the resources and motivation: the customers being served are already theirs.

Sustainable (green) innovation reduces environmental harm through cleaner energy, recycling or low emission processes. It is driven by regulation, consumers, cost savings and investors.

SustainingSustainable (green)
Meaningimproves existing products for existing customersreduces environmental harm
Who drives or wins itestablished firms usually winregulation, consumers, cost savings and investors
IP strategycontinuous follow up patenting, large portfolios, cross licensing, protection of designs and brandsIP questions concern diffusion: green patents attract investment, and wide licensing can spread clean technology
Channelsthe leader's own portfolioplatforms such as WIPO GREEN connect owners and users; technology transfer to developing countries takes place through licences and partnerships

Notice the different question IP answers. For sustaining innovation, IP strengthens the leader; for green innovation, the issue is how IP can help clean technology spread.

slides.title: Incremental innovation and its legal limits
slides.html:
Incremental innovation is small, continuous improvement; firms protect it by continuous patenting, but Indian law refuses protection to obvious or minor changes.

Incremental innovation consists of small, continuous improvements to existing products or processes, such as better features, lower cost or higher quality. It is low in risk, builds on existing knowledge and keeps firms competitive.

Granstrand shows that firms protect incremental innovation through continuous patenting throughout the product life. Minor patents, which engineers sometimes dismiss as "petty" or "junk", can still be valuable as bargaining chips, although too many weak patents waste money.

Firms also use other tools:

  1. fencing and surrounding strategies
  2. registered designs for changes in appearance
  3. secrecy for process improvements

Indian law sets four limits:

  1. obvious changes fail the inventive step test;
  2. s. 3(d) requires enhanced efficacy for new forms of known substances;
  3. India has no utility model or petty patent system;
  4. the law guards against "evergreening", meaning the extension of protection through minor changes.

Exam focus. Connect the limits to the strategy: since there is no petty patent in India and minor changes face the inventive step test and s. 3(d), firms lean on designs and secrecy alongside patents for small improvements.

Disruptivea simple, cheap, good enough offeringnewcomers displace leadersbusiness model and speed

slides.part: 3.6 Open Innovation and Its Principal Models
slides.title: Closed versus open innovation
slides.html:
Open innovation, Chesbrough's term, means using ideas from outside the firm as well as inside, and external as well as internal routes to market.

Open innovation is easiest to understand against the model it replaced. Each assumption of closed innovation is reversed:

QuestionClosed innovation assumesOpen innovation assumes
Where are the capable people?the best people work for the firmmany capable people work elsewhere
Who does the R&D?the firm must invent, develop and sell everything itselfexternal R&D can create value
What wins?being first to marketa better business model matters more than being first
What is IP for?IP should be controlled so that nobody else profitsearn from others' use of the firm's IP, and buy others' IP when it helps the business

The last row is the one that matters for IP management. In the closed model IP is only a fence; in the open model it is also a product to sell and an input to buy.

Exam focus. Define open innovation with both halves: outside ideas coming in, and external routes to market going out. Many answers give only the first half.

slides.part: 3.6 Open Innovation and Its Principal Models
slides.title: Inbound, outbound and coupled models
slides.html:
Gassmann and Enkel identify three models of open innovation: bringing knowledge in, taking ideas out, and creating knowledge jointly with partners.

Inbound (outside-in)

The firm brings in external knowledge through licensing in, acquiring start ups, crowdsourcing and working with suppliers and users.

Outbound (inside-out)

It takes internal ideas out through licensing, sale of IP and spin offs.

Coupled

It creates knowledge jointly with partners through alliances, consortia and joint development.

Common forms include collaborative research, university and industry projects, corporate venture capital, open source development, innovation contests and ecosystems built around platforms.

The idea is older than the label. Granstrand's earlier work already classified the ways firms acquire and exploit technology:

Ways listed by Granstrand
Acquire technologyown R&D, buying firms, joint ventures, buying technology and scanning
Exploit technologyown use, new units, joint ventures and selling or licensing technology

Remember: inbound = licensing in; outbound = licensing out; coupled = creating together.

slides.part: 3.6 Open Innovation and Its Principal Models
slides.title: Sharing modes, benefits and risks
slides.html:
Partners can share knowledge in four ways, from open to all to closed, and the benefits of open innovation come with real risks of losing control.

Bogers, Bekkers and Granstrand describe four ways of sharing knowledge within a collaboration:

  1. open to all;
  2. open within the group only;
  3. layered: full sharing among core members and limited sharing with outer members;
  4. closed.

Benefits

More ideas, lower cost and risk, faster launch, and income from unused IP.

Risks

Loss of control, leakage of knowledge, the "not invented here" attitude, coordination costs and disputes over ownership.

Look at the risks closely: leakage, loss of control and ownership disputes are all problems of unclear rights. That is why the next topic, open innovation and IP, is about writing those rights down before the collaboration begins.

slides.title: Why IP makes openness possible
slides.html:
Open innovation seems to conflict with IP, but clear ownership is what lets firms disclose knowledge safely and license it on agreed terms.

The apparent conflict is real: firms must share knowledge to collaborate but must protect it to profit. In fact IP makes openness possible, because clear ownership allows firms to disclose knowledge safely and to license it on agreed terms.

Every collaboration should identify four kinds of knowledge:

Background IP
brought in by each party.
Foreground IP
created in the project.
Sideground IP
developed in house in parallel with the project.
Postground IP
developed after the project ends.

Remember: Before, During, Beside, After = background, foreground, sideground, postground.

The collaboration agreement must then settle:

  1. the use of background IP;
  2. the ownership of foreground IP (sole or joint);
  3. access rights during and after the project;
  4. rights in improvements and any grant back;
  5. confidentiality;
  6. publication rights (important for universities);
  7. licensing terms and data rights;
  8. decision making, dispute resolution and exit.

slides.title: Licences as the building blocks
slides.html:
Licences are the building blocks of collaboration, and the first question about any licence is exclusivity: who besides the licensee may use the IP?

LicenceCan the licensor use it?Can others be licensed?
Exclusiveno: it excludes even the licensorno
Soleyes: only the licensor and licensee use itno
Non-exclusiveyesyes: many licensees

Firms also use cross licences, sublicences, blanket licences covering future developments, package licences, grant backs and patent pools.

Software adds a special risk, because open source code often sits inside a product. Two families of open source licence matter:

PermissiveCopyleft
ExamplesMIT, BSD and Apachethe GPL
Effectallow use in closed productsrequire modified versions to remain open

Because one copyleft component can oblige a firm to keep its modified code open, firms must track the open source code they use.

Exam focus. Exclusive versus sole is a favourite trap. Under a sole licence the licensor can still use the IP; under an exclusive licence even the licensor cannot.

slides.title: Indian law on collaboration and licensing
slides.html:
Indian law shapes open innovation through the joint ownership rule, licence formalities, void restrictive conditions and the competition law exemption for reasonable conditions.

ProvisionRuleWhat the agreement must do
Patents Act, s. 50a joint owner of a patent cannot license it or assign a share without the consent of the other ownersdeal with joint ownership expressly
Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69patent licences must be in writing and registeredbe written and registered
Patents Act, s. 140certain restrictive conditions in patent licences are void: tying arrangements, exclusive grant backs, bars on challenging validity and coercive package licensingleave these conditions out
Competition Act, 2002, s. 3(5)(i)protects only reasonable conditions needed to protect IP rightskeep every restraint reasonable

Joint ownership is the usual result of a coupled project, which is why s. 50 matters so much: without an agreement, neither co-owner can license the foreground IP alone.

India has no statute equivalent to the United States Bayh-Dole Act on publicly funded research, so universities and research institutions rely on their own IP policies and contracts.

Exam focus. In an answer on open innovation, the Indian law paragraph lifts the grade: cite s. 50 for joint ownership of foreground IP, s. 140 for grant backs and s. 3(5)(i) for the competition limit.

slides.part: 3.8 Patent Databases as a Source of IP Management Information
slides.title: Patent documents as a source of knowledge
slides.html:
Patent documents disclose technology in a standard format, often before it appears anywhere else, which makes them a unique source of management information.

Granstrand calls patent information a "tremendous and unique source of technical knowledge". He found that learning from patent documents was the most important method of tracking others' technology in large Japanese firms.

Two features explain this value. The format is standard, so documents can be searched and compared; and disclosure often comes before the technology appears anywhere else.

Knowing the parts of a patent document tells you where to look:

PartWhat it contains
Bibliographic datanumbers, dates, owners, inventors and classification
Abstract and descriptionthe technology disclosed
Claimsdefine the legal scope
Citationsthe documents cited, used in citation analysis
Family informationthe related filings that make up the patent family
Legal statuswhether the right is alive, lapsed or challenged

Exam focus. Only the claims define the legal scope. When a question asks what a competitor's patent actually protects, the answer lies in its claims, not in the description.

Patent documents disclose technology in a standard format, often before it appears anywhere else, which makes them a unique source of management information. Granstrand calls patent information a "tremendous and unique source of technical knowledge" . He found that learning from patent documents was the most important method of tracking others' technology in large Japanese firms. Two features explain this value. The format is standard, so documents can be searched and compared; and disclosure often comes before the technology appears anywhere else. Knowing the parts of a patent document tells you where to look: Part What it contains Bibliographic data numbers, dates, owners, inventors and classification Abstract and description the technology disclosed Claims define the legal scope Citations the documents cited, used in citation analysis Family information the related filings that make up the patent family Legal status whether the right is alive, lapsed or challenged Exam focus. Only the claims define the legal scope. When a question asks what a competitor's patent actually protects, the answer lies in its claims, not in the description.

slides.part: 3.8 Patent Databases as a Source of IP Management Information
slides.title: Uses of patent databases and how to search them
slides.html:
Patent databases support decisions from filing to acquisition, and good searches combine codes, keywords and names, then confirm legal status on the official register.

For IP management, patent databases support:

  1. prior art searches before filing, and patentability assessment;
  2. technology landscaping;
  3. competitor intelligence and monitoring;
  4. freedom to operate checks;
  5. identification of licensees, partners and acquisition targets;
  6. discovery of expired patents that are free to use;
  7. analysis of patent families and legal status, and citation analysis;
  8. trend analysis and portfolio benchmarking.

EspacenetEuropean Patent Office
PATENTSCOPEWIPO

Google Patents and The Lensfree services
analytics databasespaid services

Searches combine classification codes (IPC and CPC), keywords joined by AND, OR and NOT, applicant and inventor names, number searches, family searches, citation searches and date limits. Legal status should always be confirmed on the official register.

slides.part: 3.8 Patent Databases as a Source of IP Management Information
slides.title: Five searches, patent maps and pitfalls
slides.html:
Each purpose calls for its own search, results can be turned into patent maps, and database limits mean raw results must always be read with care.

SearchQuestion it asks
Novelty or patentability searchcan the invention be patented?
Freedom to operate searchdoes a product infringe live patents?
Validity searchcan a patent be revoked?
Landscape searchwho is active in a field?
Due diligence searchwhat are the ownership, status and risk in a transaction?

Patent mapping turns results into charts of technologies, owners, trends and gaps. Granstrand notes that it began at the Japan Patent Office, which published its first patent map in 1968.

Users must remember the pitfalls:

  1. coverage and data quality differ between databases;
  2. machine translations can mislead;
  3. applications are published only after about 18 months, so the newest filings cannot be seen;
  4. company names vary;
  5. legal status data may be outdated;
  6. raw counts can mislead.

Exam focus. Match the search to the purpose: novelty and validity look for prior art, freedom to operate looks for live patents a product might infringe, and due diligence looks at ownership, status and risk.

slides.title: What IP due diligence asks
slides.html:
IP due diligence is a careful legal and commercial investigation of IP before a transaction, built around four questions: own, valid, free and worth.

IP due diligence is a careful legal and commercial investigation of IP before a transaction. It answers four questions:

  1. Ownership: does the target own or validly control the IP?
  2. Validity: is the IP valid and enforceable?
  3. Freedom: is the business free to operate without infringing others' rights?
  4. Worth: what is the IP worth after taking risks into account?

Remember: Own it? Valid? Free? Worth? (O-V-F-W)

It is carried out in mergers and acquisitions, investments, licensing, technology transfer, joint ventures, loans, purchases of distressed assets in insolvency and start up funding.

The timing is the point: it is done before the deal, while a defect in title or validity can still change the price and the contract terms.

slides.title: The due diligence process
slides.html:
Due diligence runs from planning to a risk report; its findings are then written into the deal, and the transfers are registered after completion.

  1. Plan the scope and team.
  2. Send a questionnaire and document request.
  3. Review documents in a data room.
  4. Run independent searches of official registers and charge records.
  5. Interview managers and inventors.
  6. Analyse and report on risks.
  7. Reflect the findings in the deal through price adjustment, warranties, indemnities, conditions to be met before completion and escrow.
  8. After completion, register the transfers.

Why independent searches? The target's own documents show what it believes it owns; official registers and charge records show what the law recognises, including charges the target may not mention.

Each deal tool moves a risk found back to the seller, either through the price or through promises and money held back. The final registration matters because the buyer's title is only secure once the transfer is on the register.

Exam focus. Students often stop at "report". The marks are in step 7: say how each finding is reflected in the deal.

slides.title: Title, status, encumbrances and contracts
slides.html:
The core of the investigation is title: a chain of written, registered assignments from every inventor and earlier owner, free of undisclosed charges.

Chain of title requires written and registered assignments from inventors and earlier owners. Each statute has its own rule:

RightProvision on assignment
PatentsPatents Act, ss. 68 and 69
CopyrightCopyright Act, s. 19
Trade marksTrade Marks Act, s. 45

The investigation checks registration and renewal status, including filing of Form 27, and searches for encumbrances such as charges registered under s. 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 and security interests filed with CERSAI.

It then reviews contracts:

  1. licences given and taken, especially exclusivity and change of control clauses;
  2. IP and confidentiality clauses in employment and consultancy contracts, because consultants own their work unless they assign it;
  3. trade secret protection;
  4. open source licences.

Exam focus. Change of control is the hidden deal-breaker: a licence that ends when the target is acquired may remove the very IP the buyer is paying for.

slides.title: Wider risks, and how due diligence differs
slides.html:
Due diligence also tests disputes, freedom to operate, validity, tax and dependence risks, and it must be distinguished from an audit, a valuation, a legal opinion and FTO analysis.

Disputes and validity: infringement notices, pending disputes and oppositions, freedom to operate, territorial coverage and validity risks such as prior art and the exclusions in s. 3.

Wider checks: tax (withholding on royalties, GST and transfer pricing), competition law, personal data and security, dependence on one licence or customer, the link between revenue and IP, and integration after the deal.

ExerciseWhat it is
IP due diligencean investigation tied to a particular transaction
IP auditan internal and regular review, not tied to a deal
Valuationproduces a money figure
Legal opinionanswers a specific legal question
Freedom to operate analysisexamines infringement risk for a particular product

Exam focus. When asked to distinguish, use this table and stress that only due diligence is tied to a deal; an audit is regular, a valuation is a number, an opinion answers one question and an FTO analysis concerns one product.

slides.title: Licence or assignment, and what to settle first
slides.html:
A licence permits acts that would otherwise infringe while ownership stays with the licensor; an assignment transfers ownership itself.

A licence is permission from the owner (the licensor) to another person (the licensee) to do acts that would otherwise infringe the owner's IP, on agreed terms.

LicenceAssignment
What passespermission to do acts that would otherwise infringeownership
Who owns afterwardsthe licensorthe person to whom it is assigned

Before drafting, the parties must work through a checklist. It runs from purpose to exit:

  1. be clear about their business aims;
  2. complete due diligence on title, validity and freedom to operate;
  3. agree the value and royalty;
  4. define the scope of the grant;
  5. satisfy legal formalities;
  6. respect competition law;
  7. plan for tax and foreign exchange;
  8. arrange regulatory approvals;
  9. provide for quality control;
  10. plan the exit.

Remember: begin with the aims, end with the exit: the ten checks run from why the deal exists to how it will end.

slides.title: Indian legal requirements for licences
slides.html:
Each IP statute sets its own licence formalities, and every licence remains subject to competition law and to tax on royalties.

RightRequirement
Patentmust be in writing and registered (Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69)
Patent held jointlya joint owner cannot license without the consent of the others (s. 50)
Patentthe restrictive conditions listed in s. 140 are void
Copyrightmust be in writing (Copyright Act, s. 30)
Copyrightunder s. 30A the requirements of s. 19 apply, so the licence should identify the work, the rights, the duration, the territory and the royalty
Trade markmust preserve the licensor's control over quality, so that the mark continues to indicate a single trade source

Why quality control for trade marks? A mark tells the public that goods come from one trade source. If licensees could sell goods without the licensor's control over quality, the mark would stop doing that job.

Licence terms are also subject to s. 3(5)(i) of the Competition Act, 2002. Royalty payments attract tax deduction at source, GST at 18 per cent and treaty relief for cross border payments (see 3.18).

slides.title: Structuring the royalty
slides.html:
Royalties can take many shapes, from one lump sum to running percentages, and every running royalty depends on a carefully defined net sales base.

StructureHow it works
Lump suma single fixed payment
Running royaltya percentage of net sales, or an amount per unit
Upfront fee with running royaltya payment on signing combined with a running royalty
Minimum annual royaltya floor the licensee pays each year
Milestone paymentspaid as stages are reached
Step down ratesa rate that steps down over the life of the licence
Equity or a cross licenceconsideration given in shares or in rights

Net sales must be defined carefully. A running royalty is only as good as its base: every deduction allowed from the sales figure reduces what the licensor receives.

The choice between a lump sum and a running royalty is a valuation question, worked through in 3.12 Example 2. There, a running royalty worth ₹5.62 crore beats a ₹6 crore lump sum that is worth only ₹4.5 crore after tax.

Exam focus. Exclusivity is usually paired with a minimum royalty: a licensor who gives up every other licensee needs a guaranteed income from the one it keeps.

slides.title: Grant, financial and operational clauses
slides.html:
A licence agreement is built from clause families; the first three say what is granted, what is paid and how the licence is run.

The agreement opens by identifying the parties and their affiliates and defining the licensed patents, products, net sales, territory and field.

FamilyWhat it contains
Grant clausesthe licensed rights; confirmation of the licensor's ownership; the scope (make, use, sell or import); the type of exclusivity; the territory; the field of use; the duration; any right to sublicense
Financial clausesthe consideration; royalty rate and base; minimum guarantees; milestones; reports, records and audit rights; the allocation of taxes, including deduction at source and grossing up
Operational clausesquality control; technical assistance; regulatory approvals; registration of the licence

Why audit rights? The licensee calculates a running royalty itself, so the licensor needs reports, records and the right to check them. A grossing up clause decides who bears the tax deducted at source.

Remember: six families in order, "Good Financial Operations Invite Risky Exits": Grant, Financial, Operational, IP, Risk, Exit and legal.

slides.title: IP, risk and exit clauses, and how they interlock
slides.html:
The last three families decide who owns new IP, who bears the risks and how the licence ends, and every clause must be read with the others.

FamilyWhat it contains
IP clauseswho owns improvements and new IP, avoiding exclusive grant backs; protection of confidential know how
Risk clausesrepresentations; warranties on title (validity is usually not warranted); indemnities; who sues infringers and who defends claims against the licensee
Exit and legal clausestermination for breach, non payment or insolvency; the consequences of termination (stopping use, selling off stock, returning materials and dealing with sublicences); dispute resolution; governing law; cross border issues such as foreign exchange and withholding tax; force majeure; assignment and change of control; data, software and source code escrow

Exclusive grant backs are avoided because s. 140 makes them void in patent licences (3.7). The clauses also work together:

  1. exclusivity is usually paired with a minimum royalty;
  2. field and territory limits must match the improvement clauses;
  3. termination must address sublicences and stock;
  4. warranties and indemnities must be read together.

Exam focus. Note the asymmetry in the risk clauses: the licensor warrants title, but validity is usually not warranted.

slides.title: Why IP is valued, and five terms to keep apart
slides.html:
IP is valued for many purposes, and a good answer keeps value, price, consideration, carrying amount and collateral value strictly apart.

IP valuation is used in licensing, sale and purchase, investment, financial reporting, taxation, damages, insolvency, portfolio decisions and lending. Because the purpose changes the figure, several related terms must be kept apart:

Value
an estimate of worth for a purpose and date.
Price
the amount actually agreed.
Consideration
what is actually given: cash, shares or a cross licence.
Carrying amount
the figure in the accounts.
Collateral value
a lender's careful estimate of what it could recover on default.

An illustration from the notes shows how far apart they can be. In 3.16, a technology valued at ₹3.63 crore has a distressed value of only ₹1.81 crore to a lender, and supports a loan of about ₹0.91 crore.

Exam focus. Value is an estimate and price is a fact. Always say whose value, for what purpose and at what date.

slides.title: Three lives of an IP right
slides.html:
An IP right has a legal life, an economic life and a useful life, and the economic life, which drives value, is usually shorter than the legal life.

LifeMeaning
Legal lifethe term of protection
Economic lifethe period during which it earns income; usually shorter
Useful lifethe accounting estimate used for amortisation

Economic life is shortened by five forces:

  1. new technology
  2. slow market adoption
  3. weak enforcement
  4. competition
  5. regulation

Because nobody knows exactly how long the income will last, valuers handle the uncertainty through scenarios, sensitivity analysis, probability weighting, simulation and real options. Example 2 in 3.12 is a sensitivity analysis, and Example 3 is probability weighting.

Exam focus. Never value a patent over its legal life automatically. Income usually stops earlier, and a patent with a fixed term should not be given a terminal value (3.12).

slides.title: How IP is financed
slides.html:
IP can raise money directly: as security for loans, through sale or securitisation of royalties, by sale and licence back, and with government risk-sharing.

RouteHow it works
Loans secured on IPthe lender takes security over the IP (see 3.16)
Sale of future royaltiesinvestors buy the right to the royalty stream
Securitisation of royalty streamsbonds backed by royalties; an early example was bonds backed by David Bowie's music royalties in 1997
Sale and licence backthe owner sells the IP and takes a licence back, so it keeps using it
Venture debt and equityinvestors lend to or invest in the IP-rich firm
Government schemesthe state shares lenders' risks, such as Singapore's IP financing scheme

Every route depends on the same thing: a credible value and a clear title. That is why valuation (3.12 to 3.14), patent stocks (3.15) and due diligence (3.9) all feed into finance.

slides.title: Discounting, NPV, IRR and terminal value
slides.html:
Money today is worth more than the same amount later, so future cash flows are discounted to present value; a project or licence is worthwhile if its NPV is positive.

PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)t

Divide a future amount (FV) received in year t by one plus the discount rate r, raised to the power t. The further away the cash, the smaller its present value.

NPV = Σ [CFt ÷ (1 + r)t] minus initial investment

Discount each year's cash flow, add them up and subtract what is spent now. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the rate demands.

Internal rate of return (IRR)
the discount rate at which NPV is zero.
Terminal value
for an asset with no fixed end, the next year's cash flow divided by (r minus g), where g is the long term growth rate.

Terminal value = next year's cash flow ÷ (r − g)

It captures all income after the forecast years for an asset that never expires.

Exam focus. A patent with a fixed term should not be given a terminal value: its income stops when protection ends.

slides.title: Choosing the discount rate: CAPM and WACC
slides.html:
The discount rate is usually based on CAPM or WACC, with an extra premium for IP risks such as invalidity and obsolescence.

Cost of equity (CAPM) = risk free rate + beta × market risk premium

The CAPM adds to the risk free rate a premium scaled by beta, the asset's sensitivity to the market.

WACC = (equity weight × cost of equity) + (debt weight × after tax cost of debt)

The WACC is the weighted average of the cost of equity and the after tax cost of debt.

For IP, add an extra premium for IP risks such as invalidity and obsolescence, because a patent can be revoked or overtaken in ways that ordinary business assets cannot.

Worked example: the notes' WACC

Inputs: a risk free rate of 7 per cent, beta of 1.3 and a market premium of 7 per cent; 60 per cent equity and 40 per cent debt at 10 per cent before 25 per cent tax.

Step 1, cost of equity: 7 + 1.3 × 7 = 7 + 9.1 = 16.1 per cent.

Step 2, after tax cost of debt: 10 × (1 − 0.25) = 7.5 per cent.

Step 3, WACC: 0.6 × 16.1 + 0.4 × 7.5 = 9.66 + 3.00 = 12.66 per cent.

WACC = (equity weight × cost of equity) + (debt weight × after tax cost of debt) The WACC is the weighted average of the cost of equity and the after tax cost of debt. For IP, add an extra premium for IP risks such as invalidity and obsolescence , because a patent can be revoked or overtaken in ways that ordinary business assets cannot. Example 1 shows the NPV rule at work: ₹50 crore invested now returns ₹9.84 crore more than a 12 per cent discount rate demands.

Example 1: commercialising a patent

Commercialising a patent requires ₹50 crore now and brings ₹15, 20, 25 and 20 crore over four years. The discount rate is 12 per cent.

NPV = 59.84 − 50 = ₹9.84 crore. The IRR is about 20.5 per cent.

Decision: the NPV is positive and the IRR of about 20.5 per cent is well above the 12 per cent rate, so the project should go ahead.

slides.title: Example 3: risk-adjusted NPV, and NPV's limits
slides.html:
For staged projects such as a drug candidate, each cash flow is multiplied by the probability of reaching it; ignoring the probabilities gives a badly misleading NPV.

Example 3: a drug candidate, discounted at 12 per cent

StageCash flowProbabilityPresent value
Trial, now−20certain−20
Further cost, year 1−6035 per cent−18.75
Filing cost, year 3−521 per cent−0.747
Income, years 4 to 8+90 a year18.9 per cent+43.645

Adding the four present values, the risk-adjusted NPV is 4.15. Without probabilities, the NPV would be a misleading 153.79.

Why is the gap so large? The income arrives only if the drug passes every stage, and the chance of that is just 18.9 per cent; the unadjusted figure assumes success is certain.

Limits of NPV: it depends on forecasts and the discount rate, and it ignores flexibility.

Exam focus. Tie the maths to the law: legal facts such as remaining term, validity and exclusivity must decide the period and risk of the cash flows.

slides.title: Benchmarking and the 25 per cent rule
slides.html:
Benchmarking compares an IP asset, royalty rate or portfolio with similar transactions or competitors, in order to estimate value or judge performance.

Benchmarking borrows evidence from comparable deals or firms. It has several forms:

Royalty benchmarking
takes the royalty from comparable licences, adjusted for differences.
Industry norms
give typical royalty ranges.
25 per cent rule of thumb
gives the licensor about one quarter of the licensee's expected profit.
Profit split
divides profit according to each party's contribution.
Portfolio benchmarking
compares patent portfolios with competitors using counts and quality indices.
Practice benchmarking
compares IP management practices with leading firms.

Royalty (% of sales) ≈ 25 per cent × licensee's profit margin

The licensor takes about a quarter of the profit the licensee expects. It is simple but widely criticised as arbitrary.

Worked example

A 20 per cent profit margin suggests a royalty of about 0.25 × 20 = 5 per cent of sales.
