quiz.q: Before launching a new e-bike motor in India, a company wants to know whether selling it would infringe any live patents. Which search should it commission?
quiz.ok: A freedom to operate search
no: A novelty or patentability search
A validity search on its own patents
A landscape search of the whole field
quiz.why: A freedom to operate search asks whether a product infringes live patents. A novelty search asks whether the firm's own invention can be patented, which is a different question, because a product can be novel and still infringe someone else's patent. A validity search asks whether a patent can be revoked, and a landscape search shows who is active in a field.

quiz.q: A firm wants to see which companies are active in solid-state battery research, how activity is trending and where the gaps are, before deciding where to invest. What should it use?
quiz.ok: A landscape search, turned into a patent map of owners, trends and gaps
no: A freedom to operate search, listing the live patents its products would infringe
A validity search, testing whether rivals' patents in the field could be revoked
A due diligence search, checking ownership, status and risk for a transaction
quiz.why: A landscape search shows who is active in a field, and patent mapping turns the results into charts of technologies, owners, trends and gaps, which is what a strategic investment decision needs. Freedom to operate, validity and due diligence searches each answer a narrower question tied to a product, a patent or a deal.

quiz.q: In March 2026 an analyst searches the databases and finds no patent applications by a rival on a technology the rival announced in October 2025. Why is it unsafe to conclude that the rival has not filed?
quiz.ok: Applications are published only after a delay, so recent filings may not show yet
no: Databases list only granted patents and never include pending applications
A rival's filings stay confidential until the patent is granted or expires
Only the official register of the rival's home country shows its filings
quiz.why: Patent applications are published only some time after filing, so an application made a few months earlier will not yet appear in any database. Databases do contain published applications, and publication does not wait for grant. Search results must therefore be read with their dates in mind, alongside other limits such as varying company names and outdated legal status.

quiz.q: A commercial database shows a competitor's Indian patent as 'in force', and its abstract seems to cover the firm's product. Before giving a freedom to operate view, what should the IP manager do?
quiz.ok: Confirm status on the official register and read the claims, which set the legal scope
no: Rely on the database, since commercial status data is updated in real time
Rely on the abstract, since it is the part that defines the scope of protection
Count the competitor's patents, since a large count shows that this one is strong
quiz.why: Legal status data in databases may be outdated, so status should always be confirmed on the official register. The claims, not the abstract, define the legal scope of a patent, so an infringement view depends on reading them. Raw counts can mislead and say nothing about whether a particular patent covers the product.

quiz.concept: Patent family data shows foreign protection
quiz.q: An IP manager finds a competitor's Indian patent on a coating and wants to know whether the same invention is also protected in Europe and the United States. Which part of the patent record should she check first?
quiz.ok: The family information, which links filings for the same invention in other countries
no: The claims, which state the countries in which the protection applies
The citations, which list the countries whose offices examined the invention
The abstract, which summarises where and how the invention is protected
quiz.why: A patent document contains bibliographic data, an abstract, a description, claims, citations, family information and legal status. Family information links the filings for the same invention in different countries, so it shows where else protection was sought, though status in each country should then be confirmed on the official register. The claims define the legal scope of protection, not its territory, and citations point to related documents rather than countries.

quiz.concept: Owning a valid patent is not freedom to operate
quiz.q: A target owns a valid Indian patent on its flagship device, and the buyer's team concludes that the target is therefore free to make and sell the device. What is wrong with this conclusion?
quiz.ok: A patent lets its owner exclude others, but the device may still infringe others' patents
no: Nothing, since a patent owner is always free to exploit its own patented invention
Validity can be confirmed only by a court, so the patent must be treated as invalid
Freedom to operate matters only once the target's own patents have expired
quiz.why: Due diligence asks four separate questions: whether the target owns or controls the IP, whether it is valid and enforceable, whether the business is free to operate without infringing others' rights, and what the IP is worth after risks. A patent gives a right to exclude others, not a right to use, so a device can be covered by its owner's valid patent and still infringe a rival's earlier patent. That is why freedom to operate is checked separately, for the particular product.

quiz.q: A target's main revenue comes from an in-licence that ends if the target undergoes a change of control. The buyer plans to acquire all of the target's shares. What should due diligence flag?
quiz.ok: The share purchase may end the licence, so consent or deal protection is needed first
no: Nothing, since buying shares never affects the contracts of the target company
The licence passes to the buyer automatically, as the new owner of the target's IP
The clause is void, as a restrictive condition prohibited in patent licences
quiz.why: Due diligence reviews licences given and taken, especially exclusivity and change of control clauses, and checks dependence on one licence. A share purchase is exactly the event such a clause targets, so the buyer must obtain the licensor's consent or protect itself through conditions, warranties or price. Change of control clauses are not among the restrictive conditions made void in patent licences.

quiz.q: An inventor orally agreed to assign his patent to Company A, which never recorded the transfer. A later sold the patent to the target by a signed, registered deed. What does a chain-of-title review conclude?
quiz.ok: The first link lacks a written, registered assignment, so the target's title is doubtful
no: Title is sound, since only the final transfer in the chain needs to be written and registered
Title is sound, since an inventor's agreement need not be recorded if he was paid
The target owns the patent but must share its profits with the original inventor
quiz.why: Chain of title requires written and registered assignments from inventors and earlier owners, not just the last transfer. If the inventor never validly assigned to Company A, A had nothing good to pass on, so the target's title is doubtful. Due diligence should require the missing assignment to be executed and registered, often as a condition before completion. Authority: ss. 68 and 69, Patents Act.

quiz.q: Due diligence finds a pending infringement suit against the target whose outcome is uncertain. How are such findings typically reflected in the deal?
quiz.ok: Through price cuts, indemnities, warranties, escrow or conditions before completion
no: By abandoning the deal, since any pending dispute makes the IP worthless
By ignoring it, since disputes are reflected only in the valuation report
By registering the transfer at once, since registration brings the pending suit to an end
quiz.why: Due diligence ends in a risk report, and its findings are reflected in the deal through price adjustment, warranties, indemnities, conditions to be met before completion and escrow. A pending suit is a risk to price and allocate, not automatically a reason to walk away. Transfers are registered after completion, and registration does nothing to a pending dispute.

quiz.q: A search of charge records shows that the target's patents are subject to a bank's security interest registered with CERSAI and the Registrar of Companies. What does this mean for the buyer?
quiz.ok: The patents are encumbered, so the charge must be cleared or priced in the deal
no: The patents are invalid until the loan is repaid, so they cannot be enforced
Nothing, since a security interest ends automatically when the IP is sold
The bank has become a joint owner, so its consent is needed before they can be licensed
quiz.why: Due diligence searches official registers and charge records for encumbrances such as charges registered with the Registrar of Companies and security interests filed with CERSAI. A charge does not affect validity or make the bank an owner, but it gives the lender rights over the asset that a buyer must clear or price. That is why encumbrances are dealt with through release, conditions before completion or price.

quiz.q: A university wants to keep owning its patent while letting a company manufacture under it in return for royalties. Which instrument fits, and why?
quiz.ok: A licence, because it permits use while ownership stays with the university
no: An assignment, because it lets the company use the patent while paying royalties
An assignment, because royalties can be paid only where ownership passes
A licence, because it transfers ownership to the company for the agreed term
quiz.why: A licence is permission to do acts that would otherwise infringe the owner's IP, and ownership remains with the licensor, whereas an assignment transfers ownership. Royalties are common in licences, so payment does not imply transfer. A licence never transfers ownership, even for a limited term.

quiz.q: A licensor is asked to grant an exclusive licence for India to a licensee who will pay only a running royalty on its sales. What risk should the drafter address, and how?
quiz.ok: The licensee may under-exploit it, so exclusivity is paired with a minimum royalty
no: Exclusivity breaches competition law, so the grant should be made non-exclusive
Exclusivity transfers ownership, so the deal should be recorded as an assignment
Running royalties cannot apply to exclusive licences, so a lump sum is required
quiz.why: Under an exclusive licence the licensor depends entirely on the licensee's sales, so a licensee who does little leaves the licensor with almost nothing. Exclusivity is therefore usually paired with a minimum royalty, an example of clauses working together. Competition law protects reasonable conditions needed to protect IP, an exclusive licence still leaves ownership with the licensor, and running royalties are common in exclusive licences.

quiz.concept: Why trade mark licences need quality control
quiz.q: Why must a trade mark licence preserve the licensor's control over the quality of the licensee's goods?
quiz.ok: So that the mark continues to indicate a single trade source to consumers
no: So that the licensor can justify a higher royalty for a premium brand
So that the licence satisfies the writing rule that applies to IP licences
So that the licensee is barred from later challenging the mark's validity
quiz.why: A trade mark tells consumers that goods come from a single trade source. If licensees could sell goods of any quality under the mark, it would stop indicating one source, so the licensor must keep control over quality. Royalty levels, writing formalities and no-challenge terms have nothing to do with this purpose.

quiz.q: A licensee insists that the licensor warrant in the licence that the licensed patent is valid. What is the usual drafting position?
quiz.ok: Warrant title but not validity, and allocate other risks by indemnities
no: Warrant title and validity, since a granted patent is beyond any challenge
Warrant nothing, since warranties have no effect in a registered licence
Warrant validity but not title, since title is shown on the register
quiz.why: Licences usually contain warranties on title, but validity is usually not warranted, because a granted patent can still be revoked, for example on prior art. Remaining risks are handled through indemnities and rules on who sues infringers and who defends claims. Warranties and indemnities must be read together.

quiz.concept: Termination must address sublicences and stock
quiz.q: A licence allows the licensee to grant sublicences, but its termination clause says only that 'on termination the licensee shall stop using the patent'. What is the main gap?
quiz.ok: It ignores existing sublicences, unsold stock and the return of materials
no: None, since sublicences always survive automatically when the head licence ends
It should also require the licensee to assign all its improvements to the licensor
It is void, since a licence that permits sublicensing cannot be terminated
quiz.why: The consequences of termination include stopping use, selling off stock, returning materials and dealing with sublicences. Because the clauses work together, a licence that permits sublicensing must say what happens to the sublicences when it ends, and silence invites disputes with sublicensees and over stock already made. Sublicences do not survive automatically, and forcing the licensee to assign its improvements would be an exclusive grant-back, which licences should avoid.

quiz.concept: What a copyright licence must identify
quiz.q: A software developer grants a company a written copyright licence that names the program and the royalty but says nothing about which rights are licensed, for how long or where. What drafting problem does this create?
quiz.ok: The licence should also identify the rights, the duration and the territory
no: None, since a copyright licence needs only to be in writing and signed
It must be registered with the Copyright Office before it can take effect
It should be an assignment instead, since software cannot be licensed
quiz.why: A copyright licence must be in writing, and because the requirements for assignments also apply to licences, it should identify the work, the rights, the duration, the territory and the royalty. A licence that is silent on the rights, term and territory invites disputes about what was granted. Copyright licences need writing, not registration, and software can be licensed like any other copyright work. Authority: ss. 30 and 30A, Copyright Act.

quiz.concept: Royalty structure for an uncertain, staged project
quiz.q: A university licenses an early-stage drug candidate to a pharmaceutical company. Nobody knows whether it will pass its trials, and the company will not pay a large sum before results are known. Which payment structure fits best?
quiz.ok: A modest upfront fee, milestone payments at each trial stage, then a running royalty
no: A large lump sum at signing, so that the university is paid whatever the trials show
A high minimum annual royalty from the first year, whatever the trial results show
A cross licence of the company's patents, so that no money changes hands at all
quiz.why: Royalties can be structured as a lump sum, a running royalty, an upfront fee with a running royalty, a minimum annual royalty, milestone payments, step-down rates, equity or a cross licence. Where success is uncertain and staged, milestone payments tie each payment to progress, and a running royalty shares the rewards once sales begin. A large lump sum or a high minimum royalty demands payment before results are known, which the licensee has refused, and a cross licence assumes the university wants the company's patents.

quiz.q: A patent changes hands for ₹5 crore, settled by issuing shares. An independent valuer had estimated its worth at ₹6 crore for that purpose and date, the seller's books carried it at ₹1 crore, and a bank said it would lend against ₹2 crore. Which description is correct?
quiz.ok: ₹6 crore is its value, ₹5 crore its price and ₹1 crore its carrying amount
no: ₹5 crore is its value, ₹6 crore its price and ₹2 crore its carrying amount
₹6 crore is its price, ₹5 crore its value and ₹1 crore its collateral value
₹1 crore is its value, ₹5 crore its price and ₹6 crore its collateral value
quiz.why: Value is an estimate of worth for a purpose and date, price is the amount actually agreed, consideration is what is actually given (here, shares), carrying amount is the figure in the accounts and collateral value is a lender's careful estimate of what it could recover on default. The ₹2 crore is therefore the collateral value. Keeping these apart stops a book figure or a deal price being mistaken for the asset's worth.

quiz.q: A patent has 14 years of legal term left, but the product it covers is expected to be overtaken by new technology in about 5 years. Over what period should a valuer project its income?
quiz.ok: About 5 years, its economic life, since income will stop before the legal term ends
no: 14 years, its legal life, since protection lasts for the full remaining term
Indefinitely, with a terminal value, since a good patent keeps earning income forever
Its useful life in the accounts, whatever the market and technology suggest
quiz.why: Legal life is the term of protection, economic life is the period during which the right earns income and is usually shorter, and useful life is the accounting estimate used for amortisation. New technology shortens economic life, so the income projection should stop when earnings stop. A patent with a fixed term should never be given a terminal value.

quiz.q: A songwriter's estate wants cash now from a stable stream of royalties, but it does not want to borrow or to give up ownership of the copyrights. Which route fits?
quiz.ok: Sell its future royalty stream to investors
no: A sale and licence back of the copyrights to investors
A loan secured by a charge over the copyrights
Venture debt secured on the song catalogue
quiz.why: The sale of future royalties to investors is a financing route of its own, separate from loans secured on IP, venture debt and sale and licence back. Selling the royalty stream raises cash from the income without borrowing and without transferring the copyrights. A sale and licence back gives up ownership, and the other two routes are borrowing.

quiz.q: A valuer must value a patent that faces a pending revocation petition with a real chance of success. Which approach handles this uncertainty as the notes suggest?
quiz.ok: Value scenarios with and without the patent surviving, and weight them by probability
no: Ignore the petition, since valuation assumes every granted patent is valid
Use the full legal life, since revocation has not yet been ordered by anyone
Add the expected litigation cost to the value, treating it as an investment in the patent
quiz.why: Valuers handle uncertainty through scenarios, sensitivity analysis, probability weighting, simulation and real options. A real risk of revocation would end the income stream early, so it must be reflected rather than ignored. Litigation cost reduces value; it is not an addition to it.

quiz.q: Commercialising a patent needs ₹30 crore now and is expected to bring ₹10, ₹12 and ₹14 crore at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. The discount rate is 10 per cent. What is the NPV, and should the firm go ahead?
quiz.ok: About −₹0.47 crore, so reject the project
no: About ₹6.00 crore, so accept the project
About ₹2.48 crore, so accept the project
About ₹29.53 crore, so accept the project
quiz.why: The present values are 10 ÷ 1.10 = 9.09, 12 ÷ 1.10² = 9.92 and 14 ÷ 1.10³ = 10.52, a total of 29.53, so NPV is 29.53 − 30 = −0.47 and the project should not proceed. ₹6.00 crore ignores discounting, ₹2.48 crore discounts each flow one year too little, and ₹29.53 crore forgets to deduct the initial investment. Discounting turns an apparently profitable project into a loss-making one.

quiz.q: Assume a risk-free rate of 6 per cent, a beta of 1.5, a market risk premium of 6 per cent, a capital structure of 70 per cent equity and 30 per cent debt, a pre-tax cost of debt of 12 per cent and a tax rate of 25 per cent. What is the WACC?
quiz.ok: 13.2 per cent
no: 14.1 per cent
10.8 per cent
9.0 per cent
quiz.why: The cost of equity is 6 + 1.5 × 6 = 15 per cent, the after-tax cost of debt is 12 × (1 − 0.25) = 9 per cent, and WACC is 0.7 × 15 + 0.3 × 9 = 13.2 per cent. 14.1 per cent forgets the tax saving on debt, 10.8 per cent swaps the weights, and 9.0 per cent leaves the risk-free rate out of the cost of equity. An extra premium for IP risks such as invalidity and obsolescence may then be added.

quiz.concept: Risk-adjusted NPV for a staged project
quiz.q: A drug candidate's trial costs ₹10 crore now (certain). A further ₹40 crore is spent at the end of year 1, a stage with a 50 per cent chance of being reached. Income of ₹200 crore arrives at the end of year 3, with a 20 per cent chance of being reached. At a 10 per cent discount rate, what is the risk-adjusted NPV?
quiz.ok: About ₹1.87 crore
no: About ₹103.90 crore
About ₹10.00 crore
About −₹16.31 crore
quiz.why: Each flow is multiplied by the chance of reaching it and then discounted: −10, −20 ÷ 1.10 = −18.18 and 40 ÷ 1.10³ = +30.05, giving about ₹1.87 crore. ₹103.90 crore ignores the probabilities and so is misleadingly high, ₹10.00 crore applies the probabilities but forgets to discount, and −₹16.31 crore weights only the income and not the year-1 cost. Legal facts such as remaining term and validity should fix the period and risk of the flows.

quiz.concept: Lump sum versus running royalty after tax
quiz.q: A licensor can take a lump sum of ₹4.4 crore now, or a 4 per cent running royalty on a licensee's sales of ₹50 crore a year for three years, received at each year end, less its own cost of ₹0.1 crore a year. Tax is 25 per cent on either, the discount rate is 10 per cent, and there is no doubt about the licensee's credit or the patent's validity. Which is better?
quiz.ok: The royalty, worth about ₹3.54 crore after tax against ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum
no: The lump sum, worth ₹4.40 crore against about ₹3.54 crore for the royalty after tax
The royalty, worth about ₹4.28 crore after tax against ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum
The royalty, worth about ₹4.73 crore before tax against ₹4.40 crore for the lump sum
quiz.why: Each year's royalty is 4 per cent × 50 = 2.0, less the 0.1 cost and 25 per cent tax, or 1.425; discounted at 10 per cent (1 ÷ 1.10 + 1 ÷ 1.10² + 1 ÷ 1.10³ = 2.4869) it is worth about ₹3.54 crore, against 4.4 × 0.75 = ₹3.30 crore for the lump sum after tax. Setting an after-tax royalty against an untaxed lump sum wrongly favours the lump sum, ₹4.28 crore forgets to discount, and ₹4.73 crore compares both before tax. Doubt about the licensee's credit or the patent's validity could reverse the choice.

quiz.q: A trade mark with no fixed end to its life is expected to earn ₹4 crore next year, with growth of 3 per cent a year after that. The discount rate is 11 per cent. What terminal value does the notes' formula give?
quiz.ok: About ₹50.00 crore
no: About ₹36.36 crore
About ₹51.50 crore
About ₹28.57 crore
quiz.why: Terminal value is next year's cash flow divided by (r − g): 4 ÷ (0.11 − 0.03) = ₹50.00 crore. ₹36.36 crore ignores growth, ₹51.50 crore grows next year's flow a second time, and ₹28.57 crore adds g to r instead of subtracting it. The formula suits an asset with no fixed end, such as this mark; a patent with a fixed term should not be given a terminal value.

quiz.concept: Reading IRR against the discount rate
quiz.q: A licence project has conventional cash flows (an outlay now, inflows later) and an IRR of 18 per cent. The firm's discount rate is 13 per cent. What follows?
quiz.ok: Its NPV at 13 per cent is positive, since it is discounted below the IRR
no: Its NPV at 13 per cent is negative, since the return falls short of the IRR
Its NPV at 13 per cent is zero, since IRR and NPV always give the same figure
Nothing about NPV follows, since IRR ignores the timing of the cash flows
quiz.why: The IRR is the discount rate at which NPV is zero. With an outlay followed by inflows, discounting at a rate below the IRR gives a positive NPV, so at 13 per cent the project is worthwhile. IRR is built from discounted flows, so it does take timing into account.

quiz.q: A licensee expects to earn a profit equal to 16 per cent of its sales of the licensed product. What royalty does the 25 per cent rule of thumb suggest?
quiz.ok: About 4 per cent of sales
no: About 12 per cent of sales
About 25 per cent of sales
About 16 per cent of sales
quiz.why: The rule gives the licensor about one quarter of the licensee's expected profit: 25 per cent × 16 per cent = 4 per cent of sales. 12 per cent gives the licensor three quarters instead of one quarter, 25 per cent applies the fraction to sales rather than profit, and 16 per cent hands over the whole profit. The rule is simple but widely criticised as arbitrary, so it needs a cross-check.

quiz.q: Five comparable licences show royalties of 2.0, 3.0, 4.5, 5.0 and 9.0 per cent. The four lower ones were non-exclusive licences of similar proven technology without support; the 9.0 per cent deal was exclusive and bundled know-how and on-site support. The licence being priced is exclusive, for proven technology, with no support. Which conclusion follows the notes' method?
quiz.ok: Median 4.5, middle range 3.0 to 5.0 per cent; price near its top, giving the 9.0 deal little weight
no: Simple average 4.7 per cent, since every comparable licence must be weighted equally
Price near 9.0 per cent, since the only exclusive comparable sets the right level
Median 4.5, middle range 3.0 to 5.0 per cent; price near its bottom, since no support is being given
quiz.why: Sorted, the five rates give a median of 4.5 per cent and a middle range of 3.0 to 5.0 per cent. Exclusivity justifies a point near the top of a range built from non-exclusive comparables, while the 9.0 per cent deal is less comparable because it bundled know-how and support. The absence of support explains why the price stays below that deal, not why it should fall to the bottom of the range.

quiz.q: In royalty benchmarking, an analyst finds a licence granted ten years ago, non-exclusive, in a different field of use and with technical support included. What should the analyst do with it?
quiz.ok: Adjust for the differences or give it little weight, then cross-check with income methods
no: Use its royalty unchanged, since any published licence counts as a valid comparable
Prefer it over recent deals, since an older licence has been better tested
Drop benchmarking for the 25 per cent rule, which never needs comparable licences
quiz.why: Royalty benchmarking checks comparability on factors including exclusivity, territory, field, stage, remaining term, strength of protection, support included and date, then adjusts for differences and cross-checks the result with income methods. A licence that differs on date, exclusivity, field and support needs heavy adjustment or little weight. The 25 per cent rule is a rough shortcut criticised as arbitrary, not a cure for scarce comparables.

quiz.q: What is the essential difference between benchmarking methods and discounted methods of valuing IP?
quiz.ok: Benchmarking reasons from comparable deals; discounted methods from the asset's future benefits
no: Benchmarking relies on after-tax cash flows, while discounted methods rely on pre-tax royalty rates
Benchmarking suits only portfolios; discounted methods suit only single patents
Benchmarking yields a present value; discounted methods yield a royalty range
quiz.why: Benchmarking compares an asset, royalty rate or portfolio with similar transactions or competitors, so it reasons from the market. Discounted methods value IP as the present value of its future benefits and together form the income approach. The option saying benchmarking yields a present value reverses the roles: benchmarking produces a rate or range, which a discounted method such as relief from royalty can then turn into a present value.

quiz.q: An Indian subsidiary pays its foreign parent a royalty for a trade mark licence, and the tax officer asks whether the rate is at arm's length. Which licence is the most reliable comparable?
quiz.ok: A recent licence of a similar mark, field and territory between unrelated parties
no: A licence of a similar mark between two other companies in the same group
The rate that the parent charges its other subsidiaries for the same mark
An old licence of a patent in an unrelated industry between unrelated parties
quiz.why: Royalties between related companies must be at arm's length, so the benchmark must come from licences between unrelated parties, checked for comparability on industry, exclusivity, territory, field, stage, remaining term and date. Rates set within a group, whether between sister companies or by the parent to other subsidiaries, are not themselves at arm's length. An old patent licence in an unrelated industry fails comparability even though its parties are independent. Authority: ss. 161 to 173, Income Tax Act, 2025.

quiz.q: A brand's revenue is expected to be ₹200 crore in year 1, growing by 5 per cent a year over a three-year period. Assume a royalty rate of 3 per cent, tax of 25 per cent and a discount rate of 12 per cent, with all flows at each year end. What is the brand's value by relief from royalty?
quiz.ok: About ₹11.32 crore
no: About ₹15.09 crore
About ₹14.19 crore
About ₹10.81 crore
quiz.why: The after-tax royalties saved are 200 × 3% × 0.75 = 4.50, then 4.73 and 4.96, and dividing them by 1.12, 1.12² and 1.12³ gives a total of about ₹11.32 crore. ₹15.09 crore forgets the tax, ₹14.19 crore forgets to discount, and ₹10.81 crore ignores the 5 per cent growth. The method values the after-tax royalties the owner avoids by not having to license the asset.

quiz.q: A core technology supports revenue of ₹100, ₹120 and ₹110 crore at the end of years 1 to 3. After-tax profit is 20 per cent of revenue, and fair charges for all the other assets used are 7 per cent of revenue. At a 15 per cent discount rate, what is the technology worth by the excess earnings method?
quiz.ok: About ₹32.50 crore
no: About ₹50.00 crore
About ₹42.90 crore
About ₹37.38 crore
quiz.why: Excess earnings are 13 per cent of revenue, or 13.0, 15.6 and 14.3, which divided by 1.15, 1.15² and 1.15³ total about ₹32.50 crore. ₹50.00 crore skips the charge for the other assets and so credits their contribution to the technology, ₹42.90 crore forgets to discount, and ₹37.38 crore treats the year-1 flow as received today. The contributory charge is what isolates the main asset's own earnings.

quiz.q: A key supply contract protects cash flows of ₹80, ₹85 and ₹90 crore at the end of years 1 to 3. Without it, they would fall to ₹70, ₹72 and ₹75 crore. At a 10 per cent discount rate, what is the contract worth by the with and without method?
quiz.ok: About ₹31.10 crore
no: About ₹38.00 crore
About ₹34.21 crore
About ₹28.28 crore
quiz.why: The differences are 10, 13 and 15, which divided by 1.10, 1.10² and 1.10³ give 9.09, 10.74 and 11.27, about ₹31.10 crore. ₹38.00 crore forgets to discount, ₹34.21 crore treats the first difference as received today, and ₹28.28 crore discounts each flow for one year too many. The method values an asset by the cash flows it protects.

quiz.q: A valuer applies relief from royalty to a patent with 8 years of term left, projecting royalty savings for 20 years and then adding a terminal value 'because good technology lasts'. What is the main flaw?
quiz.ok: It gives a patent an unlimited life, though its legal and economic lives are fixed
no: Relief from royalty can never be used for patents, only for trade marks
The terminal value is right, but it should be based on this year's cash flow instead
Royalty savings are tax-free, so the length of the projection does not matter
quiz.why: Giving a patent an unlimited life is a common mistake in discounted methods: income should stop by the end of the remaining term, or earlier if economic life is shorter, and a patent with a fixed term should not get a terminal value. Relief from royalty suits technologies with observable royalty rates as well as trade marks. Royalties saved are taken after tax.

quiz.q: A valuer counts the same price premium once in valuing a company's brand and again in valuing its patented technology, and discounts pre-tax royalty savings at an after-tax rate. Which pair of mistakes is this?
quiz.ok: Counting the same income twice, and mixing before-tax flows with after-tax rates
no: Borrowing royalty rates from unlike deals, and giving a patent an unlimited life
Counting the same income twice, and giving a patent an unlimited life
Mixing before-tax flows with after-tax rates, and borrowing rates from unlike deals
quiz.why: The common mistakes in discounted methods are counting the same income twice, mixing before-tax cash flows with after-tax rates, giving a patent an unlimited life and borrowing royalty rates from unlike deals. Crediting one price premium to both the brand and the patent counts it twice and overstates their combined value. Discounting pre-tax flows at an after-tax rate is the tax mismatch.

quiz.concept: Choosing excess earnings for a core asset
quiz.q: A software company's profit comes mainly from one core platform, but the business also uses working capital, servers, a skilled workforce and a brand. No royalty rates exist for platforms like it. Which method isolates the platform's value?
quiz.ok: Excess earnings, deducting fair charges for the other assets before discounting
no: Relief from royalty, borrowing a rate from licences of unrelated products
Premium profit, crediting the whole of the company's profit to the platform
With and without, comparing the company with a rival that has no platform
quiz.why: The multi-period excess earnings method values the main asset of a business by taking the profit it generates, deducting a fair charge for all other assets used (working capital, machinery, workforce and brand) and discounting the remaining excess earnings. Relief from royalty suits assets with observable royalty rates, and borrowing rates from unlike deals is a common mistake. Crediting the whole profit to the platform ignores the other assets' contribution, which is exactly what the contributory charge removes.

quiz.q: Portfolio X has twelve patent families, most of them weak or lapsed. Portfolio Y has four strong, active families, two of which are crown jewels. A lender must choose which to accept as primary collateral. What does the notes' approach suggest?
quiz.ok: Portfolio Y, since active, quality-adjusted families matter more than raw counts
no: Portfolio X, since a larger count spreads the lender's risk over more patents
Portfolio X, since lenders always prefer several patent families to only a few
Neither, since patent stocks play no part in valuation or finance
quiz.why: Simple counts mislead because a few patents carry most of the value and many are weak, unused or lapsed. Lenders prefer several strong patent families to a single patent, and the word 'strong' is what matters, so a smaller strong portfolio beats a larger weak one. Patent stocks do have uses in valuation and finance, but only after adjusting for quality.

quiz.q: An acquirer is valuing a target's portfolio of 200 patents. Which approach is better than relying on the simple count?
quiz.ok: Count active families, adjust for quality, and value crown jewels by income methods
no: Multiply the number of granted patents by an industry average value per patent
Add applications, grants and families together, so that no activity is missed
Keep the count but add the decoy filings, since they deter rivals from entering
quiz.why: A better approach counts families and active patents, adjusts for quality, depreciates older patents, values crown-jewel patents separately by income methods and confirms ownership and validity through due diligence. Multiplying by an average ignores that value is concentrated in a few patents. Adding applications, grants and families mixes counting units and counts the same invention more than once.

quiz.concept: Why lenders prefer several strong families
quiz.q: A start-up offers a lender, as collateral, either its single strongest patent or a package of four strong, active patent families of similar total quality. Which does the lender usually prefer, and why?
quiz.ok: The four families, since several strong families spread the risk of any one failing
no: The single patent, since one strong right is simpler to value and to enforce
The single patent, since a package of families counts the same invention twice
Neither, since lenders judge patent collateral only by its raw count of patents
quiz.why: Lenders prefer several strong patent families to a single patent, because a lender worries about invalidity, obsolescence and a thin resale market, and one patent that fails takes all the security with it. Spreading the security over several strong families reduces that risk. A family counts one invention once across countries, so four families are four inventions, and lenders look at strength, not raw counts.

quiz.concept: Flooding and decoy filings inflate patent stocks
quiz.q: Firm R's patent count doubled in a year after it filed hundreds of near-identical applications it does not intend to use. Firm S has a smaller stock of actively used families. How should a valuer treat R's jump before comparing the two?
quiz.ok: Discount the flood and decoy filings, and compare active, quality-adjusted families
no: Rank R higher, since a fast-rising count shows strong and growing innovation
Count each of R's applications in full, since every filing deters rivals equally
Rank them on raw counts, since filing motives cannot affect a patent stock's value
quiz.why: Flooding and decoy filings inflate patent counts, and many patents are unused or weak, so a better approach counts families and active patents and adjusts for quality. On that basis S's smaller, active stock may well be the stronger. Filings made only to crowd the field add numbers without adding the income that a valuer or lender relies on.

quiz.q: A lender values a borrower's patent portfolio at ₹8 crore. Assume it applies a 40 per cent haircut to reach a distressed value, and then lends 50 per cent of that distressed value. How much will it lend?
quiz.ok: ₹2.4 crore
no: ₹4.0 crore
₹4.8 crore
₹1.6 crore
quiz.why: The distressed value is 8 × (1 − 0.40) = ₹4.8 crore, and lending half of it gives ₹2.4 crore. ₹4.0 crore skips the haircut, ₹4.8 crore lends the whole distressed value, and ₹1.6 crore treats the 40 per cent haircut as the share kept. The result shows why IP alone rarely supports a large loan.

quiz.q: A bank takes a written mortgage over a borrower company's patents and files the charge with the Registrar of Companies, but does nothing more. What do the notes say is still missing?
quiz.ok: Registration with CERSAI and registration of the mortgage under the Patents Act
no: Nothing, since the company charge filing covers every asset the company owns
A court order, since security over IP cannot be enforced without one
Registration with CERSAI only, since the patent register records ownership, not security
quiz.why: Security interests over intangible assets must be registered with CERSAI, a patent mortgage must be in writing and registered under the Patents Act, and a company must register charges with the Registrar of Companies, so a lender registers in every relevant registry. The patent register records mortgages as well as ownership, so CERSAI alone is not enough, and no court order is needed because secured creditors can enforce without going to court. Authority: ss. 68 and 69, Patents Act; s. 77, Companies Act, 2013; s. 13, SARFAESI Act, 2002.

quiz.q: A borrower defaults on an IP-backed loan and the bank starts to enforce its security out of court. Before enforcement is complete, insolvency resolution begins and a moratorium takes effect. What is the position?
quiz.ok: Enforcement must stop while the moratorium lasts, though it began lawfully
no: Enforcement continues, since SARFAESI security overrides the insolvency moratorium
Enforcement was unlawful from the start, since IP security needs a court order
Enforcement continues, since IP rights fall outside insolvency proceedings
quiz.why: Secured creditors may enforce their security without going to court, so the bank acted lawfully at first. The moratorium under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 stops enforcement during insolvency resolution, which is why a lender must plan for insolvency when taking IP security. Authority: s. 13, SARFAESI Act, 2002.

quiz.q: A start-up gives a bank a charge over its patents and the royalties they produce. Which concern is it most likely to have?
quiz.ok: Losing freedom to license, since the lender may restrict licensing and transfer
no: Losing ownership at once, since a charge transfers title in the patents to the bank
Losing the right to keep using the patents in making its own products
Losing validity, since charged patents cannot be renewed by their owner
quiz.why: When IP is used as collateral the borrower usually keeps ownership and use, but the lender may restrict licensing and transfer. Borrowers therefore worry about losing the freedom to license and about strict covenants. A charge does not transfer ownership or affect validity.

quiz.q: Assume an audit scores each risk as likelihood (1 to 5) × impact (1 to 5), with 15 to 25 rated high, 8 to 14 medium and 1 to 7 low. Finding A has likelihood 2 and impact 5, B has likelihood 4 and impact 4, and C has likelihood 3 and impact 2. How are they rated?
quiz.ok: A medium, B high, C low
no: A low, B medium, C low
A high, B high, C low
A high, B medium, C low
quiz.why: The scores are A = 2 × 5 = 10 (medium), B = 4 × 4 = 16 (high) and C = 3 × 2 = 6 (low). Adding likelihood and impact instead of multiplying gives 7, 8 and 5, which understates every risk. Rating on impact alone overrates A, whose severe impact is offset by its low likelihood.

quiz.q: Before its public issue of shares, a company commissions a review of its own IP. Separately, it checks whether a licensee has paid the right royalties. How are these two audits classified?
quiz.ok: The first is an event based audit; the second is a royalty audit
no: The first is a general audit; the second is a compliance audit
The first is a focused audit; the second is a royalty audit
The first is a compliance audit; the second is a focused audit
quiz.why: An event based audit is done before a merger, investment, public issue, loan or product launch, and a royalty audit checks a licensee's payments. A focused audit examines one area, such as trade secrets or software licences, and a compliance audit checks filings and legal duties. Classifying the audit fixes its scope and the team it needs.

quiz.q: A company's statutory auditors have just signed off its annual accounts, and no transaction is planned. The board asks whether it still needs an IP audit. What is the best answer?
quiz.ok: Yes: a financial audit tests the accounts, whereas an IP audit checks ownership, protection and risk
no: No: the financial audit already confirms who owns the IP and whether it is valid
No: an IP audit is needed only once the firm's IP has been valued in money terms
Yes, but only to rank the assets for keep or drop, which is all an IP audit does
quiz.why: An IP audit is a systematic review that finds out what IP a firm owns or uses, confirms ownership and protection, assesses use and value, and identifies legal and commercial risks. A financial audit tests the accounts, so clean accounts say nothing about whether assignments are signed or deadlines tracked. Ranking assets for keep or drop decisions is a portfolio review, and valuation, which produces a money figure, is a separate exercise.

quiz.q: An audit finds that a registered trade mark has cost renewal fees for years without being used or licensed, and that a little-used patent is being exploited by a competitor without a licence. Which follow-up best reflects the purpose of an IP audit?
quiz.ok: Cut the idle mark's cost and turn the patent's unlicensed use into licensing income
no: Renew both as usual, since an audit's job ends once the IP has been listed
Value both in money terms, since an audit is essentially a valuation exercise
Drop both at once, since any right that is not earning money should go
quiz.why: An audit asks which rights earn money and which only cost money, and its report includes commercial opportunities and an action plan, after which problems are fixed and monitoring set up. Its benefits include cost savings and new licensing income, so the idle mark's cost should be cut and the exploited patent turned into income. Dropping the patent would throw away the very opportunity the audit found, and valuation is a separate exercise.

quiz.concept: Licence income versus sale of IP
quiz.q: Company A grants a five-year licence of its trade mark for an annual fee. Company B sells its patent outright for a lump sum. Neither deals in IP as a business. How is the income generally treated?
quiz.ok: A's fees are revenue income; B's sale may give rise to capital gains
no: Both give rise to capital gains, since both involve a transfer of IP rights
Both are revenue income, since every receipt from IP counts as royalty
A's fees give rise to capital gains; B's lump sum is taxed as royalty
quiz.why: Licence fees and royalties are revenue income, while an outright sale of IP may give rise to capital gains, or business income for a dealer. A licence keeps ownership with the licensor and earns recurring income, whereas a sale transfers the asset itself. The tax line mirrors the line between a licence and an assignment.

quiz.concept: Software copy versus right to copy
quiz.q: Indian Company P pays a foreign vendor for copies of off-the-shelf software for its staff's own use, with no right to copy or modify. Indian Company Q pays a foreign developer for the right to modify and redistribute its code. How are these payments generally treated under tax treaties?
quiz.ok: P's payment is generally not royalty, but Q's payment for the right to modify is
no: Both are royalty, since software is copyright and any payment for it is royalty
Neither is royalty, since software payments are always taxed as business income
P's payment is royalty, but Q's payment is a fee for technical services
quiz.why: Payment for a copy of software for the buyer's own use, without any transfer of copyright rights, is generally not treated as royalty under tax treaties. Payment for the right to copy or modify software is royalty, because it is a payment for rights in the copyright. The test is whether copyright rights pass, not whether software is involved.

quiz.concept: Patent box taxes the gross royalty
quiz.q: An eligible resident inventor-patentee opts for the patent box. Its royalty from the Indian patent is ₹3 crore gross, and it spent ₹1.2 crore in earning it. Assume the patent box rate is 10 per cent and its normal rate on net income is 25 per cent. What tax is payable on the royalty?
quiz.ok: ₹0.30 crore
no: ₹0.18 crore
₹0.45 crore
₹0.75 crore
quiz.why: The patent box taxes the royalty at 10 per cent of the gross amount without any deduction of expenses: 10% × 3 = ₹0.30 crore. ₹0.18 crore wrongly deducts the expenses first, ₹0.45 crore applies normal taxation to net income although the patentee opted for the box, and ₹0.75 crore applies the normal rate to the gross royalty. The choice binds: departing from the regime in any of the following five years loses the benefit for the next five.

quiz.concept: Who can use the patent box
quiz.q: Assume the patent box requires a resident patentee who is the true and first inventor, a patent developed and registered in India, and at least 75 per cent of the invention's spending incurred in India. Which royalty earner qualifies?
quiz.ok: A resident inventor whose Indian patent was developed with 80 per cent of spending in India
no: A resident company that bought an Indian patent from its inventor, with all spending in India
A non-resident inventor whose patent was developed and registered in India
A resident inventor whose patent, developed fully in India, is registered only abroad
quiz.why: The regime is confined to a resident patentee who is the true and first inventor, with the patent developed and registered in India and at least 75 per cent of the spending incurred there. A buyer of a patent is not its true and first inventor, a non-resident fails the residence test, and a patent registered only abroad is not registered in India. The option is exercised in Form 65 by the due date of the return.

quiz.q: An Indian company pays ₹1 crore of royalty to a non-resident licensor that has no permanent establishment in India. Assume domestic law taxes such royalty at 20 per cent of the gross amount and the applicable treaty rate is 15 per cent. What is the position?
quiz.ok: Tax of ₹0.15 crore at the treaty rate, deducted at source by the Indian payer
no: Tax of ₹0.20 crore, since domestic law always prevails over a tax treaty
Tax at normal business rates on net income, since the licensor earns it from India
No Indian tax at all, since the licensor has no permanent establishment in India
quiz.why: Royalty earned by a non-resident is taxed at 20 per cent of the gross amount, or at a lower treaty rate where the treaty is more beneficial, and the payer must deduct the tax at source. Here the treaty gives ₹0.15 crore. Taxation as business income applies only where the royalty is connected with a permanent establishment in India, and having no such establishment does not remove the royalty charge. Authority: ss. 207, 159 and 393(2), Income Tax Act, 2025.

quiz.q: An Indian licensor grants an Indian manufacturer a three-year licence to use its patented process. How does GST treat this?
quiz.ok: As a supply of services, since it is a temporary permission to use an IP right
no: As a supply of goods, since the licence is used to manufacture goods for sale
As outside GST, since the royalty already suffers income tax deduction at source
As a zero-rated supply, since an IP right is intangible and has no location
quiz.why: A temporary transfer of an IP right, or permission to use it, is a supply of services and is taxed at 18 per cent. Income tax deduction at source is a separate regime and does not displace GST. Zero rating is available only for exports of services that meet the conditions, not for a licence between two Indian parties. Authority: CGST Act, Schedule II, para 5(c).

quiz.q: A group's patent is legally owned by a company in a low-tax country that has no staff, while an Indian subsidiary carries out its development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation. Where should the IP profit be allocated?
quiz.ok: To the Indian subsidiary, which performs the functions that create the value
no: To the low-tax owner, since legal ownership alone decides where IP profit is taxed
Equally between the two, since both companies belong to the same group
To whichever company first applied for the patent in any country
quiz.why: Profit from IP should be allocated to the group company that performs the DEMPE functions, and anti-avoidance rules prevent shifting IP income to low-tax companies without real activity. Legal title held by a company with no staff does not attract the profit. Royalties between the related companies must also be at arm's length. Authority: ss. 161 to 173, Income Tax Act, 2025.

cards.f: Why can IP law decide what accounting recognises as an intangible asset?
cards.b: Ind AS 38 requires the business to control the asset, which in practice usually means owning a legal or contractual right. A right that is not legally secured is often not controlled, and what is not controlled cannot be an asset.

cards.f: Distinguish the four levels of measuring intangible assets.
cards.b: Identification lists what the firm has (an IP register); classification groups it by type, technology, business or legal status; quantification uses non money indicators such as patents, citations, staff turnover or customer retention; valuation puts a money value on it for a stated purpose and date.

cards.f: Ind AS 38: research, internally generated brands and goodwill
cards.b: Research cost: always an expense (para 54). Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists: never recognised (para 63). Internally generated goodwill: never recognised (para 48). Bought intangibles: at cost, amortised over a finite useful life.

cards.f: Ind AS 38, para 57: the six conditions for capitalising development cost
cards.b: Technical feasibility; intention to complete; ability to use or sell; probable future benefits; adequate resources; reliable measurement of cost.

cards.f: Why can’t the market to book gap be treated as the value of a firm’s IP?
cards.b: The gap (for example ₹10,000 crore ÷ ₹2,000 crore = 5) partly reflects unrecorded intangibles, but it also reflects growth expectations and market mood. So it cannot be treated as an exact value of the firm’s IP.

cards.f: What is the relevance and reliability choice, and how do most standard setters resolve it?
cards.b: Recognising more intangibles makes accounts more realistic and lowers knowledge firms’ cost of capital, but the values are estimates that are hard to audit, open to manipulation and volatile. Most standard setters keep recognition strict and encourage better disclosure of non money indicators and narrative.

cards.f: Who must value intangibles for company law purposes, and under which standard?
cards.b: Registered valuers: s. 247, Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017. ICAI Valuation Standards 2018 include VS 302 on intangible assets.

cards.f: Income Tax Act, 2025: acquired intangibles and patent royalty
cards.b: s. 33(1)(b): depreciation on acquired intangibles such as know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences and franchises, but not goodwill. s. 194(1): royalty from patents developed and registered in India taxed at a concessional 10 per cent.

cards.f: Indian law lets IP secure a loan, so why does IP backed lending remain small?
cards.b: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 includes intangibles in the definition of property, and security interests are registered with CERSAI. But strict recognition means lenders find little security on the balance sheet, so IP backed lending remains small.

cards.f: Why do start-ups report losses and depend on equity under the present accounting rules?
cards.b: Research cost is always expensed and development is capitalised only on strict conditions, so a start-up’s R&D shows up as losses rather than assets. With little to offer lenders, it depends on equity, and government must use tax incentives and grants to encourage R&D.

cards.f: IC accounting is voluntary. Is a company free to publish whatever IC claims it likes?
cards.b: No. IC accounting is voluntary and outside the statutory financial statements, but IC information published in a prospectus must not be untrue or misleading, because ss. 34 and 35 of the Companies Act, 2013 impose liability for misstatements in a prospectus.

cards.f: Distinguish the Balanced Scorecard, the Skandia Navigator and the Intangible Assets Monitor.
cards.b: Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton): four perspectives linked by cause and effect. Skandia Navigator (Edvinsson and Malone): five focus areas with human capital at the centre. Intangible Assets Monitor (Sveiby): external structure, internal structure and competence, each read through growth, efficiency and stability.

cards.f: How does Tobin’s q differ from the market to book ratio, and what does q above 1 suggest?
cards.b: Both put market value on top. The market to book ratio divides by the book value of net assets; Tobin’s q divides by the replacement cost of the firm’s assets. A q above 1 suggests valuable intangibles that replacement cost does not capture.

cards.f: VAIC: formula and the notes’ worked example
cards.b: VAIC = HCE + SCE + CEE, where HCE = VA ÷ HC, SCE = (VA − HC) ÷ VA and CEE = VA ÷ CE. With VA 200, HC 80 and CE 400: 2.5 + 0.6 + 0.5 = 3.6.

cards.f: Calculated Intangible Value: the notes’ worked example
cards.b: Profit 90 on tangible assets of 500; industry return 12 per cent gives 60. Excess profit 30; after 25 per cent tax, 22.5; divided by a 15 per cent cost of capital, CIV = 150.

cards.f: According to Teece, when may imitators capture most of the profit from an innovation?
cards.b: When the appropriability regime is weak and the imitators own the complementary assets (manufacturing, distribution, service and brand). Once a dominant design emerges, competition moves to price and scale.

cards.f: Formalities for licences and assignments
cards.b: Patent licence: in writing and registered to be relied upon (ss. 68 and 69). Copyright licence: in writing (s. 30). Assignment: patents, writing and registration; copyright, writing (s. 19); trade marks, registration (Trade Marks Act, s. 45).

cards.f: Distinguish Granstrand’s policy from a strategy, and give three features of his model IP policy.
cards.b: A policy is a long lasting general guideline; a strategy is a specific plan of action. The model policy makes business managers responsible for IP, seeks a strong patent position in core businesses and encourages “speed to patent”; it also uses several protections, checks others’ patents, licenses openly and respects others’ IP.

cards.f: Patents Act, s. 140: restrictive licence conditions made void
cards.b: Tying the licensee to buy unpatented goods from the licensor; exclusive grant backs; preventing challenges to validity; coercive package licensing.

cards.f: Why is the Form 27 statement of working important for a patentee extracting value?
cards.b: A patent that is not worked in India may attract a compulsory licence under s. 84 after three years from grant. The working statement in Form 27 is the record of working, and unused patents carry this legal risk.

cards.f: Why is ownership the first question in measuring a start-up’s intellectual capital?
cards.b: Investors pay for IP the company actually holds. Founders must assign inventions in writing (s. 6; ss. 68 and 69), and a freelancer’s copyright stays with the freelancer unless assigned in writing (s. 19). Unclear ownership is one of the main reasons start-up IC is hard to measure.

cards.f: Scorecard method: weights and the notes’ example
cards.b: Team 30 per cent; size of opportunity 25; product and technology 15; competition 10; sales channels 10; need for further funding 5; others 5. Average value ₹20 crore × weighted score 1.155 = ₹23.1 crore.

cards.f: Venture capital method: the notes’ worked example
cards.b: Exit ₹200 crore in five years at a 50 per cent target return; investment ₹10 crore. Post money = 200 ÷ 1.55 (7.594) = ₹26.34 crore; pre money = ₹16.34 crore; investor’s share about 38 per cent.

cards.f: Distinguish the Berkus method from the First Chicago method.
cards.b: The Berkus method gives value for five risk reducing elements: a sound idea, a prototype, a good team, strategic relationships and a product launch or sales. The First Chicago method weights values in best, normal and worst cases by their probabilities.

cards.f: How does a large portfolio protect freedom to operate, and why does it not deter a “patent extortionist”?
cards.b: Firms depend on each other’s patents, so a strong portfolio gives retaliatory power: others hesitate to sue a firm that can sue back. A party holding one patent with no manufacturing to be counter attacked is beyond that threat, so it can make demands on large firms.

cards.f: What does offensive blocking secure, and what does defensive blocking secure?
cards.b: Offensive blocking secures market freedom; defensive blocking secures design freedom.

cards.f: Distinguish fencing from surrounding.
cards.b: Fencing places a row of patents across several research paths. Surrounding places many small patents around a rival’s key patent to force a cross licence.

cards.f: Legal options against a blocking patent
cards.b: Opposition before grant (s. 25(1)); opposition within one year from publication of the grant (s. 25(2)); revocation (s. 64); compulsory licence where the conditions of s. 84 are met. Commercial options: invent around, buy or license, cross licence, wait for expiry, leave the field.

cards.f: Why is the size of a portfolio not a measure of its value?
cards.b: A few patents usually carry most of the value. Strength depends on validity, claim scope, use in products, countries covered, remaining life, fit with strategy and cost of maintenance, and unused patents risk a compulsory licence. Leading Japanese firms moved from quantity to quality.

cards.f: How has the IA manager’s role evolved through Granstrand’s four stages?
cards.b: IP is first ignored; then inventors are rewarded and IP is left to the legal department; then patenting becomes selective and positions are reviewed; finally IP becomes part of business strategy, with engineers rotating through the IP department. The role moves from legal administration to business strategy.

cards.f: The IA manager’s compliance checklist
cards.b: Form 27 once for every period of three financial years (rule 131, as amended in 2024); renewal fees on time, with a 10 per cent reduction for online payment four or more years ahead; registration of patent assignments and licences (s. 69); permission before filing abroad first (s. 39); trade marks renewed every ten years; records for CARO 2020.

cards.f: What skills does an IA manager need, and how can the function be organised?
cards.b: Skills: IP law, technical understanding, business and financial skills, negotiation and communication. Organisation: centrally, within business units, or a mix of central policy and unit level managers.

cards.f: Why might an Indian software firm rely on copyright, secrecy and contracts rather than patents?
cards.b: Because s. 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes computer programs as such and business methods. With the patent route often closed, the firm protects code through copyright, confidentiality and contract.

cards.f: Distinguish a patent from a trade secret on disclosure, duration and scope.
cards.b: A patent needs full public disclosure, lasts 20 years and binds even independent inventors. A trade secret needs no disclosure and can last indefinitely, but protects only against misuse of confidential information, not independent discovery or reverse engineering.

cards.f: A firm's new process leaves no trace in the final product. Why might Granstrand advise secrecy rather than a patent?
cards.b: A secret that is hard to discover is one of Granstrand's four situations favouring secrecy; the others are a large lead, patent infringement hard to detect and a patent easily invented around. A patent would demand full disclosure yet add little real protection.

cards.f: Why is defensive publication a cheap way of keeping freedom to operate?
cards.b: Published matter forms prior art that defeats later patent claims, so no rival can patent the invention and block the firm, and the firm avoids the cost of filing.

cards.f: Filing abroad: Paris priority, PCT and s. 39
cards.b: 12 months (patents) and 6 months (designs and trade marks) under the Paris Convention; PCT entry into the Indian national phase at 31 months from priority; a resident needs permission before filing abroad first (s. 39).

cards.f: What does categorisation add to a bare list of registrations?
cards.b: It turns the list into information for decisions: which rights matter to the business, which only cost money, where the legal risks lie and what action each asset needs.

cards.f: A patent covers the firm's best product but has narrow claims rivals can invent around. Where does it sit in the portfolio matrix, and what should the firm do?
cards.b: High business value, weak legal position: the weak core. Strengthen it through further filings, secrecy or better contracts. (Crown jewels are maintained, enforced and extended; strong but low-value rights are licensed or sold; rights weak on both are dropped.)

cards.f: Why must joint ownership be flagged in the legal categorisation?
cards.b: Under s. 50, Patents Act, a joint owner of an Indian patent cannot grant a licence or assign a share without the consent of the other owners, so one co-owner cannot exploit the patent alone.

cards.f: What is the risk of abandoning a patent to save renewal fees?
cards.b: Abandonment saves money but may free the technology for competitors, and a lapsed patent can be restored only within the period and conditions allowed by law (s. 60). Renew only where the expected benefit exceeds the cost.

cards.f: Why must evaluation come before valuation?
cards.b: Because a valuation of a weak or invalid right is meaningless. Evaluation first checks the legal, technical, commercial, strategic and risk factors, and only then is a money value worth fixing.

cards.f: Legal bases for IP valuation in India
cards.b: Companies Act, 2013, s. 247 (registered valuers); Income Tax Act, 2025, ss. 161 to 173 (arm's length royalties); Ind AS 103, 36 and 113 (fair values); ICAI VS 302 (intangible assets).

cards.f: Distinguish relief from royalty from excess earnings.
cards.b: Relief from royalty values the royalties saved by owning the asset rather than licensing it; it suits established brands and technologies. Excess earnings takes business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used; it suits the core technology of a business.

cards.f: A start-up's early patent has no income yet. Which method suits it?
cards.b: The cost approach or real options. With no income yet there is little to discount, while cost or an option model can still give a value.

cards.f: Why might a buyer reject a cost-approach value, and why is the market approach often hard to use?
cards.b: Because cost is not the same as value: what was spent proves nothing about what the asset will earn. The market approach needs comparables, but true comparables are rare and deal terms are usually confidential.

cards.f: Patent Asset Index formula
cards.b: Competitive Impact = Technology Relevance × Market Coverage; Patent Asset Index = Σ Competitive Impact.

cards.f: Portfolio A has three families (3.6, 0.15, 1.08); Portfolio B has ten families of 0.2. Which is stronger?
cards.b: A scores 4.83 and B scores 2.0, so the smaller portfolio is stronger: quality per family, not the number of families, drives the index.

cards.f: Why can't an IP value index fix a price?
cards.b: It is a relative quality score for screening and comparison. It gives no money value, citations take years to accumulate, weights are subjective, indicators can be manipulated and legal validity is not checked.

cards.f: Patent X is cited by many later patents and protected in many countries. What does each fact suggest about its value?
cards.b: Many forward citations signal technical importance; a large family size (number of countries where protection is sought) signals expected commercial value.

cards.f: Why can't patent data alone value a portfolio, according to Granstrand?
cards.b: Because patent values are highly uneven, so counts mislead. Patent data must be combined with stock market data, panel data or survey evidence.

cards.f: Market value model
cards.b: V = q × (A + γK): V market value, A tangible assets, K knowledge stock (R&D or patents), and γ how the market values knowledge relative to tangible assets.

cards.f: What do renewal models reveal, and how?
cards.b: Owners pay renewal fees only while a patent is worth more than the fee, so renewal data show how values are spread: most patents are worth little while a few are worth a great deal.

cards.f: A renewal study shows that the average patent in a field is worth little. Can you conclude that your client's patent is worth little?
cards.b: No. Empirical models give averages rather than the value of one patent, depend on available data and show association rather than cause. Patent values are highly uneven, so one patent may be worth a great deal.

cards.f: Why can discounted cash flow undervalue early, uncertain IP?
cards.b: DCF assumes a fixed plan and ignores the flexibility a patent gives: the right but not the obligation to wait, expand, license, switch use or abandon.

cards.f: Black and Scholes worked example (S 100, K 120, T 3, σ 0.40, r 0.07)
cards.b: d1 0.3864; d2 −0.3065; N(d1) 0.6504; N(d2) 0.3796; PV of K 97.27; C = 65.04 − 36.93 = 28.11, against an NPV of −20 for investing now.

cards.f: Binomial worked example (S 100, u 1.4, d 0.7, r 7 per cent, K 110)
cards.b: Payoff 30 up, nothing down; p = (1.07 − 0.7) ÷ (1.4 − 0.7) = 0.5286; value = 0.5286 × 30 ÷ 1.07 = 14.82.

cards.f: Decision tree example: pilot 20, good 180 or bad 40, launch 80, 10 per cent
cards.b: Commit to launch in both cases: NPV 7.27. Launch only if good: 25.45. Flexibility is worth 18.18.

cards.f: Why does a patent's option value rise as uncertainty rises?
cards.b: The owner keeps the upside if things go well and need not invest if they go badly, so wider uncertainty raises the possible gain without raising the loss.

cards.f: Distinguish measuring from monitoring intellectual capital.
cards.b: Measuring gives a picture at one point in time; monitoring tracks IC regularly through indicators and targets so that management can act early.

cards.f: Classify: R&D spending, invention disclosures, patents granted, licence income.
cards.b: An input, a process, an output and an outcome indicator respectively.

cards.f: Staff file many weak patents to hit a patent-count target. What is this problem, and why does it matter?
cards.b: Gaming: people improve the number rather than the reality. The indicator rises while real innovation does not, so the monitoring system misleads management.

cards.f: A firm's IC report is only a table of indicators. What would the Danish model add?
cards.b: The Danish model IC statement combines a knowledge narrative, management challenges and initiatives with the indicators, so the figures are read against the firm's strategy and the actions it is taking.

cards.f: How does Arrow's information paradox explain why IP rights matter?
cards.b: A buyer cannot judge knowledge without seeing it, but once it is seen it has been given away. Patents and confidentiality agreements allow disclosure without loss of protection.

cards.f: A firm's know-how is valuable and rare, but rivals can copy it easily. Does it give lasting competitive advantage?
cards.b: No. Barney's VRIN test requires knowledge to be valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable. Easily copied know-how fails the hard-to-imitate limb.

cards.f: An engineer writes her tacit know-how into a manual. Which SECI mode is this, and what are the other three?
cards.b: Externalisation (tacit to explicit). The others are socialisation (tacit to tacit), combination (explicit to explicit) and internalisation (explicit to tacit), from Nonaka and Takeuchi.

cards.f: Why do Indian firms rely on confidentiality and retention rather than non compete clauses?
cards.b: s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872 makes post employment non compete clauses generally void, so firms rely on confidentiality duties and retention through incentives, career paths and succession planning.

cards.f: Distinguish dynamic capabilities from absorptive capacity.
cards.b: Dynamic capabilities (Teece): the ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure resources. Absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal): the ability to recognise and use outside knowledge.

cards.f: What IP actions belong at the design and testing stages of product development?
cards.b: Design: decide between patenting and secrecy and file before any disclosure. Testing: non disclosure agreements bind testers and improvements are filed.

cards.f: What is "speed to patent" and why does Indian law make it matter?
cards.b: Granstrand's advice to file early. In India public disclosure before filing usually destroys novelty, so a late filing can lose the right altogether.

cards.f: Why does joint development need clear agreement on ownership?
cards.b: Because under s. 50, Patents Act, a joint owner cannot license or assign a share without the consent of the other owners.

cards.f: How can patent maps help a firm plan its product development?
cards.b: Granstrand: patent maps help to generate ideas, track rivals, plan R&D and strengthen bargaining, alongside his advice to check others' patents before entering a new field.

cards.f: Depreciated patent stock formula
cards.b: Kt = (1 − δ) × Kt−1 + Pt, with δ often about 15 per cent.

cards.f: Patent stock example: 10, 12, 15, 9, 20, 18 and 22 patents from 2019 to 2025
cards.b: Simple count 106; depreciated stock in 2025 74.20.

cards.f: Revealed technological advantage: formula and example
cards.b: (Firm's patents in a field ÷ firm's total) ÷ (world patents in the field ÷ world total). 20 per cent ÷ 5 per cent = 4.0, strong specialisation.

cards.f: Why can't you simply compare two firms' raw patent counts?
cards.b: Industries patent at different rates, values are highly uneven, strategic filing inflates counts, publication is delayed by about 18 months and company names vary. So Granstrand insists the counting unit must always be stated.

cards.f: Why does copyright need collective management?
cards.b: Users such as broadcasters, hotels and platforms use thousands of works; negotiating with every owner would be impossibly costly, and owners cannot monitor use across the country. A society grants blanket licences over its whole repertoire.

cards.f: s. 33, Copyright Act, 1957
cards.b: Licensing business only by or through a registered copyright society; owners may still license their own works individually; ordinarily one society per class of works; registration lasts five years.

cards.f: ss. 33A, 34, 35 and 36, Copyright Act, 1957
cards.b: 33A: publish the tariff scheme. 34: administration of rights entrusted. 35: owners' and authors' control over the society. 36: returns and audited accounts.

cards.f: How did the 2012 amendments shift power within copyright societies?
cards.b: Societies had to register afresh, the control of authors was strengthened, and authors of works used in films and sound recordings gained a right to share in royalties.

cards.f: Indian collective management organisations and their fields
cards.b: IPRS: music and lyrics. PPL and RMPL: sound recordings. ISRA: performers. IRRO: reprographic rights. Current registration status should be checked with the Copyright Office.

cards.f: Why do the financial statements of knowledge companies understate their value?
cards.b: Research and brand building are expensed under Ind AS 38, employees are not shown as assets, assets are carried at historical cost, and network effects, data and future opportunities are not captured.

cards.f: Enterprise value
cards.b: Equity value plus net debt: the value of the business to all providers of capital.

cards.f: Why is the residual method unreliable? Use the notes' numbers.
cards.b: Market value ₹10,000 crore − book value ₹2,000 crore = ₹8,000 crore. A 20 per cent share price fall makes it ₹6,000 crore though nothing inside the firm changed. The gap reflects mood and hidden items, and changes daily.

cards.f: A loss-making pharmaceutical company has a promising research pipeline. How might it be valued?
cards.b: Not from its accounts. Use DCF with scenarios, multiples such as EV to revenue, a sum of the parts, real options for the research pipeline and customer lifetime value, sometimes after treating R&D as an investment.

cards.f: Why is an invention not yet an innovation?
cards.b: An invention is a new idea or device. It becomes an innovation only when it is successfully introduced into the market as a new or improved product, process, service or business model; diffusion is its later spread among users.

cards.f: Distinguish modular from architectural innovation (Henderson and Clark).
cards.b: Modular: core ideas replaced, links between components unchanged. Architectural: core ideas kept, links changed. Incremental changes neither; radical changes both.

cards.f: Rogers' adopter groups and their shares
cards.b: Innovators 2.5 per cent, early adopters 13.5 per cent, early majority 34 per cent, late majority 34 per cent, laggards 16 per cent.

cards.f: What is the "sailing ship effect", and what does Granstrand pair it with?
cards.b: Old technologies may improve under threat from a new one. Granstrand also observes that firms strong in an old technology are often slow to build patent positions in a new one, which gives entrants an opening.

cards.f: What does Granstrand's strategy ladder imply for IP?
cards.b: IP strategy sits below the business, innovation, technology and commercialisation strategies, so IP choices should follow business choices.

cards.f: Why should a radical innovator file early with broad claims, and what is the risk?
cards.b: Early broad claims and strategic patents secure the pioneer position before the second race for surrounding patents. But broad claims attract opposition and revocation, so drafting must withstand the inventive step requirement of s. 2(1)(ja).

cards.f: Why does radical innovation need patient finance?
cards.b: It involves high uncertainty and cost and long development, so it needs venture capital, government grants or staged corporate investment. It risks technical failure, slow adoption, lack of complementary assets and regulatory delay.

cards.f: Besides patents, how does a radical innovator protect its processes and its new brand?
cards.b: Processes may be protected as trade secrets and the new brand by trade marks, alongside early broad filings, strategic patents and follow up (surrounding) patents.

cards.f: Where does a disruptive entrant start, and when is disruption complete?
cards.b: At the low end (customers the leaders neglect) or in a new market (people not buying at all), with a simpler, cheaper or more convenient "good enough" product. It improves and moves up; disruption is complete when mainstream customers adopt it.

cards.f: Why, on Christensen's analysis, was Uber not disruptive?
cards.b: Because it began in the main market with a better service, not at the low end or in a new market.

cards.f: Why do disrupters in India rely less on patents?
cards.b: Their edge lies in business models, speed and network effects, and business methods as such are not patentable (s. 3(k)). Protection comes mainly from copyright in software, trade secrets, brands and contracts.

cards.f: How should incumbents respond to disruptive entrants?
cards.b: Their portfolios, built for sustaining innovation, may not block a new business model, so they must watch low end and new market entrants, create separate units, or invest in or acquire the newcomers.

cards.f: The syllabus says "sustaining and sustainable innovation". What must your answer do first?
cards.b: State which meaning it uses: sustaining innovation in Christensen's sense (the likely meaning beside radical, disruptive and incremental) or environmentally sustainable (green) innovation.

cards.f: What is the main IP question for green innovation?
