cards.b: Diffusion: green patents attract investment, wide licensing can spread clean technology, WIPO GREEN connects owners and users, and transfer to developing countries takes place through licences and partnerships.

cards.f: Who usually wins sustaining innovation contests, and with what IP?
cards.b: Established firms, which have the resources and motivation. They use continuous follow up patenting, large portfolios, cross licensing and protection of designs and brands.

cards.f: Why can "petty" or "junk" patents still be valuable?
cards.b: Granstrand shows that minor patents from continuous patenting can serve as bargaining chips, although too many weak patents waste money.

cards.f: What four limits does Indian law place on protecting incremental innovation?
cards.b: Obvious changes fail the inventive step test; s. 3(d) requires enhanced efficacy for new forms of known substances; India has no utility model or petty patent system; the law guards against evergreening.

cards.f: Match each innovation type to the IP it relies on.
cards.b: Radical: pioneer and strategic patents. Disruptive: business model and speed. Sustaining: follow up patents. Incremental: continuous patents, designs and secrets.

cards.f: How do closed and open innovation differ in their view of IP?
cards.b: Closed: control IP so that nobody else profits. Open: earn from others' use of the firm's IP and buy others' IP when it helps the business.

cards.f: Distinguish the inbound, outbound and coupled models.
cards.b: Inbound (outside-in): bring in external knowledge by licensing in, acquiring start ups or crowdsourcing. Outbound (inside-out): take ideas out by licensing, sale of IP or spin offs. Coupled: create knowledge jointly through alliances, consortia and joint development.

cards.f: What is "layered" knowledge sharing?
cards.b: One of the four sharing modes of Bogers, Bekkers and Granstrand: full sharing among core members and limited sharing with outer members. The others are open to all, open within the group only, and closed.

cards.f: What are the risks of open innovation?
cards.b: Loss of control, leakage of knowledge, the "not invented here" attitude, coordination costs and disputes over ownership.

cards.f: Why does IP make open innovation possible rather than block it?
cards.b: Clear ownership allows firms to disclose knowledge safely and to license it on agreed terms.

cards.f: Distinguish background, foreground, sideground and postground IP.
cards.b: Background: brought in by each party. Foreground: created in the project. Sideground: developed in house in parallel with it. Postground: developed after it ends.

cards.f: Exclusive, sole or non-exclusive licence: who may use the IP?
cards.b: Exclusive: the licensee only, excluding even the licensor. Sole: only the licensor and the licensee. Non-exclusive: many licensees.

cards.f: Patents Act, ss. 50 and 140 in collaborations
cards.b: s. 50: a joint owner cannot license the patent or assign a share without the consent of the other owners. s. 140: tying arrangements, exclusive grant backs, bars on challenging validity and coercive package licensing in patent licences are void.

cards.f: Permissive versus copyleft open source licences?
cards.b: Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache) allow use in closed products; copyleft licences (GPL) require modified versions to remain open, so firms must track the open source code they use.

cards.f: Why is patent information a unique management resource?
cards.b: It discloses technology in a standard format, often before it appears anywhere else. Granstrand found it the most important method of tracking others' technology in large Japanese firms.

cards.f: Which search answers which question?
cards.b: Novelty: can it be patented? Freedom to operate: does a product infringe live patents? Validity: can a patent be revoked? Landscape: who is active in a field? Due diligence: ownership, status and risk in a transaction.

cards.f: First patent map
cards.b: Published by the Japan Patent Office in 1968 (Granstrand).

cards.f: Why must patent search results be read with care?
cards.b: Coverage and data quality differ, machine translations mislead, applications are published only after about 18 months, company names vary, legal status may be outdated and raw counts mislead. Confirm status on the official register.

cards.f: What four questions does IP due diligence answer?
cards.b: Does the target own or validly control the IP? Is it valid and enforceable? Is the business free to operate without infringing? What is the IP worth after taking risks into account?

cards.f: How are due diligence findings reflected in the deal?
cards.b: Through price adjustment, warranties, indemnities, conditions to be met before completion and escrow; after completion, the transfers must be registered.

cards.f: Why must consultancy contracts be checked in due diligence?
cards.b: Consultants own their work unless they assign it, so without a written assignment the chain of title is broken.

cards.f: Chain of title and encumbrance provisions
cards.b: Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69; Copyright Act, s. 19; Trade Marks Act, s. 45. Charges: Companies Act, 2013, s. 77; security interests filed with CERSAI.

cards.f: Distinguish IP due diligence from an IP audit.
cards.b: Due diligence investigates IP before a particular transaction; an IP audit is an internal and regular review not tied to a deal.

cards.f: Licence or assignment: what is the difference?
cards.b: A licence permits the licensee to do acts that would otherwise infringe, on agreed terms, while ownership remains with the licensor; an assignment transfers ownership.

cards.f: Copyright licence formalities
cards.b: Must be in writing (Copyright Act, s. 30); under s. 30A the s. 19 requirements apply, so identify the work, rights, duration, territory and royalty.

cards.f: Why must a trade mark licence preserve quality control?
cards.b: So that the mark continues to indicate a single trade source.

cards.f: How do licence clauses interlock?
cards.b: Exclusivity is usually paired with a minimum royalty; field and territory limits must match the improvement clauses; termination must address sublicences and stock; warranties and indemnities are read together.

cards.f: What does a licensor usually warrant, and what not?
cards.b: It warrants title; validity is usually not warranted.

cards.f: Distinguish value, price and consideration.
cards.b: Value: an estimate of worth for a purpose and date. Price: the amount actually agreed. Consideration: what is actually given, such as cash, shares or a cross licence.

cards.f: Distinguish legal, economic and useful life.
cards.b: Legal life: the term of protection. Economic life: the period during which the right earns income, usually shorter. Useful life: the accounting estimate used for amortisation.

cards.f: Early securitisation of royalties
cards.b: Bonds backed by David Bowie's music royalties, 1997.

cards.f: What shortens economic life, and how do valuers handle the uncertainty?
cards.b: New technology, slow market adoption, weak enforcement, competition and regulation. Valuers use scenarios, sensitivity analysis, probability weighting, simulation and real options.

cards.f: The notes' CAPM and WACC
cards.b: Cost of equity = 7 + 1.3 × 7 = 16.1 per cent; WACC = 0.6 × 16.1 + 0.4 × 7.5 = 12.66 per cent.

cards.f: Example 1 (commercialising a patent)
cards.b: ₹50 crore now; ₹15, 20, 25 and 20 crore over four years at 12 per cent: PV 59.84, NPV ₹9.84 crore, IRR about 20.5 per cent. Go ahead.

cards.f: Example 2 (running royalty)
cards.b: PV ₹5.62 crore at 14 per cent (₹5.92 crore at 12, ₹5.34 crore at 16); a ₹6 crore lump sum is worth ₹4.5 crore after tax.

cards.f: Why does Example 3's NPV fall from 153.79 to 4.15?
cards.b: Each cash flow is multiplied by the probability of reaching it; the income in years 4 to 8 has only an 18.9 per cent chance, so the risk-adjusted NPV is 4.15.

cards.f: Why should a patent not be given a terminal value?
cards.b: Terminal value (next year's cash flow ÷ (r − g)) is for assets with no fixed end; a patent has a fixed term, so its income stops when protection ends.

cards.f: 25 per cent rule of thumb
cards.b: The licensor gets about one quarter of the licensee's expected profit: a 20 per cent margin suggests about 5 per cent of sales. Simple but criticised as arbitrary.

cards.f: Royalty benchmarking example
cards.b: Royalties of 3.5, 4.0, 5.5, 6.0 and 8.0 per cent: median 5.5 per cent, middle range 4.0 to 6.0 per cent; the 8 per cent licence is less comparable (it included know how and support).

cards.f: Why is royalty benchmarking routine in Indian tax law?
cards.b: Royalties between related companies must be at arm's length under the Income Tax Act, 2025, ss. 161 to 173.

cards.f: What limits benchmarking?
cards.b: Scarce true comparables, confidential licence terms and subjective adjustments; Granstrand warns that patent and R&D figures must refer to the same group of companies before comparison.

cards.f: Relief from royalty
cards.b: Value = Σ [Revenue × Royalty rate × (1 minus tax rate) ÷ (1 + r)<sup>t</sup>]. Notes' example: 11.66. Suits trade marks and technologies with observable royalty rates.

cards.f: How does the multi-period excess earnings method work?
cards.b: Take the profit of the main asset, deduct a fair charge for all other assets (working capital, machinery, workforce and brand) and discount the remaining excess earnings. Notes' example: 39.98.

cards.f: With and without example
cards.b: Cash flows of 50, 55 and 60 would fall to 42, 46 and 50; the differences of 8, 9 and 10 discounted at 15 per cent give 20.34.

cards.f: What are the common mistakes in discounted methods?
cards.b: Counting the same income twice, mixing before tax cash flows with after tax rates, giving a patent an unlimited life and borrowing royalty rates from unlike deals.

cards.f: Why can simple patent counts mislead?
cards.b: A few patents carry most of the value, counting units differ, flooding and decoy filings inflate numbers, many patents are unused or weak, and some may have lapsed or face challenge.

cards.f: Portfolio A (3 strong families, index 4.83) or Portfolio B (10 weak families, index 2.0)?
cards.b: A is stronger even though B is larger: quality, not size, decides value.

cards.f: How should patent stocks be counted so that they do not mislead?
cards.b: Count families and active patents, adjust for quality, depreciate older patents, value the "crown jewel" patents separately by income methods, and confirm ownership and validity through due diligence.

cards.f: SARFAESI Act, 2002
cards.b: s. 2(1)(t): property includes know how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences and franchises; s. 13: secured creditors enforce without going to court.

cards.f: Where must security over IP be registered?
cards.b: With CERSAI; for a patent mortgage, in writing and on the register under ss. 68 and 69 of the Patents Act; and charges with the Registrar of Companies under s. 77 of the Companies Act, 2013.

cards.f: Collateral haircut example
cards.b: ₹3.63 crore value; 50 per cent haircut gives ₹1.81 crore; lending half gives about ₹0.91 crore.

cards.f: Why is IP-backed lending still limited in India?
cards.b: Lenders face uncertain values, thin resale markets, obsolescence, territorial limits, licence restrictions and invalidity; the IBC moratorium stops enforcement; and as on 7 November 2026 there is no dedicated RBI framework.

cards.f: What are the five types of IP audit?
cards.b: General (whole portfolio), event based (before a merger, investment, public issue, loan or launch), focused (one area), royalty (a licensee's payments) and compliance (filings and legal duties).

cards.f: Audit risk score
cards.b: Likelihood (1 to 5) × impact (1 to 5): 15 to 25 high, 8 to 14 medium, 1 to 7 low.

cards.f: What compliance points does an IP audit check?
cards.b: Renewals, Form 27 and the record keeping that auditors examine under CARO 2020.

cards.f: Tax on royalty: residents and non-residents
cards.b: Residents: TDS 10 per cent (2 per cent for film royalty and fees for technical services) where payments exceed ₹50,000 a year, s. 393(1). Non-residents: 20 per cent of gross (s. 207) or a lower treaty rate (s. 159), deducted under s. 393(2); PE-connected royalty is business income.

cards.f: Patent box
cards.b: s. 194(1): 10 per cent of gross royalty, no expenses; resident patentee who is true and first inventor, at least 75 per cent of spending in India, option in Form 65; five-year lock-out.

cards.f: Depreciation on acquired IP
cards.b: 25 per cent under s. 33(1)(b) on know how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences and franchises; not on goodwill.

cards.f: When is a payment for software royalty?
cards.b: A copy for the buyer's own use without any transfer of copyright rights is generally not royalty under tax treaties; payment for the right to copy or modify software is royalty.

cards.f: A group company licenses its IP to an Indian affiliate. Which two further regimes apply, and how?
cards.b: Transfer pricing: the royalty must be at arm's length (ss. 161 to 173), with IP profit going to the company performing the DEMPE functions. GST: the licence is a supply of services (Schedule II, para 5(c)) at 18 per cent; imports fall under reverse charge, exports can be zero rated.

about:
Welcome to IPR Management: the study of intellectual property as a business asset that a firm must find, measure, protect, use and account for within the limits of Indian law.

The notes are in three Parts. Each one builds on the one before, so it pays to study them in order.

Part One: Measuring and Extracting Value (1.1 to 1.7)

What intangible assets are and why accounts show so few of them; public policy and India’s legal framework; intellectual capital and its frameworks and formulas; the routes for earning from IP and their legal limits; start-ups; the portfolio as a competitive tool; and the intellectual asset manager.

Part Two: Portfolio Management (2.1 to 2.12)

Choosing protection, including patent or trade secret; categorising a portfolio from business, technical and legal perspectives; evaluation and valuation; IP value indices, empirical and option models; monitoring intellectual capital; knowledge assets; patent stocks; copyright collective management; and valuing knowledge companies.

Part Three: Innovation and IP Protection (3.1 to 3.18)

Radical, disruptive, sustaining and incremental innovation; open innovation and IP; patent databases; due diligence and licence drafting; valuation and finance through NPV, benchmarking and discounted methods; patent stocks; IP as collateral; IP audit; and IP taxation.

How the Parts build. Part One gives the vocabulary and the reasons: why intangibles are hard to see in the accounts, how they can still be measured, and how value is extracted. Part Two applies those ideas to running a portfolio, from choosing the right form of protection to putting a value on it. Part Three puts both to work in innovation and in transactions: licences, due diligence, finance, audit and tax.

How to read the references.

  1. s. means section and ss. sections. The Act is named with the section, for example s. 84, Patents Act, 1970 or s. 247, Companies Act, 2013. Where a slide gives a bare section just after naming an Act, it belongs to that Act.
  2. Ind AS is an Indian Accounting Standard, notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015; AS is the standard for other entities; IAS is the international standard. para means a paragraph of a standard, as in Ind AS 38, para 57.
  3. VS is an ICAI Valuation Standard, such as VS 302 on intangible assets. CARO 2020 is the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020. Form 27 and rule 131 refer to the Patents Rules.
  4. Names such as Granstrand, Teece, Sveiby, Kaplan and Norton are the authors of the models discussed, not cases.
  5. The law, standards and tax position are stated as on 7 November 2026. Boxes marked “Law update” flag points that may change.

Each Part ends with quick revision, practice questions and answer plans. Use recall mode to test yourself on the bold terms, and the Memory Lab to drill the lists, frameworks and formulas.
appB:
1. Intangible asset (Ind AS 38): an identifiable non monetary asset without physical substance; identifiable, controlled, with expected future economic benefits
  2. Ind AS 38 recognition: research always expensed (para 54); development only on six conditions (para 57); internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists never (para 63); internally generated goodwill never (para 48)
  3. Market to book ratio: Market value of equity ÷ Book value of net assets; ₹10,000 crore ÷ ₹2,000 crore = 5
  4. Tobin’s q: Market value of the firm ÷ Replacement cost of its assets; above 1 suggests valuable intangibles
  5. VAIC: HCE + SCE + CEE = VA ÷ HC + (VA − HC) ÷ VA + VA ÷ CE; VA 200, HC 80, CE 400 gives 3.6
  6. Calculated Intangible Value: (90 − 12 per cent of 500) × (1 − 25 per cent) ÷ 15 per cent = 150
  7. Scorecard method: Average value × weighted score; weights team 30, opportunity 25, product 15, competition 10, sales channels 10, further funding 5, others 5 per cent; ₹20 crore × 1.155 = ₹23.1 crore
  8. Venture capital method: Post money = Exit value ÷ (1 + target return)years; pre money = post money − investment; ₹200 crore, 50 per cent, five years, ₹10 crore gives ₹26.34 crore, ₹16.34 crore and about 38 per cent
  9. Registered valuers: s. 247, Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017; ICAI VS 302 on intangible assets
  10. Prospectus liability for IC information: ss. 34 and 35, Companies Act, 2013
  11. Income Tax Act, 2025: s. 33(1)(b) depreciation on acquired intangibles, not goodwill; s. 194(1) concessional 10 per cent on royalty from patents developed and registered in India
  12. IP as security: SARFAESI Act, 2002 includes intangibles in property; security interests registered with CERSAI
  13. Licence and assignment formalities: Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69 (writing and registration); Copyright Act, s. 30 (licence in writing) and s. 19 (assignment in writing); Trade Marks Act, s. 45 (assignment registered)
  14. Competition limit: s. 3(5)(i), Competition Act, 2002 protects only reasonable conditions needed to protect IP rights
  15. Void licence conditions: s. 140, Patents Act: tying to unpatented goods, exclusive grant backs, no-challenge clauses, coercive package licensing
  16. Compulsory licence: s. 84, Patents Act: patent not worked in India, after three years from grant
  17. Opposition and revocation: s. 25(1) before grant; s. 25(2) within one year from publication of grant; s. 64 revocation
  18. Start-up ownership: Patents Act, s. 6 (true and first inventor or assignee); Copyright Act, s. 17 (employer owns employee’s work), s. 19 (freelancer’s work only by written assignment)
  19. Form 27: once for every period of three financial years (Patents Rules, rule 131, as amended in 2024)
  20. Patent renewal fees: 10 per cent reduction when paid online four or more years in advance
  21. Foreign filing: s. 39, Patents Act: permission before filing abroad first, for inventions made in India by residents
  22. Trade mark renewal: every ten years
  23. SIPP scheme: facilitators and fee support for start-ups; extended up to 31 March 2026
  24. IAS 38 review: IASB research project; no change by 7 November 2026
  25. Terms of rights: patent 20 years from filing; design 10 years, extendable by 5; trade mark renewable 10-year periods without limit; copyright generally life of the author plus 60 years; trade secret as long as it remains secret
  26. Paris Convention priority: 12 months for patents; 6 months for designs and trade marks
  27. PCT route: entry into the Indian national phase at 31 months from priority
  28. s. 3(d), Patents Act, 1970: no patents on new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy
  29. s. 3(k), Patents Act, 1970: excludes computer programs as such and business methods
  30. s. 39, Patents Act, 1970: a resident inventor needs permission before filing abroad first
  31. s. 50, Patents Act, 1970: a joint owner cannot license or assign a share without the other owners' consent
  32. s. 60, Patents Act, 1970: a lapsed patent can be restored only within the period and conditions allowed by law
  33. s. 27, Indian Contract Act, 1872: most post employment non compete restraints are void
  34. s. 247, Companies Act, 2013: registered valuers for statutory valuations
  35. ss. 161 to 173, Income Tax Act, 2025: related party royalties must be at arm's length
  36. Ind AS 103, Ind AS 36 and Ind AS 113: fair values in acquisitions and impairment tests
  37. ICAI VS 302: the valuation standard dealing specifically with intangible assets
  38. Patent Asset Index: Competitive Impact = Technology Relevance × Market Coverage; index = Σ Competitive Impact (A 4.83 against B 2.0)
  39. Market value model: V = q × (A + γK)
  40. Black and Scholes: C = S × N(d1) − K × e−rT × N(d2); notes' example 28.11, against an NPV of −20
  41. Binomial model: p = (1 + r − d) ÷ (u − d) = 0.5286; option value 0.5286 × 30 ÷ 1.07 = 14.82
  42. Decision tree: NPV 7.27 if committed, 25.45 if flexible; flexibility worth 18.18
  43. Depreciated patent stock: Kt = (1 − δ) × Kt−1 + Pt, δ about 15 per cent; example 74.20 against a simple count of 106
  44. Revealed technological advantage: (firm's patents in field ÷ firm's total) ÷ (world patents in field ÷ world total); 20 per cent ÷ 5 per cent = 4.0
  45. Patent publication delay: about 18 months
  46. Copyright societies: ss. 33, 33A, 34, 35 and 36, Copyright Act, 1957; registration lasts five years; Copyright Rules, 2013; 2012 amendments
  47. Enterprise value: equity value + net debt
  48. Residual method example: ₹10,000 crore − ₹2,000 crore = ₹8,000 crore; after a 20 per cent price fall, ₹6,000 crore
  49. Directive 2014/26/EU: EU rules on governance and transparency of collective management
  50. Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: applies to knowledge assets that include personal data
  51. Rogers' adopter groups: innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34%, laggards 16%
  52. Inventive step: s. 2(1)(ja), Patents Act: broad radical claims must withstand it
  53. Business methods: not patentable as such, s. 3(k), Patents Act
  54. New forms of known substances: s. 3(d), Patents Act: enhanced efficacy required
  55. Joint owners of a patent: no licence or assignment of a share without the others' consent, s. 50
  56. Patent licence or mortgage formalities: in writing and registered, Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69
  57. Void licence conditions: s. 140, Patents Act: tying, exclusive grant backs, no-challenge clauses, coercive package licensing
  58. Reasonable IP conditions: protected by s. 3(5)(i), Competition Act, 2002
  59. Copyright licence: in writing, s. 30; s. 19 requirements apply via s. 30A
  60. Chain of title: Patents Act, ss. 68 and 69; Copyright Act, s. 19; Trade Marks Act, s. 45
  61. Registration of charges: s. 77, Companies Act, 2013; security interests with CERSAI
  62. First patent map: Japan Patent Office, 1968
  63. Publication of applications: only after about 18 months
  64. PV: FV ÷ (1 + r)t
  65. NPV: Σ [CFt ÷ (1 + r)t] minus initial investment; positive = worthwhile
  66. Terminal value: next year's cash flow ÷ (r − g); none for a fixed-term patent
  67. CAPM: risk free rate + beta × market risk premium; 7 + 1.3 × 7 = 16.1%
  68. WACC (notes): 0.6 × 16.1 + 0.4 × 7.5 = 12.66%
  69. Example 1: NPV ₹9.84 crore (PV 59.84 − 50), IRR about 20.5%
  70. Example 2: running royalty ₹5.62 crore at 14% (₹5.92 crore at 12%, ₹5.34 crore at 16%); lump sum ₹6 crore = ₹4.5 crore after tax
  71. Example 3: risk-adjusted NPV 4.15; unadjusted 153.79
  72. 25 per cent rule: royalty ≈ 25% × licensee's profit margin; 20% margin → 5%
  73. Benchmark example: median 5.5%, middle range 4.0 to 6.0%
  74. Arm's length royalties: Income Tax Act, 2025, ss. 161 to 173
  75. Relief from royalty: Σ [Revenue × Royalty rate × (1 − tax) ÷ (1 + r)t]; example 11.66
  76. Excess earnings / with and without: 39.98 / 20.34
  77. SARFAESI Act, 2002: s. 2(1)(t) intangibles are property; s. 13 enforcement without court
  78. Collateral example: ₹3.63 crore → 50% haircut → ₹1.81 crore → loan about ₹0.91 crore
  79. Audit risk bands: likelihood × impact: 15–25 high, 8–14 medium, 1–7 low
  80. Income Tax Act, 2025: applies from 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act; royalty defined in s. 9
  81. TDS on royalty to residents: 10% (2% films and FTS) above ₹50,000 a year, s. 393(1)
  82. Non-resident royalty: 20% of gross, s. 207, or treaty rate, s. 159; deduction under s. 393(2)
  83. Depreciation on acquired IP: 25%, s. 33(1)(b); not on goodwill
  84. Patent box: 10% of gross, s. 194(1); resident true and first inventor; ≥ 75% spending in India; Form 65; five-year lock-out
  85. GST on IP licensing: 18%, supply of services, CGST Act, Schedule II, para 5(c)
  86. Compliance filings: Form 27; record keeping under CARO 2020

glossary.def: A resource with no physical form that is expected to bring future benefits to a business. Under Ind AS 38: an identifiable non monetary asset without physical substance.
Under Ind AS 38, an intangible is identifiable if it can be separated from the business or arises from contractual or legal rights.
The business’s power over an intangible asset, which in practice usually means owning a legal right or a contractual right.
The first level of measuring: listing what the firm has, usually through an IP register.
The second level of measuring: grouping assets by type, technology, business or legal status.
The third level of measuring: using non money indicators such as the number of patents, citations, staff turnover or customer retention.
The fourth level of measuring: putting a money value on an asset for a stated purpose and date.
The risk that the right behind a value fails: a patent may be revoked, a mark may become generic and a trade secret may leak.
The Indian Accounting Standard on intangible assets, notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015; it applies a conservative recognition rule.
The accounting standard on intangible assets for companies outside Ind AS; it takes an approach similar to Ind AS 38.
Voluntary measurement of all intangibles, including human capital, aimed at better decisions rather than audited reliability.
Market value of equity ÷ book value of net assets. It shows the gap that partly reflects unrecorded intangibles, growth expectations and market mood.
Rules made by government, regulators and standard setters on how intangible assets are recognised, valued, disclosed, audited, taxed, financed and counted in national statistics.
The central policy choice: recognising more intangibles makes accounts more realistic (relevance), while strict recognition avoids hard-to-audit, manipulable estimates (reliability).
A professional who must carry out valuations required under company law: s. 247, Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Registered Valuers and Valuation) Rules, 2017.
The ICAI Valuation Standard on intangible assets, part of the ICAI Valuation Standards 2018.
The Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020, which requires the auditor to report whether proper records of intangible assets are kept and on any revaluation.
The finance statute that includes intangible assets in the definition of property, so IP can be secured.
The registry with which security interests over intangible assets are registered.
India’s IP policy, which lists commercialisation of IPR as an objective, including valuation and IP based financing.
A scheme supporting start-ups with IP filings through facilitators and fee support; the notes record that it was extended up to 31 March 2026.
The Quick Revision’s name for the concessional 10 per cent tax on royalty from patents developed and registered in India (s. 194(1), Income Tax Act, 2025).
A reporting approach that encourages firms to report on six capitals: financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, and natural.
The knowledge, skills, systems and relationships of a firm that can be converted into value.
The knowledge and skill of employees, which the firm does not own and which leaves when people leave.
What remains in the firm, such as processes, databases, systems, culture and IP rights.
The value of relationships with customers, suppliers and partners, including brand and reputation.
Market value = financial + intellectual capital; IC = human + structural capital; structural = customer + organisational capital; organisational = innovation + process capital.
The identification, measurement and reporting of intellectual capital, mainly for internal management; voluntary and not part of the statutory financial statements.
Kaplan and Norton’s framework measuring performance from financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth perspectives, linked through cause and effect.
Edvinsson and Malone’s framework of five focus areas (financial, customer, process, renewal and development, and human), with human capital at the centre.
Sveiby’s framework measuring external structure, internal structure and the competence of people, each through indicators of growth, efficiency and stability.
Brooking’s framework dividing IC into market assets, human centred assets, IP assets and infrastructure assets.
Roos’s method that combines indicators into one index and tracks changes over time.
Market value of the firm ÷ replacement cost of its assets. A q above 1 suggests valuable intangibles that replacement cost does not capture.
HCE + SCE + CEE, where HCE = VA ÷ HC, SCE = (VA − HC) ÷ VA and CEE = VA ÷ CE; VA is value added, HC employee cost, CE capital employed.
A method that takes profit above the industry’s return on tangible assets, deducts tax and divides by the cost of capital to value intangibles.
The production of new knowledge and inventions.
The conversion of knowledge into money or market power.
Teece’s first condition: the strength of legal protection, such as valid patents or well kept secrets. Strong protection lets the innovator profit; weak protection helps imitators.
Teece’s second condition: once a standard design emerges, competition moves to price and scale.
Manufacturing, distribution, service and brand. If imitators own these and protection is weak, they may capture most of the profit (Teece).
Harrison and Sullivan’s ladder: using IP defensively, controlling IP costs, IP as a profit centre, integrating IP with business strategy, and a visionary stage.
Extracting value by using IP oneself: it keeps competitors out, and protected features, designs and marks support higher prices.
Allowing others to use IP for a royalty while the licensor keeps ownership.
Transfer of ownership of IP for a price.
Licensing a business system with marks and know-how; the franchisor must control quality to protect the mark.
A combination of patent licences with know-how and technical assistance.
A collaborative method in which firms buy in outside ideas and sell out unused ones.
A financial method of extracting value by securitising royalty streams.
Making an invention public so that nobody can patent it, keeping the field free.
An arrangement letting several owners license related patents together.
A long lasting general guideline.
A specific plan of action.
Granstrand’s model-policy principle of encouraging early filing.
A licence that a patent not worked in India may attract under s. 84 of the Patents Act after three years from grant.
The statement of working of patents, filed once for every period of three financial years (Patents Rules, rule 131, as amended in 2024).
Granstrand’s term for founders’ tendency to overvalue their own ideas.
The ability to make and sell a product without infringing others’ patents; a freedom to operate check shows whether it may infringe.

Start-up valuation that adjusts the average value of similar funded start-ups by weighted factors (team 30, opportunity 25, product 15, competition 10, sales channels 10, funding 5, others 5 per cent).
Start-up valuation that gives value for five risk reducing elements: a sound idea, a prototype, a good team, strategic relationships and a product launch or sales.
Start-up valuation working backwards from expected exit value: post money = exit value ÷ (1 + target return)^years; pre money = post money − investment.
Start-up valuation that weights values in best, normal and worst cases by their probabilities.
The whole group of IP rights a firm owns or controls, managed together; legally, a bundle of territorial rights with different terms, owners and conditions.
The deterrent effect of a strong portfolio: because firms depend on each other’s patents, others hesitate to attack a firm that can sue back.
Granstrand’s term for a party that holds a patent but has no manufacturing to be counter attacked, and so can make demands on large firms.
What offensive blocking secures.
What defensive blocking secures.
A patent strategy using a few patents for one use; easy to invent around.
One patent that is too costly for rivals to invent around.
A patent strategy covering a field with many patents.
A patent strategy placing a row of patents across several research paths.
A patent strategy placing many small patents around a rival’s key patent to force a cross licence.
A deliberate combination of different patents.
Patenting only key inventions.
Filing throughout the product life; it costs more but gives wider and longer protection.
Also IP manager or chief IP officer: the person who manages IP as a business asset by identifying, protecting, using and defending it in line with business strategy.
A right under the Patents Act, 1970 over an invention that is new, involves an inventive step and is capable of industrial application, for 20 years from filing, subject to the exclusions in s. 3.
A right under the Designs Act, 2000 protecting the shape, pattern or appearance of an article for 10 years, extendable by 5.
A right under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 protecting signs that distinguish goods or services, for renewable periods of 10 years without limit.

A right under the Copyright Act, 1957 arising automatically in literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, films, sound recordings and software, generally for the life of the author plus 60 years.
A right protecting goods linked to a place.
Confidential information protected in India not by statute but through contracts and the equitable duty of confidence, for as long as it remains secret.
The decision of which IP right to use, when, where and how much, so that IP supports the business at the lowest total cost and risk.
Granstrand's recommendation to combine several rights around one business, such as a secret formula, patented machinery, a registered design and a registered trade mark.
The time after a first filing within which protection can be sought abroad under the Paris Convention: 12 months for patents, 6 months for designs and trade marks.
One international patent application, with entry into the Indian national phase at 31 months from priority.
Categorising rights as core or non core, strategic, defensive or offensive, revenue earning or cost generating, and by product line, business unit or market.
Categorising rights by technology field (IPC or CPC classes), basic technology or application, product or process, basic invention or improvement, and stage of maturity.
Categorising rights by type, registration, legal status, countries and remaining term, ownership, licences and security interests granted, and strength (validity, claim scope, enforceability).
A tool that scores each IP asset for business value and legal strength to decide whether to maintain, strengthen, license or sell, or drop it.
Rights high in both business value and legal strength, which should be maintained, enforced and extended.
Rights of high business value but weak legal position, to be strengthened through further filings, secrecy or better contracts.
A judgement of the quality and importance of an IP asset, usually expressed through scores or ratings and used for portfolio decisions and screening.
Fixing a value in money for an IP asset for a stated purpose and date, used in sales, licences, accounts, tax, loans and damages.
Values an asset at what it would cost to recreate or replace it, less obsolescence.
Values an asset by reference to prices or royalty rates in comparable transactions.
Values an asset as the present value of the future income it will generate.
An income method valuing the royalties saved by owning the asset rather than licensing it.
An income method: business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used.
An income method: the difference in business value with and without the asset; suits non compete agreements.
An income method valuing the extra price or cost saving due to the asset.
A single score that ranks patents or portfolios by quality by combining several indicators; a tool for screening and comparison, not for fixing a price.
Later patents citing a patent; a sign of its technical importance.
The number of countries in which protection is sought for an invention; a sign of expected commercial value.
Ernst and Omland's index: the sum across patent families of Competitive Impact, which is Technology Relevance multiplied by Market Coverage.
In the Patent Asset Index, a family's citation-based score, with an average of 1.
In the Patent Asset Index, a family's score for the size of the markets in which it is protected, with a granted United States patent equal to 1.
Technology Relevance multiplied by Market Coverage for one patent family.
Models that estimate the value of IP from real data on large numbers of patents and firms rather than from forecasts for a single asset.
V = q × (A + γK): relates the stock market value of firms to their tangible assets and knowledge stock, with γ showing how the market values knowledge.
Models that read the spread of patent values from renewal data, since owners pay renewal fees only while a patent is worth more than the fee.
Empirical models showing that highly cited patents tend to be more valuable.
Empirical models that ask owners to estimate the value of their patents.
Empirical models measuring share price reactions to patent grants or court outcomes.
Empirical models using prices from patent sales and licences.
Viewing a patent as the right but not the obligation to exploit an invention exclusively, like a call option, so the owner can wait, expand, license, switch use or abandon.
An option pricing formula, C = S × N(d1) − K × e^(−rT) × N(d2), used to value the flexibility a patent gives.
An option model assuming that value moves up or down by set factors, valued with a risk neutral probability and discounted at the risk free rate.
In the binomial model, (1 + r − d) ÷ (u − d); 0.5286 in the notes' example.
A model that maps choices and outcomes over time to show the value of flexibility, such as launching only if the market is good.
Giving a picture of intellectual capital at one point in time.
Tracking intellectual capital regularly through indicators and targets so that management can act early.
An indicator that predicts the future.
An indicator that reports the past.
An IC statement combining a knowledge narrative, management challenges, initiatives and indicators.
Improving the number rather than the reality, for example by filing weak patents to raise patent counts.
The stocks of useful knowledge a firm holds: know how, skills, processes, designs, software, customer insight and IP.
Knowledge that lives in people's heads and is hard to express.
Knowledge that is written or coded and easy to transfer.
Arrow's point that a buyer cannot judge knowledge without seeing it, but once it is seen it has been given away.
Barney's test: knowledge gives competitive advantage when it is valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.
Prahalad and Hamel's forms of collective learning that open many markets, add customer value and are hard to copy.
Teece's ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure resources.
Cohen and Levinthal's ability to recognise and use outside knowledge.
Creating, capturing, storing, sharing, using and protecting knowledge.
Nonaka and Takeuchi's model of knowledge creation through socialisation, externalisation, combination and internalisation.
Maps of patents used to generate ideas, track rivals, plan research and strengthen bargaining.
The accumulated number of patents of a firm, industry or country, used as a measure of its stock of technical knowledge.
One invention counted once across the countries in which it is protected.
A patent stock giving less weight to older patents because knowledge becomes outdated: Kt = (1 − δ) × Kt−1 + Pt, with δ often about 15 per cent.
A firm's share of its patents in a field divided by that field's share of world patents; values above 1 show specialisation.
The system in which copyright societies license works on behalf of many owners, collect royalties and distribute them.
A registered body that licenses works on behalf of many owners, sets tariffs, collects and distributes royalties and enforces rights.
A licence from a copyright society covering its whole repertoire.
Collective management extended to non members by law, as in Nordic countries.
Software, pharmaceutical, media, platform and similar businesses that derive most of their value from technology, data, brands, people and relationships; Granstrand calls them IC firms.
The value of the business to all providers of capital; equity value plus net debt.
The value of the business to shareholders.
The value of individual assets.
The value of the legal rights and the income they protect.
Non money measures of intellectual capital.
Treating market value minus book value as the value of intellectual capital; unreliable because the gap includes market mood, ignores hidden items and changes every day.
A new idea or device.
The successful introduction of a new or improved product, process, service or business model into the market.
The spread of an innovation among users.
Schumpeter's term for the process in which new products and firms replace old ones.
Innovation in which core ideas and links between components are unchanged.
Innovation in which core ideas are replaced but the links between components are unchanged.
Innovation in which core ideas are kept but the links between components are changed.
Innovation in which both the core ideas and the links between components are changed.
Innovation arising where new science creates products.
Innovation arising where customer needs drive development.
The path a technology usually follows: improving slowly, then rapidly, then levelling off.
The improvement of an old technology under threat from a new one (Granstrand).
Granstrand's ordering that places IP strategy below business, innovation, technology and commercialisation strategies, so IP choices follow business choices.
A major technical change that creates a new technology base, a large jump in performance or an entirely new market.
Patents that rivals cannot easily invent around.
Follow up patents filed around a key patent in a second race (Granstrand).
Christensen's process by which a smaller firm with fewer resources successfully challenges established firms, starting at the low end or in a new market.
Entry by serving customers whom the leaders neglect, with a simpler, cheaper "good enough" product.
Entry by serving people who were not buying at all.
Improvement of existing products for existing customers, by small steps or major breakthroughs; established firms usually win.
Innovation that reduces environmental harm through cleaner energy, recycling or low emission processes.
A platform that connects owners and users of green technology.
Small, continuous improvements to existing products or processes, such as better features, lower cost or higher quality.
The extension of protection through minor changes, which Indian law guards against.
Chesbrough's term: using ideas from outside as well as inside the firm, and external as well as internal routes to market.
The model in which the firm invents, develops and sells everything itself and controls IP so nobody else profits.
Bringing in external knowledge through licensing in, acquiring start ups, crowdsourcing and working with suppliers and users.
Taking internal ideas out through licensing, sale of IP and spin offs.
Creating knowledge jointly with partners through alliances, consortia and joint development.
Full sharing of knowledge among core members of a collaboration and limited sharing with outer members.
IP brought into a collaboration by each party.
IP created in the collaboration project.
IP developed in house in parallel with the project.
IP developed after the project ends.
A licence that excludes everyone else, even the licensor.
A licence under which only the licensor and the licensee may use the IP.
A licence that allows many licensees.
An open source licence (such as MIT, BSD or Apache) that allows use in closed products.
An open source licence (such as the GPL) that requires modified versions to remain open.
A search asking whether an invention can be patented.
A search asking whether a product infringes live patents.
A search asking whether a patent can be revoked.
A search showing who is active in a field.
A search checking ownership, status and risk in a transaction.
Turning search results into charts of technologies, owners, trends and gaps; begun at the Japan Patent Office (first map 1968).
A careful legal and commercial investigation of IP before a transaction.
The written and registered assignments from inventors and earlier owners that prove ownership.
A charge or security interest over IP, such as a charge under s. 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 or an interest filed with CERSAI.
A systematic review of a firm's IP to find what it owns or uses, confirm ownership and protection, assess use and worth, and identify risks.
An examination of infringement risk for a particular product.
Advice answering a specific legal question.
Permission from the owner (licensor) to another (licensee) to do acts that would otherwise infringe the owner's IP, on agreed terms; ownership stays with the licensor.
The base on which a running royalty is calculated; it must be defined carefully.
A royalty calculated as a percentage of net sales or an amount per unit.
A licence term giving the licensor rights in the licensee's improvements; exclusive grant backs are void under s. 140.
An estimate of worth for a purpose and date.
The amount actually agreed.
What is actually given, such as cash, shares or a cross licence.
The figure for an asset in the accounts.
A lender's careful estimate of what it could recover on default.
The term of protection of an IP right.
The period during which an IP right earns income; usually shorter than its legal life.
The accounting estimate of life used for amortisation.
A future amount discounted to today: FV ÷ (1 + r)<sup>t</sup>.
The sum of discounted cash flows minus the initial investment; a project is worthwhile if it is positive.
The discount rate at which NPV is zero.
For an asset with no fixed end, next year's cash flow ÷ (r − g); not given to a fixed-term patent.
Cost of equity = risk free rate + beta × market risk premium.
The weighted average of the cost of equity and the after tax cost of debt.
NPV in which each cash flow is multiplied by the probability of reaching it; used for staged projects.
Comparing an IP asset, royalty rate or portfolio with similar transactions or competitors to estimate value or judge performance.
Taking the royalty from comparable licences, adjusted for differences.
Typical royalty ranges for an industry.
Giving the licensor about one quarter of the licensee's expected profit; simple but criticised as arbitrary.
Dividing profit according to each party's contribution.
Comparing patent portfolios with competitors using counts and quality indices.
Comparing IP management practices with leading firms.
Methods valuing IP as the present value of its future benefits; together they form the income approach.
Valuing the main asset by its profit after fair charges for all other assets used, discounted.
Valuing the extra price or cost saving that a brand or patent allows.
The most valuable patents in a portfolio, valued separately by income methods.
A security interest given to a lender over IP rights, and often their royalties, to recover a loan on default.
The reduction a lender applies to IP value to reach a distressed value.
The limited share of the (distressed) value that a lender will lend.
An IP audit covering the whole portfolio.
An IP audit done before a merger, investment, public issue, loan or product launch.
An IP audit of one area, such as trade secrets or software licences.
An audit checking a licensee's royalty payments.
An audit checking filings and legal duties.
The single year used by the Income Tax Act, 2025, equal to the financial year.
Under s. 9, payment for the transfer or licence of rights in patents, designs, secret formulas, trade marks, copyright and similar property, or for imparting technical or commercial knowledge.
Development, enhancement, maintenance, protection and exploitation: the functions that decide which group company should get IP profit.
The GST mechanism under which imports of IP services are taxed.

sort.title: Methods of extracting value
sort.intro: Five families for revision. Own use is the notes’ own term, and the notes name the collaborative and financial groups; “transactional” and “defensive” are study labels. Enforcement, standards, pools, copyright societies and spin-offs are left out because they fit no single family.
sort.prompt: Which family of extraction method is this?

items.text: Using your own patents to keep competitors out of the market
items.why: Own use: the firm exploits the IP itself, keeping rivals out.

items.text: Protected features, designs and marks that let the firm charge higher prices
items.why: Own use: the IP supports the firm’s own pricing; nothing is transferred.

items.text: Letting another firm use a patent for a royalty while keeping ownership
items.why: Licensing: a transfer of permission to use, for a royalty; the licensor keeps title.

items.text: Transferring ownership of a patent for a price
items.why: Assignment: ownership passes to the assignee, in writing and registered for patents.

items.text: Licensing a business system with marks and know-how, with quality control
items.why: Franchising: a licence of a whole business system; the franchisor controls quality to protect the mark.

items.text: Patent licences combined with know-how and technical assistance
items.why: Technology transfer: rights and knowledge pass to the recipient under contract.

items.text: Partners contributing IP to a new company
items.why: Joint venture: one of the notes’ collaborative methods.

items.text: A contract-based strategic alliance
items.why: Strategic alliances are listed among the collaborative methods.

items.text: A research collaboration with a university
items.why: Research collaborations with universities and firms are collaborative methods.

items.text: Buying in outside ideas and selling out unused ones
items.why: Open innovation is listed among the collaborative methods.

items.text: Offering IP as security for a loan
items.why: One of the notes’ financial methods; SARFAESI treats intangibles as property and CERSAI registers the security.

items.text: Selling future royalties
items.why: A financial method: the royalty stream is turned into money.

items.text: Securitising a royalty stream
items.why: Securitisation is listed among the financial methods.

items.text: Making an invention public so that nobody can patent it
items.why: Defensive publication keeps a field free rather than earning income.

items.text: Using patents as bargaining chips to obtain cross licences and freedom to operate
items.why: The patents are used to protect the firm’s freedom to operate, not to earn royalties.

sort.title: Which valuation approach?
sort.prompt: Which valuation approach does each method or feature belong to?

items.text: What it would cost to recreate the asset, less obsolescence
items.why: Recreation or replacement cost less obsolescence is the definition of the cost approach.

items.text: Simple, and suits early stage technology and software
items.why: The notes give these as the cost approach's strengths.

items.text: Weakness: cost is not the same as value
items.why: Spending a lot to build an asset does not make it valuable, the cost approach's main flaw.

items.text: Royalty rates in comparable licences
items.why: The market approach values by reference to prices or royalty rates in comparable transactions.

items.text: Prices paid in comparable transactions
items.why: Comparable deal prices are the market approach's evidence.

items.text: Weakness: true comparables are rare and deal terms are usually confidential
items.why: The market approach is only as good as its comparables.

items.text: Discounted cash flow
items.why: DCF takes the present value of future cash flows, the income approach.

items.text: Royalties saved by owning rather than licensing the asset
items.why: This is relief from royalty, an income method.

items.text: Business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used
items.why: This is excess earnings, an income method.

items.text: Difference in business value with and without the asset
items.why: The with and without method is an income method.

items.text: Extra price or cost saving due to the asset
items.why: This is premium profit, an income method.

items.text: Present value of the future income the asset will generate
items.why: This is the definition of the income approach.

sort.title: Input, process, output or outcome?
sort.prompt: What kind of IC indicator is each of these?

items.text: R&D spending
items.why: Resources put into innovation are inputs.

items.text: Training hours
items.why: Time invested in people is an input.

items.text: Projects running
items.why: Activity under way is a process measure.

items.text: Invention disclosures
items.why: Disclosures show the innovation process working, before any right is granted.

items.text: Patents granted
items.why: A granted right is a direct output of the process.

items.text: Products launched
items.why: A launched product is an output.

items.text: Revenue from new products
items.why: Money earned from outputs is an outcome.

items.text: Licence income
items.why: Income earned from IP is an outcome.

sort.title: Which type of innovation is this?
sort.prompt: Sort each example or description by type of innovation.

items.text: Transistors replace vacuum tubes
items.why: A new technology base replaces the old one: the notes' example of radical innovation.

items.text: Digital technology replaces analogue mobile telephony
items.why: A new technology base and a large performance jump: radical.

items.text: A change with high uncertainty and cost, long development, obsolete skills and frequent entry by newcomers
items.why: These are the listed features of radical innovation, which often creates new industries.

items.text: Steel minimills against integrated mills
items.why: A classic disruption: a cheaper, good enough entrant that moved up into the main market.

items.text: Personal computers against minicomputers
items.why: One of Christensen's classic examples of disruption in the notes.

items.text: Netflix against video rental chains
items.why: Listed in the notes as a classic disruptive example.

items.text: A simpler, cheaper product for people who were not buying at all
items.why: New market disruption: the entrant serves non-buyers with a good enough product.

items.text: A leader improves its product for its most demanding and profitable customers
items.why: Improving existing products for existing customers is sustaining innovation, which established firms usually win.

items.text: An established firm wins with a major breakthrough for its current customers, backed by follow up patents and cross licensing
items.why: Sustaining innovation can be a major breakthrough; what matters is that it serves existing customers.

items.text: Better features, lower cost or higher quality in small, continuous steps
items.why: Small, continuous improvements are the definition of incremental innovation.

items.text: A change in a product's appearance protected by a registered design
items.why: Firms register designs for changes in appearance when protecting incremental innovation.

items.text: Minor "petty" patents kept as bargaining chips
items.why: Granstrand: continuous patenting of incremental changes yields minor patents that can be bargaining chips.

sort.title: Which clause family does this term belong to?
sort.prompt: Sort each licence term into its clause family.

items.text: Field of use
items.why: The grant defines what is licensed, including the field of use.

items.text: Right to sublicense
items.why: Whether the licensee may sublicense is part of the scope of the grant.

items.text: Scope: make, use, sell or import
items.why: The acts licensed are the heart of the grant clauses.

items.text: Royalty rate and base
items.why: Consideration, rate and base are financial terms.

items.text: Reports, records and audit rights
items.why: These let the licensor check a royalty the licensee calculates; they sit in the financial clauses.

items.text: Deduction at source and grossing up
items.why: The allocation of taxes is a financial clause.

items.text: Quality control
items.why: How the licence is run day to day is operational; quality control is essential for trade marks.

items.text: Technical assistance
items.why: Support given by the licensor is an operational term.

items.text: Registration of the licence
items.why: Registration (ss. 68 and 69 for patents) is listed among the operational clauses.

items.text: Ownership of improvements and new IP
items.why: IP clauses decide who owns improvements, avoiding exclusive grant backs.

items.text: Protection of confidential know how
items.why: Know how protection belongs to the IP clauses.

items.text: Warranties on title
items.why: Warranties allocate risk; title is warranted, validity usually not.

items.text: Who sues infringers and who defends claims against the licensee
items.why: Enforcement and defence decide who bears litigation risk.

items.text: Termination for non payment or insolvency
items.why: Grounds of termination are exit clauses.

items.text: Selling off stock after termination
items.why: A consequence of termination, dealt with in the exit clauses.

items.text: Source code escrow
items.why: Data, software and source code escrow is listed with the exit and legal clauses.

sort.title: Which patent search is needed?
sort.prompt: Pick the search that answers each question.

items.text: A start up asks whether its new device can be patented before it files
items.why: Whether an invention can be patented is the novelty or patentability question.

items.text: An inventor checks prior art before spending on a filing
items.why: Prior art searches before filing support patentability assessment.

items.text: A manufacturer asks whether its product infringes live patents
items.why: Infringement of live patents by a product is the freedom to operate question.

items.text: A firm looks for expired patents it is free to use
items.why: Freedom to operate is about which patents are live; expired ones are free to use.

items.text: A defendant in an infringement suit looks for grounds to revoke the patent
items.why: Whether a patent can be revoked is the validity question.

items.text: A licensee doubts whether the licensed patent would survive a challenge
items.why: This is a validity question; bars on challenging validity are void under s. 140.

items.text: A strategist wants to know who is active in a technology field
items.why: Landscape searches show who is active in a field, often presented as patent maps.

items.text: Charting technologies, owners, trends and gaps in a field
items.why: Patent mapping turns landscape results into charts.

items.text: An acquirer checks the ownership, status and risk of the target's patents
items.why: Ownership, status and risk in a transaction is the due diligence search.

items.text: A lender verifies title and legal status of patents offered as security
items.why: A loan is a transaction; the lender must verify ownership and status before lending.

sort.title: Which valuation method fits?
sort.prompt: Choose the method that each situation describes.

items.text: Value a trade mark by the royalties its owner avoids paying
items.why: Relief from royalty values the after tax royalties saved by owning rather than licensing.

items.text: A technology whose royalty rates can be observed in comparable deals
items.why: Relief from royalty suits assets with observable royalty rates.

items.text: Value the main asset of a business after charging for working capital, machinery, workforce and brand
items.why: Deducting fair charges for all other assets and discounting the excess is the excess earnings method.

items.text: Excess earnings of 20.5, 18.45 and 15.375 discounted at 18 per cent
items.why: The notes' excess earnings example, giving 39.98.

items.text: A non compete agreement that keeps cash flows at 50, 55 and 60 instead of 42, 46 and 50
items.why: The difference between cash flows with and without the asset is the with and without method (20.34).

items.text: Compare the business's cash flows if the asset exists and if it does not
items.why: That is the definition of the with and without method.

items.text: Value a brand by the extra price customers pay for it
items.why: The premium profit method values the extra price a brand allows.

items.text: Value a patent by the cost saving it allows
items.why: Premium profit covers extra price or cost saving.

items.text: A drug candidate whose income depends on passing trials
items.why: Staged projects are valued by multiplying each cash flow by the probability of reaching it.

items.text: An NPV of 153.79 that falls to 4.15 once probabilities are applied
items.why: Example 3: the risk-adjusted NPV is 4.15.

items.text: A review of the whole IP portfolio
items.why: A general audit covers the whole portfolio.

items.text: An audit before a merger
items.why: Event based audits are done before a merger, investment, public issue, loan or product launch.

items.text: An audit before a public issue of shares
items.why: A public issue is one of the listed triggering events.

items.text: An audit before taking a loan secured on IP
items.why: A loan is a listed triggering event.

items.text: A review of the firm's trade secrets only
items.why: A focused audit examines one area such as trade secrets.

items.text: A review of software licences only
items.why: Software licences are the notes' other example of a focused audit.

items.text: Checking that a licensee has paid the right royalties
items.why: A royalty audit checks a licensee's payments.

items.text: Checking filings, renewals and Form 27
items.why: A compliance audit checks filings and legal duties.

mnemonics.title: Components of intellectual capital

items.text: Human capital: the knowledge and skill of employees, which the firm does not own and which leaves when people leave.
Structural capital: what remains in the firm, such as processes, databases, systems, culture and IP rights.
Relational capital: the value of relationships with customers, suppliers and partners, including brand and reputation.

mnemonics.note: In the Skandia scheme, customer capital sits inside structural capital.

mnemonics.title: The four levels of measuring
mnemonics.hook: I Can Quote Value = Identification, Classification, Quantification, Valuation

items.text: Identification: listing what the firm has, usually through an IP register.
Classification: grouping assets by type, technology, business or legal status.
Quantification: non money indicators such as the number of patents, citations, staff turnover or customer retention.
Valuation: a money value on an asset for a stated purpose and date.

mnemonics.note: Valuation is only the fourth level of measuring.

mnemonics.title: Ind AS 38, para 57: capitalising development cost
mnemonics.hook: Tired Interns Always Prefer Adequate Rest

items.text: Technical feasibility
Intention to complete
Ability to use or sell
Probable future benefits
Adequate resources
Reliable measurement of cost

mnemonics.note: Research cost is always an expense (para 54); only development can qualify.

mnemonics.title: The IP value hierarchy (Harrison and Sullivan)
mnemonics.hook: Don’t Count Pennies, Imagine Victory = Defensive, Cost control, Profit centre, Integrated, Visionary

items.text: Defensive: using IP defensively.
Cost control: controlling IP costs.
Profit centre: treating IP as a profit centre.
Integrated: integrating IP with business strategy.
Visionary: IP shapes the future of the firm and the industry.

mnemonics.title: Granstrand’s four stages of corporate IP management
mnemonics.hook: I Leave Selection to Strategy = Ignored, Legal department, Selective, Strategy

items.text: IP is ignored.
Inventors are rewarded and IP is left to the legal department.
Patenting becomes selective, licensing happens when needed and patent positions are reviewed.
IP becomes part of business strategy, engineers rotate through the IP department and licensing is based on business needs.

mnemonics.note: The role moves from legal administration to business strategy.

mnemonics.title: When secrecy beats patenting
mnemonics.hook: HIDE = Head start, Invisible, Detection hard, Easy to invent around

items.text: Head start: the firm has a large lead over rivals.
Invisible: the secret is hard to discover, for example a process that leaves no trace in the product.
Detection: infringement of a patent would be hard to detect.
Easy to invent around: a patent could easily be invented around.

mnemonics.note: Granstrand's four situations. Legal protection of secrets is weak, so firms must rely on their own measures.

items.text: Crown jewels (high business value, strong legal position): maintained, enforced and extended.
Weak core (high business value, weak legal position): strengthened through further filings, secrecy or better contracts.
Strong legal position, low business value: candidates for licensing or sale.
Weak on both: dropped by abandonment, sale or donation.

mnemonics.title: Factors in IP evaluation
mnemonics.hook: Let The Company See Risk = Legal, Technical, Commercial, Strategic, Risk

items.text: Legal factors: validity, scope, enforceability, remaining term, territory and ownership.
Technical factors: novelty, substitutes and ease of inventing around.
Commercial factors: market size, growth, margins and competition.
Strategic factors: fit with business plans and blocking power.
Risk.

mnemonics.title: Income approach methods
mnemonics.hook: DREW a Profit = DCF, Relief from royalty, Excess earnings, With and without, Premium profit

items.text: Discounted cash flow.
Relief from royalty: the royalties saved by owning the asset rather than licensing it.
Excess earnings: business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used.
With and without: the difference in business value with and without the asset.
Premium profit: extra price or cost saving due to the asset.

mnemonics.title: Barney's VRIN test
mnemonics.hook: VRIN = Valuable, Rare, Inimitable, Non substitutable

items.text: Valuable.
Rare.
Hard to imitate.
Not substitutable.

mnemonics.note: Knowledge gives competitive advantage when all four hold.

mnemonics.title: The SECI model of knowledge creation

items.text: Socialisation: tacit to tacit.
Externalisation: tacit to explicit.
Combination: explicit to explicit.
Internalisation: explicit to tacit.
Innovators (2.5 per cent)
Early adopters (13.5 per cent)
Early majority (34 per cent)
Late majority (34 per cent)
Laggards (16 per cent)

mnemonics.title: Four kinds of IP in a collaboration

items.text: Background IP: brought in by each party
Foreground IP: created in the project
Sideground IP: developed in house in parallel with the project
Postground IP: developed after the project ends

mnemonics.title: The four questions of IP due diligence
mnemonics.hook: O-V-F-W: Own it? Valid? Free? Worth?

items.text: Whether the target owns or validly controls the IP
Whether the IP is valid and enforceable
Whether the business is free to operate without infringing others' rights
What the IP is worth after taking risks into account

mnemonics.title: IP due diligence stages
mnemonics.hook: Plan, Question, Data room, Search, Interview, Analyse, Reflect, Register

items.text: Planning the scope and team
A questionnaire and document request
Review of documents in a data room
Independent searches of official registers and charge records
Interviews with managers and inventors
Analysis and a report on risks
Findings reflected in the deal: price adjustment, warranties, indemnities, conditions before completion, escrow
After completion, transfers registered

mnemonics.title: Before drafting a licence
mnemonics.hook: Begin with the aims, end with the exit (ten checks)

items.text: Be clear about business aims
Complete due diligence on title, validity and freedom to operate
Agree the value and royalty
Define the scope of the grant
Satisfy legal formalities
Respect competition law
Plan for tax and foreign exchange
Arrange regulatory approvals
Provide for quality control
Plan the exit

mnemonics.title: Licence clause families
mnemonics.hook: Good Financial Operations Invite Risky Exits

items.text: Grant clauses: rights, ownership, scope, exclusivity, territory, field, duration, sublicensing
Financial clauses: consideration, rate and base, minimums, milestones, reports and audit, taxes
Operational clauses: quality control, technical assistance, approvals, registration
IP clauses: improvements and new IP (no exclusive grant backs), confidential know how
Risk clauses: representations, warranties on title, indemnities, enforcement and defence
Exit and legal clauses: termination and its consequences, disputes, governing law, cross border issues, force majeure, assignment, escrow

mnemonics.note: Then check the interlocks: exclusivity with minimum royalty, field and territory with improvements, termination with sublicences and stock, warranties with indemnities.

items.text: Scope and team fixed
Identify all IP through registers, interviews and records
Verify ownership and assignments
Check status, deadlines and territorial coverage
Review licences and other contracts
Compliance: renewals, Form 27, CARO 2020 record keeping
Commercial use of the IP reviewed
Assess risks
Report findings
Fix the problems found
Monitor regularly

mnemonics.title: DEMPE functions

items.text: Development
Enhancement
Maintenance
Protection
Exploitation

mnemonics.note: Profit from IP should be allocated to the group company that performs these functions (transfer pricing, ss. 161 to 173).

formulas.title: Market to book ratio
formulas.meaning: The further above 1, the more of the firm’s value the accounts do not record. The gap partly reflects unrecorded intangibles but also growth expectations and market mood, so it is not an exact value of the IP.

formulas.title: Tobin’s q
formulas.intro: Your notes give this formula without a worked example: enter your own figures to see how it behaves.
formulas.meaning: A q above 1 suggests that the market sees valuable intangibles that replacement cost does not capture.

formulas.title: VAIC
formulas.meaning: VAIC = HCE + SCE + CEE. HCE is value added per unit of employee cost, SCE the share of value added left after employee cost, CEE value added per unit of capital employed. A higher total means more value added from people and capital.

example.note: The notes’ example: HCE 2.5 + SCE 0.6 + CEE 0.5.

formulas.title: Calculated Intangible Value
formulas.meaning: Profit above the industry’s normal return on tangible assets is treated as earned by intangibles; after tax, it is capitalised at the cost of capital.

formulas.title: Scorecard method

vars.name: A
vars.label: Average value of similar funded start-ups

formulas.meaning: A weighted score above 1 means the start-up scores better than the average on the weighted factors (team 30, opportunity 25, product 15, competition 10, sales channels 10, funding 5, others 5 per cent).

formulas.title: Venture capital method: post money value
formulas.meaning: The exit value discounted at the investor’s target return. Pre money value = post money value − investment.

example.note: The notes’ example: 200 ÷ 7.594 = ₹26.34 crore; pre money ₹16.34 crore after a ₹10 crore investment.

formulas.title: Venture capital method: investor’s share
formulas.meaning: The investment as a share of the post money value: the part of the company the investor must own to reach the target return at exit.

example.note: The notes’ example: 10 ÷ 26.34 = about 38 per cent.

formulas.title: Competitive Impact of a patent family
formulas.intro: The defaults are the index’s reference points from your notes: an average Technology Relevance is 1, and a granted United States patent has Market Coverage 1.
formulas.meaning: A family scores highly only when it is both technically relevant and protected in large markets; a zero on either scale makes the product zero.

formulas.title: Patent Asset Index of Portfolio A
formulas.meaning: The index is the sum of the families' Competitive Impact. One strong family (3.6) carries most of A's score.

example.note: The notes' Portfolio A: 4.83, stronger than Portfolio B's 2.0.

formulas.title: Patent Asset Index of Portfolio B
formulas.meaning: Ten weak families score only 2.0, less than Portfolio A's three families (4.83): size is not value.

formulas.title: Market value model
formulas.intro: Your notes give this formula without a worked example: enter your own figures to see how it behaves.

vars.name: gamma
vars.label: γ: market value of knowledge relative to tangible assets

formulas.meaning: Raise γ to see how much more the market pays for the same knowledge stock; estimated across many firms, γ shows how the market values knowledge relative to tangible assets.

vars.name: T

vars.name: sigma

vars.name: sigma

formulas.title: Black and Scholes: option value of a patent
formulas.intro: C = S × N(d1) − K × e^(−rT) × N(d2). Work out d1 and d2 with the d1 and d2 calculators, read N(d1) and N(d2) from a normal table, and enter them here.

vars.name: T
vars.label: T: years until the decision must be taken

formulas.meaning: Investing now is worth S − K (−20 in the example), yet the right to wait is worth about 28.11. K × e^(−rT) is the present value of K (97.27 in the example).

example.note: The notes: 65.04 − 36.93 = 28.11. With N values rounded to four places the calculator shows 28.12; the notes round the second term from unrounded values.

formulas.title: Binomial model: risk neutral probability
formulas.meaning: The probability of the up move that lets the expected payoff be discounted at the risk free rate.

formulas.title: Binomial model: option value
formulas.meaning: The option pays 30 in the up state (140 − 110) and nothing in the down state; weighting by the risk neutral probability and discounting gives its value.

vars.name: G
vars.label: Value next year if the market is good

vars.name: B
vars.label: Value next year if the market is bad

formulas.meaning: Committing now means launching even into a bad market, where the launch cost exceeds the value.

formulas.title: Decision tree: NPV with flexibility

vars.name: G
vars.label: Value next year if the market is good

vars.name: B
vars.label: Value next year if the market is bad

formulas.meaning: Waiting to see the market and launching only when it is good avoids the loss in the bad state.

formulas.title: Decision tree: value of flexibility

vars.name: G
vars.label: Value next year if the market is good

vars.name: B
vars.label: Value next year if the market is bad

formulas.meaning: The difference between the flexible and committed NPVs: the discounted, probability-weighted loss avoided by not launching into a bad market.

formulas.title: Depreciated patent stock in 2025
formulas.intro: Kt = (1 − δ) × Kt−1 + Pt, unrolled from 2019 (stock zero before then).
formulas.meaning: Each older year is multiplied once more by (1 − δ), so old patents count for less. Set δ to 0 to get the simple count of 106.

example.note: The notes: simple count 106, depreciated stock 74.20.

formulas.title: Revealed technological advantage

vars.name: F
vars.label: Firm's patents in the field, as a share of its total patents

formulas.meaning: A value of 1 means the firm patents in the field in the same proportion as the world; above 1 shows specialisation.

formulas.title: The residual method and a falling share price
formulas.meaning: Set the fall to 0 and the gap is ₹8,000 crore; a 20 per cent fall cuts it to ₹6,000 crore although nothing inside the firm has changed.

formulas.title: Enterprise value
formulas.intro: Your notes give this formula without a worked example: enter your own figures to see how it behaves.
formulas.meaning: Enterprise value is the value of the business to all providers of capital, so net debt is added to the shareholders' equity value.

formulas.title: Present value of a future amount
formulas.meaning: The further away the cash and the higher the rate, the smaller its value today.

example.note: Example 1, year 3: ₹25 crore at 12 per cent has a present value of 17.79.

formulas.title: NPV of commercialising a patent (Example 1)
formulas.meaning: Positive NPV: go ahead. Set the rate to 20.5 per cent and the NPV falls to about zero, which is the IRR.

formulas.intro: Your notes give this formula without a worked example: enter your own figures to see how it behaves.
formulas.meaning: Only for assets with no fixed end. A patent with a fixed term should not be given a terminal value.

formulas.title: Cost of equity (CAPM)
formulas.meaning: The return equity investors require; add an IP premium for invalidity and obsolescence when valuing IP.

formulas.title: WACC
formulas.meaning: A weighted average of the cost of equity and the after tax cost of debt; often the base discount rate.
