result.label: Present value of after tax royalties (₹ crore)

formulas.meaning: Compare with a lump sum after tax (₹6 crore × 0.75 = ₹4.5 crore). Try r = 12 (₹5.92 crore) and r = 16 (₹5.34 crore) to see the sensitivity.

example.note: After tax royalties 1.35, 1.50, 1.665, 1.8465 and 2.0462 discounted at 14 per cent: ₹5.62 crore.

formulas.title: Lump sum after tax (Example 2)
formulas.meaning: Compare with the running royalty value of ₹5.62 crore: the royalty is better unless the licensee's credit or the patent's validity is doubtful.

formulas.title: Risk-adjusted NPV of a drug candidate (Example 3)
formulas.meaning: Set all three probabilities to 100 to see the misleading unadjusted NPV of 153.79.

formulas.title: 25 per cent rule of thumb
formulas.meaning: A quick starting point only; it is widely criticised as arbitrary, so cross-check with comparables and income methods.

example.note: A 20 per cent margin suggests a royalty of about 5 per cent of sales.

formulas.title: Relief from royalty
formulas.meaning: The present value of the after tax royalties the owner avoids by owning, not licensing, the asset.

example.note: Royalties saved 3.00, 3.30, 3.63, 3.99 and 4.39 discounted at 16 per cent: 11.66.

formulas.title: Multi-period excess earnings

vars.name: c
vars.label: Charges for other assets (% of revenue)

formulas.meaning: What is left after every other asset has been paid a fair charge belongs to the main asset.

example.note: Excess earnings 20.5, 18.45 and 15.375 at 18 per cent: 39.98.

formulas.title: With and without method
formulas.meaning: The asset is worth the cash flow it protects or adds.

formulas.title: How much will a lender lend against IP?
formulas.meaning: IP alone rarely supports a large loan: the haircut and the loan to value ratio cut the value twice.

example.note: ₹3.63 crore → distressed value ₹1.81 crore → loan about ₹0.91 crore.

formulas.title: IP audit risk score
formulas.intro: Your notes give this formula without a worked example: enter your own figures to see how it behaves.
formulas.meaning: 15 to 25 is high, 8 to 14 is medium and 1 to 7 is low.

flows.title: Choosing the route to extract value
flows.intro: Run the notes’ tests in order. Whatever the answer, tax, competition law and foreign exchange rules still apply.

q1.q: Is the IP a core asset of the business?

q2.q: Does the firm own manufacturing and distribution?

options.label: No: it lacks capital or market access

r_noncore.detail: Core assets are kept; non-core assets are licensed or sold. Selling or donating non-core patents also saves renewal fees.

r_own.detail: A firm that owns manufacturing and distribution usually earns most by using its IP itself.

r_license.detail: A firm lacking capital or market access does better through licensing or partnership, and strong legal protection makes licensing safer.

r_weak.detail: Weak protection favours speed, secrecy and own use, because licensing is safer only when protection is strong. Teece warns that where protection is weak and imitators own the complementary assets, they may capture most of the profit.

q1.q: Is the appropriability regime strong (valid patents or well kept secrets)?

q3.q: Who owns the complementary assets (manufacturing, distribution, service, brand)?

r_strong.result: The innovator is well placed to profit
r_strong.detail: Strong legal protection allows the innovator to profit, and it makes licensing safer.

r_early.result: Competition has not yet moved to price and scale
r_early.detail: Only once a standard design emerges does competition move to price and scale. With weak protection, the notes advise speed, secrecy and own use.

r_imitators.result: Imitators may capture most of the profit
r_imitators.detail: Weak protection helps imitators; if they own the complementary assets, they may capture most of the profit.

r_innovator.result: The contest moves to price and scale, where the innovator holds the assets
r_innovator.detail: After the dominant design, competition moves to price and scale. The notes’ warning is about imitators owning the complementary assets; a firm that owns manufacturing and distribution usually earns most by using its IP itself.

q1.q: Has the patent been granted yet?

q2.q: Is it within one year from publication of the grant?

q3.q: Is the patent not worked in India, with the conditions of s. 84 met?

r_pre.detail: Pre-grant opposition is available only before grant. The commercial options remain open too.

r_post.result: Oppose after grant: s. 25(2), or seek revocation: s. 64
r_post.detail: Post-grant opposition lies within one year from publication of the grant; revocation under s. 64 is a separate route. The commercial options remain open too.

r_cl.result: Seek revocation (s. 64) or apply for a compulsory licence (s. 84)
r_cl.detail: A patent not worked in India may attract a compulsory licence after three years from grant. The commercial options remain open too.

r_commercial.result: Seek revocation (s. 64) or use the commercial options
r_commercial.detail: Invent around it, buy or license it, offer a cross licence, wait for expiry or leave the field. A cross licence needs patents the other side wants.

flows.title: Patent or trade secret?
flows.intro: Built from the notes: the s. 3 exclusions, the scope of each right and Granstrand's four situations.

q1.q: Is the invention excluded from patents in India, such as a new form of a known substance without enhanced efficacy (s. 3(d)) or a computer program as such (s. 3(k))?

q2.q: Could rivals learn the invention by examining the product (reverse engineering) or discover it independently?

q3.q: Would infringement of a patent be hard to detect?

q4.q: Could a patent easily be invented around?

q5.q: Does the firm have a large lead over rivals?

rExcluded.result: Rely on copyright, secrecy and contracts
rExcluded.detail: The patent route is closed. The exclusions push firms, such as software firms under s. 3(k), towards copyright, secrecy and contracts.

rPatentCopy.result: Patent it, filing before any disclosure
rPatentCopy.detail: A trade secret gives no protection against independent discovery or reverse engineering, while a patent gives a strong 20-year right even against independent inventors.

rSecret.result: Keep it as a trade secret
rSecret.detail: This is one of Granstrand's situations in which secrecy may be better. Legal protection of secrets is weak, so use confidentiality clauses, NDAs and access controls; s. 27 of the Contract Act makes most non competes void.

rSecretLead.detail: A large lead over rivals and a secret that is hard to discover are two of Granstrand's four situations. Back the secret with confidentiality clauses, NDAs and access controls.

rPatent.detail: None of Granstrand's situations for secrecy applies, so the strong 20-year right is worth the price of full disclosure. Consider multi protection around the same business.

flows.title: What should we do with this IP asset?

q1.q: Does the asset have high business value?

q2.q: Is its legal position strong in validity, claim scope and enforceability?

q3.q: Is its legal position strong in validity, claim scope and enforceability?

rCrown.result: Crown jewel: maintain, enforce and extend
rCrown.detail: High on both business value and legal strength. Keep renewing while the expected benefit exceeds the cost.

rWeak.detail: Valuable but legally weak: strengthen through further filings, secrecy or better contracts.

rLicense.detail: Strong legally but of low value to this business. If it is jointly owned, s. 50 requires the other owners' consent to license or assign.

rDrop.result: Drop it: abandon, sell or donate
rDrop.detail: Weak on both. Abandonment saves money but may free the technology for competitors, and a lapsed patent can be restored only within s. 60.

q1.q: What are you valuing, or for what purpose?

options.label: An early patent with no income
The core technology of a business

rEarly.detail: With no income yet there is little to discount; cost or an option model can still value the right. Use at least two methods.

rBrand.detail: Value the royalties saved by owning the brand or technology rather than licensing it.

rCore.detail: Take business profit minus a fair return on all other assets used.

rNonCompete.detail: Compare business value with and without the agreement.

rLicence.result: Comparable royalties combined with discounted cash flow
rLicence.detail: Comparables anchor the rate and DCF tests it against the expected income. Test sensitivity and state assumptions.

q1.q: Has the invention already been publicly disclosed?

q2.q: Is the inventor resident in India and planning to file abroad first?

q3.q: Has permission to file abroad first been obtained?

q4.q: Is protection wanted in many countries through one application?

rDisclosed.detail: Filing must come before any public disclosure; Indian law allows only limited exceptions, and disclosure before filing usually destroys novelty.

rPermission.detail: A resident inventor must obtain permission before filing abroad first.

rPct.detail: One international application, entering the Indian national phase at 31 months from priority. Seek rights where the firm sells, manufactures and meets competitors.

rParis.result: File abroad within the Paris priority period
rParis.detail: 12 months for patents and 6 months for designs and trade marks from the first filing. Choose countries where the firm sells, manufactures and meets competitors.

options.label: At the low end or in a new market
In the main market with a better product or service

q2.q: Is its product simpler, cheaper or more convenient, "good enough" though worse at first on conventional measures?

options.label: No, it is simply technically new

q3.q: Has it improved and moved into the main market, with mainstream customers adopting it?

r1.detail: Christensen and his co authors say Uber was not disruptive because it began in the main market with a better service.

r2.detail: Disruption should not be confused with novelty: a disruptive product is cheaper or easier, and usually worse at first.

r3.detail: Mainstream customers have adopted it. The disrupter relied on business model, speed and network effects rather than patents (s. 3(k)).

r4.detail: Incumbents should watch low end and new market entrants, create separate units, or invest in or acquire the newcomers.

flows.title: Is this IP acceptable as collateral?
flows.intro: Walk through the lender's checklist from the notes.

q1.q: Are the exact rights identified, and are ownership and the chain of title verified?

q2.q: Is the IP valid and in force, with renewals, licences and disputes under control?

q3.q: After a haircut and a limited loan to value ratio, does the distressed value cover the loan sought?

q4.q: Is the security created by a written deed and registered everywhere relevant: CERSAI, the patent register (ss. 68 and 69) and the Registrar of Companies (s. 77)?

q5.q: Do earlier charges have priority over this security?

q6.q: Is the borrower in insolvency resolution under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?

r1.detail: A lender must identify the exact rights and verify ownership and the chain of title before anything else.

r2.detail: Lenders worry about invalidity and obsolescence; renewals, licences and disputes must be monitored.

r3.result: Only a small loan is possible
r3.detail: E.g. ₹3.63 crore value → ₹1.81 crore after a 50 per cent haircut → about ₹0.91 crore loan. IP alone rarely supports a large loan.

r4.detail: Security over intangibles must be registered with CERSAI; a patent mortgage must be written and registered (ss. 68 and 69); company charges go to the ROC (s. 77).

r5.detail: The lender must check priority against earlier charges; its recovery comes after theirs.

r6.detail: SARFAESI treats IP as property (s. 2(1)(t)) and allows enforcement without court (s. 13). Define default, plan for insolvency and cover future IP and royalties.

r7.detail: The IBC moratorium stops enforcement during insolvency resolution.

flows.title: How is this IP payment taxed?

q1.q: Does the buyer get the right to copy or modify the software?

options.label: No, only a copy for its own use

q2.q: Is the recipient of the royalty a resident?

q3.q: Is it royalty on films or a fee for technical services?

q4.q: Is the royalty connected with a permanent establishment in India?

r0.detail: A copy for the buyer's own use without any transfer of copyright rights is generally not treated as royalty under tax treaties.

r1.detail: Under s. 393(1), where payments exceed ₹50,000 in a year. GST at 18 per cent also applies to licensing.

r2.detail: Under s. 393(1) for royalty on films and fees for technical services, where payments exceed ₹50,000 in a year.

r3.detail: Royalty connected with a permanent establishment in India is taxed as business income.

r4.result: 20 per cent of gross, or the treaty rate
r4.detail: Taxed at 20 per cent on the gross amount under s. 207, or at a lower treaty rate if more beneficial (s. 159); the payer deducts under s. 393(2).

q1.q: Is the taxpayer a resident patentee who is the true and first inventor?

q2.q: Was the patent developed and registered in India?

q3.q: Was at least 75 per cent of the expenditure on the invention incurred in India?

q4.q: Was the option exercised in Form 65 by the due date of the return?

q5.q: Did the patentee depart from the regime in any of the following five years?

r1.detail: All conditions of s. 194(1) must be met; otherwise the ordinary rules apply.

r2.detail: Royalty is taxed at 10 per cent of the gross amount without any deduction of expenses (s. 194(1)).

r3.detail: A patentee that departs from the regime in any of the following five years loses the benefit for the next five years.
